The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating. Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated. Warning: This article contains distressing details The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window. To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition. The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder. Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible. Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings. "I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented." Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind. "We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said. The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster". She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity." Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side". But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial. The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations. Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday. In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began. He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them". During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis. Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong. A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children. However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association. Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility. The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial. Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial. He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy. He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset." The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

item.title: North Korean anthem played for South Korea at Asian Games
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.30
- Published Organisers have apologised for playing the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men's hockey team at the Asian Games in Japan. South Korea, who thrashed Bangladesh 5-0, looked confused as the incorrect national anthem was played. South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported that Bangladesh's national anthem followed before South Korea's actual anthem was played. A stadium announcer did apologise for the mistake. "This is a really serious problem. When we protested, they said, 'We're sorry. It wasn't that it wasn't prepared; there was a mistake on the part of those responsible for playing it'," South Korea coach Min Tae-seok said. "But this is something that simply should never happen." North Korea's national anthem, along with other symbols of the secretive state, are banned in South Korea. The two countries are still technically at war, after the 1950-53 conflict between the two ended without a peace treaty. The build-up to the Asian Games, which officially starts on Saturday, has already seen complaints from teams about the quality and amount of accommodation. A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me." Some teams were also stranded at the airport for up to six hours when they landed this week. Field hockey at the Asian Games started on Friday and runs until 3 October.

item.title: Shark attack prompts rare kill order in Western Australia as victim named
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.97
- Published A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia after 63-year-old swimmer Greg O'Neill was killed at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found. Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues. It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year. The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia. In a statement, Greg O'Neill's family said they were "deeply shocked and devastated by the terrible tragedy." "Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy." On Saturday, his family visited the scene, where locals have been laying flowers. Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water. Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish". Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time. Joondalup authorities, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday. Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter. Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species. WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident". The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark". It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past. The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers. Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks. The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC. There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year. A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.

item.title: Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.91
- Published Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast. Saudi authorities said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired at Riyadh on Saturday, without confirming any further strikes or causalities. Earlier, a column of black smoke was seen rising from fuel tanks near the Saudi capital's international airport, where flights were disrupted temporarily on Saturday. Air raid alerts had sounded in the capital for the first time since the Iran-backed Houthis increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia in July. The US state department urged Americans in the Middle East to "exercise vigilance and be prepared for potential flight cancellations and other travel disruptions". "Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," it said in a statement. It added that Americans "should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region". Air defences also stopped "hostile attempts to target civilians" in the cities of Bish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu, an official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement. In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones" had been used to attack "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco state oil and gas company facilities in Yanbu on the coast. He added that the attacks were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts" to target the Yemeni capital Sanaa, which is currently controlled by the Houthis. Earlier, Sarea had accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week. The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen. According to an unconfirmed report from AFP news agency, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday. The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency. On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796, external. A number of apparent explosions were heard in Riyadh and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport earlier on Saturday, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations., external An AFP journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to Aramco. The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts. "I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this." The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe. The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen. Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

item.title: Is the Kennedy Center losing 'hundreds of millions of dollars'?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.43
Is the Kennedy Center losing 'hundreds of millions of dollars'? US President Donald Trump has claimed the Kennedy Center in Washington DC has been losing "tens of millions of dollars, even hundreds of millions of dollars" for years. Trump, who wants his name on the famous performing arts venue, was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site. Federal audit records for 2024 show that, despite having "an operating deficit", it had a surplus of millions of dollars - as Aisha Sembhi explains. Design by Mesut Ersöz and Henry Esterson. Additional reporting by Tom Edgington.

item.title: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the same
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.41
- Published Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch. The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner". But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland. So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit. Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps. "It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her. They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting. 'Mary, your video is going viral' From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own. She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen". Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says. When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up". A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media." She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home. Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker. That's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world. Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand. But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out. Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night. "My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby. So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her. 'Conversation just flowed' "I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing. "Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.' "It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you." He didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out. "It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer. What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves. When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going. "It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit." They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal. "We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited." The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival. "So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay." Timby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success. "I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland. "I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator." So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560. The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary. "You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan. "It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know." Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees. "I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."

item.title: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.40
August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House. It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance. In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa. Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued. Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will." Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does. A casualty of war The conflict in Ukraine is just one of the panoply of wars in recent years that have revealed once again the disastrous impact of conflict on cultural heritage. Tareq Abu Dayyeh sells craftwork, souvenirs and antiquities in Gaza. The Great Omari Mosque features on many of the items he sells. It represents the very identity of Gaza - charting its history through the building's many manifestations from ancient pagan temple to Byzantine church to Seventh Century mosque to Crusader Cathedral and then back to being a mosque. The Great Omari Mosque was all but destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023. The Israeli military said the strike was targeting Hamas. Now Dayyeh says his heart is broken every time he sees the ruins. "When your past is destroyed, you have no present." The war in Gaza has claimed tens of thousands of lives and an estimated 200,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli bombardment. But despite the overwhelming death and devastation, such cultural losses run deep. This is a sentiment expressed throughout history by people living through war. In Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, the alarm has been raised time and time again. More than 100 sites in Iran are reported to have been damaged during the aerial war launched by the US and Israel back in February. They include the Unesco-listed Golestan Palace in the capital, Tehran, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan. The civil war in Sudan has further imperilled one of the ancient wonders of the world - the Meroe Pyramids, built during the flourishing civilisation of the Kingdom of Kush. Unesco, which designated Meroe as a World Heritage Site in 2011, has warned that the fighting has halted all preservation work there, leaving the fragile ancient structures prey to erosion from the encroaching sand and vegetation. A difficult task In response to the massive destruction of World War Two, the first-ever international treaty exclusively dedicated to protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict was adopted in The Hague in 1954. It applies to monuments and architecture, but also works of art and books, requiring states to safeguard and respect cultural property and refrain from any actions that might endanger it. Since the Hague Convention, there have been several additional moves to strengthen protective measures for cultural heritage. A Second Protocol to the Convention in 1999 said that any site that has been placed under enhanced protection due to its immense cultural significance must not be made a military target even if it is being used in such a way as to have become a 'military objective' - unless there is no other feasible way of ending its use in that way. When the International Criminal Court was established in The Hague in 2002, part of its remit was to bring accountability for deliberate attacks in war against buildings of religious, artistic and educational value as well as historical monuments, which had been defined as war crimes. But this has been a complex and difficult task. So far, only one case has been successfully brought at the ICC. Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was a jihadist militant leader in Mali who was found guilty of directing attacks that destroyed mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu. He was sentenced to nine years in prison. Rouhani says that without the full backing of the major powers and a genuine commitment to international law and its enforcement, the world will simply keep watching the same devastating pattern repeat itself. "For most governments, heritage is a secondary concern, unless it becomes useful for propaganda," Rouhani says. "The Hague Convention requires states to build protection into their military rules and to respect cultural property abroad as well as at home. Looking at the scale of damage in recent conflicts, it is difficult to conclude that these obligations are taken seriously." In conflicts from Ukraine to Iran to Gaza, where schools and hospitals are seen as permissible military targets by combatants, how likely is it that a museum or pile of ancient stones, however freighted with beauty and history and memory, will be spared? Heritage ambulances In an isolated position in open countryside, a museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed by Russian shelling during an overnight attack in 2022. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said it had left him speechless: "Targeted strikes against museums - not even terrorists would think of this. But this is the kind of army we are fighting against." The building was set ablaze and a caretaker was injured, but much of the collection had already been removed. Joe Biden, then the US president, said that Russian President Vladimir Putin was not only trying to take over Ukraine, but "literally trying to wipe out the culture and identity of the Ukrainian people". That pattern has been repeated across much of the frontline in Ukraine where local organisations have worked with international groups to try to safeguard their national heritage from Russian attack. One international group that's played a big role is the Aliph Foundation, which was set up in Geneva in 2017 to protect and repair cultural heritage. Alexandra Fiebig, a project manager with Aliph, says that her group provided millions of dollars in funds to Ukrainian museums scrambling to move their most valuable items to safety. This has involved the use of what she describes as 'heritage ambulances': "These vehicles that have specialised equipment and space with specialised teams and equipment, they were in the beginning travelling a lot to affected museums that were damaged through military action." Now, she says the teams also check on the artefacts that were transported in great haste to safer places to make sure they remain in good condition. Blue Shield International is a group that operates in multiple war zones, working with armed forces and local heritage officials to such an extent that it's come to be known as the Red Cross for culture. Dr Emma Cunliffe, the head of operations for the group, says Ukrainians are risking their lives to protect their heritage. "They are taking great measures to document the damage even when they are risking their own lives to do it. In fact one of the things we really see is that the government is taking huge steps despite the many many competing priorities and the struggles they are facing." Other conflicts have seen civilians take similar measures to protect their culture. In February 2015, Isis turned its attention from hacking down ancient statues and artefacts in Mosul in northern Iraq to ransacking its written heritage as its fighters laid waste to the city's much treasured public libraries. They burned the Central Library and destroyed or stole many thousands of books - many of them rare manuscripts that told the story of the city. "These were not simply books or shelves, they represented decades of knowledge and research and formed an important part of the intellectual heritage of Mosul University and the wider community… Within days, everything was gone," Dr Mohammed Jasim Mohammed al-Hamdani says. The main library in Mosul has played a key role in his life - to such an extent that he is now the director there. "Seeing it destroyed felt like losing a part of myself. Many people in the city had a story connected to the University of Mosul and therefore the loss felt very close to home. And this is why when that part of Mosul was liberated from Isis, young people, old people rushed to the library to save what they could." A lucrative trade The obverse of communities taking it into their own hands to protect cultural property is the looting of those same sites. Again, this is a byproduct of war that dates back to the dawn of history. Cunliffe says that understanding the reasons for looting - which can vary from place to place - is a necessary starting point: "That might then in turn result in greater sanctions, greater prosecutions to take it seriously as a threat." She says that it's important if possible to convey a sense to local communities that by assisting this, they are selling their own heritage. In Iraq and Syria for example, both during and after the Isis rampage, looting of priceless artefacts was carried out on an industrial scale. The precious objects were spirited out and trafficked abroad, including to the US. A years-long investigation by the US Justice Department traced and tracked the smuggling routes and resulted in thousands of looted artefacts being returned to Iraq. In Europe and elsewhere, co-ordinated, multi-national police and customs operations take place regularly, seizing large numbers of stolen antiquities and arresting some of the traffickers. But the trade remains highly lucrative and the plethora of conflicts provides ever more opportunities. In Sudan, the national museum in Khartoum was stripped of its treasures in 2023 when it came under the control of one of the warring factions, the RSF, which loaded them onto trucks and left the display rooms bare. As in other conflict zones like Ukraine, specialised training has been provided for those involved in trying to recover the antiquities, which has had some success. But much of the museum's display - which told the story of the region over thousands of years - may have disappeared for good. Slim chance of deterrence The challenges of trying to limit the scale of destruction and looting of cultural heritage are huge. At an international or state level, there are regulations in place, but putting them into practice in a timely fashion is difficult enough - and often there isn't even the will to attempt this. Local initiatives backed by organisations like Aliph and Blue Shield International can make a difference on a small scale. But if - as seems the case right now - the chances of anyone facing consequences for destroying a heritage site are close to zero, then there is all but no real deterrent. "What would change the calculation is not harsher sentences," says Dr Bijan Rouhani, "but a real prospect of being named - arrest warrants for the commanders who authorise these strikes, prosecutions in national courts under universal jurisdiction, and targeted sanctions on named individuals. Those measures don't require a new treaty. They require states to be willing to use the instruments they already have, against allies as well as adversaries." Of all the recent attempts to erase the cultural past embodied in stone, Palmyra in Syria still stands out. Isis blew up temples there and might have done far worse if it had not been defeated. One man became emblematic for standing up to them. For 40 years, the archaeologist Khaled al-Asaad had been the principal custodian of Palmyra. He was in his eighties when Isis descended on the ancient city. They captured him and tortured him to try to find out where its most valuable artefacts had been hidden. When he refused to tell them, they beheaded him in a public square and hung his corpse from a traffic light. Al-Asaad was celebrated across the world as a heroic defender of culture against the forces of darkness. He was awarded the Order of Civil Merit in Syria and in Palmyra, a school was named in his honour. But nothing is free from political complications. Years later, under the new authorities in Syria, his name has now been removed from the school. More from InDepth BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day. Emma Barnett and John Simpson bring their pick of the most thought-provoking deep reads and analysis, every Saturday. Sign up for the newsletter here

item.title: Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.23
- Published Residents in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh have been given the all-clear after air raid alerts were issued and explosions were reported in the capital. It was the first time alerts have been issued in Riyadh since the Houthis increased their attacks and declared a "maritime embargo" on the Saudis in July. The Saudi Civil Defence sent alerts for the capital and several other regions late on Friday night and Saturday morning (local time) as the Kingdom's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate. Journalists from Reuters and AFP reported hearing explosions in the capital, but authorities have since said the danger has passed. Residents were urged to avoid gathering in crowds. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe. The Iran-backed group's military spokesman said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen. Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the Houthis attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted. The attacks on Saudi oil assets have directly impacted global energy markets and the price of petrol and diesel in many countries has sharply risen in recent weeks, compounding already elevated costs caused by the blockades of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally asked US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said. A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability." Earlier this week, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week. The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN. Additional reporting by Tabby Wilson.

item.title: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.20
- Published Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists". He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments. O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders. Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC. O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe". He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate. "British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added. Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime". In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair". "I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors. "I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors." O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again". "I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future." Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments. She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said". She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise. "I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote. In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape." He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training". It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business. In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges. He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories". In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

item.title: Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.12
Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished The BBC's Caitríona Perry spoke to Kerry Kennedy, the niece of late president John F Kennedy, about demolition threats to the performance centre named after him. A US federal judge ruled the Trump administration must give 30 days' notice before any "demolition" occurs to the Kennedy Center, as President Donald Trump warned the Washington DC performing arts venue could be "ripped down". The order comes after Trump was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site. Protesters also gathered at the venue on Friday to demonstrate against demolition threats.

item.title: Ukraine's defense companies say soldiers want drones that do more on their own so one operator can control more at once
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 6.20
Ukraine's soldiers want drones and robots that can handle more of the flying and driving themselves, letting one operator oversee multiple systems instead of manually controlling each one. Ukraine's rapidly expanding arsenal of aerial drones and ground robots has become central to its fight against Russia's larger military. Defense technology companies say they're increasingly automating certain tasks while keeping humans responsible for decisions about using force. In practice, that means shifting more routine work from the operator to the drone. Newer systems can increasingly navigate, return to base, and help identify targets independently, allowing operators to focus on other tasks, from target confirmation to swarm control. Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer at Ukrainian defense technology company Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that his company's innovation has come from soldier' requests. "Our soldiers are coming to us with a request of: 'How can you provide us with the capability to have different robots controlled by one person?' or 'Can we make a shift of our UAV pilots easier?'" The company responded to these requests by developing software that lets drones handle more of the flight themselves, including traveling to and from an area of interest with minimal input. "In the new version of a drone that we produce right now and supply, there is an autonomy layer installed in the drone itself," Rozhkov explained. "So it can go autonomously to the area of interest, then come back with basically one button." A "pilot can bring the system home with a push of a button," and the drone can figure out the shortest way back, he said. Autonomy is also being built into the company's product updates. The latest version of its Linza drone — the 3.0 released this year — has more onboard autonomy, so it can operate when GPS is unavailable because of Russian electronic warfare. It puts less "mental demand on a soldier so they can do more stuff." It took eight months to develop, but it offers "a huge upper hand," Rozhkov said. Frontline's Zoom reconnaissance drone also has AI navigation, so it can work when it loses satellite navigational signals. These changes, likewise, were driven by soldier feedback, the executive said. Unlike many Western defense firms, Ukrainian companies often work directly with soldiers, even talking to them from the front lines over FaceTime and listening to their insights. The broader shift toward artificial intelligence and autonomy is also a priority for Ukraine's government. Ukraine's defense ministry said in August that units were using "more than 70 different systems powered by AI and computer vision technologies to strike enemy targets." And it said that the aim is to eventually have 100% of drones on the front line equipped with computer vision and AI capabilities. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, battlefield technology has moved from one pilot fully manually controlling one drone, to AI helping pilots find targets and providing autopilot capabilities, to now enabling one operator to oversee multiple drones while AI assists with basic tasks, like flying and driving, and helps take over when Russian electronic warfare cuts the connection. Former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov predicted last month that "we will reach a stage where autonomous drones will fight autonomous drones." A host of Ukrainian companies are pursuing that vision, and some are working toward larger swarms of autonomous weapons that can communicate with one another. Achi, the CEO of Ukrainian defense firm Ark Robotics, told Business Insider that the evolution toward a single pilot controlling many drones is "kind of a prerequisite to be successful in the total drone warfare that is coming to all of us." The defense technology company is developing a system that allows thousands of aerial drones and ground robots, including those not made by Ark Robotics, to work together with minimal human intervention, and enables an operator to be thousands of kilometers away. Achi said that to have the advantage on the battlefield, "you need these asymmetrical systems that allow you to work with multiple drones at the same time." Ukraine's combat systems need to be able to work amid Russia's heavy electronic warfare. Ukraine's Twist Robotics makes hardware and software that allow drones to navigate and track designated targets when Russia disrupts GPS. It does that "by default" because the problem is so common, co-founder Rostyslav Olenchyn told Business Insider. Most of the company's products have AI assistance, allowing the drone to "accomplish the mission" even if an operator makes a mistake or loses control. How much autonomy is in use remains somewhat limited by both technical and ethical constraints. Many companies and experts describe what is often portrayed as autonomy as exaggerated in practice, resembling advanced automation rather than independently acting AI. Ukraine says it has not removed human oversight. Its defense ministry said last month that "algorithms are now being entrusted with critical combat tasks, ranging from navigation and object identification to autonomous target engagement. However, the final decision on target selection and engagement is made by a human operator." It said it will keep humans in the loop on principle, and while technology helps to identify a target, "the final decision to engage remains with a human, while the system's level of autonomy is limited based on the potential cost of an error." Ukraine is rapidly advancing to match Russia's volume and allow its human soldiers to stay farther from the fight. Rozhkov described the general trend as "trying to get people outside of the danger zone."

item.title: Inside airlines' panic as FAA pushed new AI tool
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.11
Airline industry officials have finally stopped panicking about the Federal Aviation Administration's soon-to-launch artificial intelligence tool for managing flights and easing congestion in air travel, multiple people familiar with the situation told POLITICO. Weeks of industry confusion over the FAA's vague description of its much-hyped plans eased in the past week when agency officials told them they would use the tool in just a limited way at first, said the people, who were granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations. The tool, dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Trajectories, or SMART, is set to debut in coming days, offering advice to air traffic controllers managing flights for the three airports that serve the nation's capital, according to two industry officials. The hope, according to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, is that after a 90-day testing period the tool will be rolled out on a wider scale. Before the FAA eased the airlines officials' concerns, one of their biggest worries was how extensively the AI would be integrated into day-to-day air traffic management, one of the industry people said. "I think that's what people were freaking out about," the person said. Instead, according to another industry official, the SMART tool is not expected to create any new procedures for air traffic controllers or for the airlines. It will simply generate alternative route information that is passed through the FAA's existing systems and procedures. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has touted the tool, aimed at easing congestion in the skies. But three airline officials said the industry was bewildered for weeks about how the system would work, and that a sustained series of meetings with the FAA had left them with more questions than answers. "We've been requesting and … talking to [FAA] and saying, 'Let's narrow the scope of this. Start, crawl, walk, run.' And I think ultimately that's what they decided to do," said one airline industry official, who like the others, was granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations with the agency. In a statement, FAA spokesperson Hannah Walden said the agency is "moving at record speed to modernize America's National Airspace System, and SMART will fundamentally change the way we manage our skies." "Instead of waiting for congestion or weather to cause delays, SMART helps us see problems coming and act before they do," she said. Walden added that airlines have been "at the table" since the very beginning and FAA is "welcoming their feedback as we deploy SMART, which is why we're taking a slow, methodical approach to the rollout." With Duffy and Bedford leading the charge, the FAA has fully embraced artificial intelligence to help tackle some of its persistent problems following a series of high-profile aviation disasters, highlighted by the deadly midair collision over Washington in January 2025 and a fatal March runway crash at LaGuardia Airport in New York. It's part of a wider overhaul aimed at bolstering the nation's rickety air traffic control system. During the discussions, some airline officials fretted that the AI tool could inject chaos by prompting increases in flight cancellations and reschedulings in the name of preventing aviation bottlenecks and avoiding weather-related delays. That could become a costly headache for both airlines and passengers, though nobody involved alleged that the system would compromise safety. As confusion continued to reign across the airline industry, the FAA convened several meetings last week, including one on Sept. 10 between the major airline CEOs and Bedford. It helped ease many of the airlines' concerns, two of the airline officials said. According to a fourth airline official, granted anonymity to discuss the executives' meeting, Bedford presented the FAA's vision and strategy, and the CEOs' reception to the plan was "exceptionally favorable and supportive of the effort." The CEOs of United Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and Southwest Airlines were among those who attended the meeting, several airline and one government officials said. Duffy hinted this week at the modest ambitions for the tool, which is part of a larger 12-year, $875 million contract effort to modernize air traffic control. "We have to do a slow roll into the airspace," he said at a Tuesday talk at the National Artificial Intelligence Association in Washington. And in a recent interview with POLITICO, Bedford said the rollout's roughly 90-day first phase will focus mainly on testing the system and building airlines' confidence in its predictions. How SMART? Bedford said Tuesday that the FAA will work with airlines to examine specific flights, compare flight paths and assess how accurately SMART's predictive analytics perform. SMART will focus, in part, on forecasting where weather systems are headed rather than simply assessing where they are in real time, Bedford said. "That is a big difference between whether we keep airspace closed too long," he said. "So how can we make more space available safely, based on better data and better decision-making tools." He said the 90-day testing window will give the agency time to determine whether the system performs as expected and whether airlines can trust its recommendations. While the industry has generally acknowledged the potential of predictive analytics to help manage disruptions, airline industry officials who spoke to POLITICO in recent weeks have also cast doubt on the notion that the technology is ready to immediately transform flight operations. That raises questions about how much the system can actually accomplish at launch and how it will fit into existing airline and FAA processes. The technology is being developed by Air Space Intelligence, a Boston-based software company that won the contract in June. The company did not respond to a request for comment Thursday, but previously referred questions back to DOT and FAA. To their understanding, the official who described FAA's effort to now "narrow the scope" said that the new tool won't create any new procedures for air traffic controllers. SMART will identify alternative routes, such as in cases of bad weather, and send those recommendations from the "SMART center" — headquartered at the Transportation Department — to an established command center through the FAA's existing processes. From there, the information will reach controllers though systems they already use to receive routing information. The key difference is that SMART will generate additional routing options. That could be particularly useful when traffic is backed up at airports, giving the FAA more options to move aircraft out of those bottlenecks and reduce disruptions for passengers, the official said. That the system will not be integrated in day-to-day air traffic management is "a big relief," added another airline industry official, who said airlines were approaching SMART with some trepidation over how the system would integrate with their own scheduling and operations systems. Down to the wire In the weeks leading up to the rollout, however, these airline officials familiar with the project weren't completely convinced the FAA had all the details figured out. The industry officials said at the time they were asking questions such as whether the air traffic controllers themselves would use the AI, whether the software's developer would be in charge of feeding routing information to both airlines and controllers, and whether airlines needed to train their employees to understand the technology. They also weren't clear if the airlines could opt out of using the AI system. Even now, the three airline industry officials said the FAA has yet to answer some of those questions in granular detail, despite the airlines holding almost weekly group meetings with the agency to discuss implementation over the course of three months. Bedford's in-person meeting with airline CEOs on Sept. 10 helped quell some of the industry's concerns about the rollout and offered additional clarity on how the FAA envisions the technology working. 'When done thoughtfully…' Top airline officials have publicly expressed measured optimism about the initiative. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement on Sept. 9 that SMART could significantly reduce delays and cancellations during bad weather. "If it works as we think it can, it will do more to reduce delays and cancellations than anything that's happened in decades," he said. Similarly, American Airlines CEO Robert Isom said in a statement that he applauded Duffy and Bedford "for their efforts to leverage technology to make the airspace more efficient and safer." He said the airline is working closely with the FAA on SMART, "which when done thoughtfully and methodically will offer enhanced benefit to the traveling public." Airlines for America, the trade group for the many of the major carriers in the airline industry, similarly touted SMART as a potentially transformative tool, saying its ability to strengthen safety, increase capacity and improve efficiency could reduce delays and cancellations nationwide. "We're just in the initial stages, but it's one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades," a statement from the group said. In a statement, Delta Air Lines also said it "fully supports" the FAA's modernization effort, including the SMART program, and said it appreciated the FAA's "collaborative approach," adding that the airline is "actively engaged in the development process." This story originally appeared on POLITICO and is courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms.

item.title: Disney has a new tech chief — read the memo from CEO Josh D'Amaro
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.84
Disney has hired its first-ever companywide tech chief as its leadership shuffle under CEO Josh D'Amaro continues. Karandeep Anand is joining Disney as chief technology officer and a senior EVP, D'Amaro told employees on Friday. "Karandeep brings a rare mix of experience across infrastructure, consumer technology, and AI," D'Amaro said in a memo, which was obtained by Business Insider. The hire comes a day after Disney promoted Adam Smith to the head of its streaming business and moved Joe Earley, who'd shared the direct-to-consumer co-president title with Smith, to the president of franchise and content strategy for Disney's Entertainment TV arm. As tech chief, Anand will oversee the enterprise tech, infrastructure, data and AI platforms, product, and engineering teams, D'Amaro said. This aligns with the "One Disney" initiative designed to unify the company, which D'Amaro has made a priority. Friday marks D'Amaro's six-month anniversary at the helm of the Mouse House. Anand has been the CEO of Character.AI, an AI startup to which Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter last September. Disney had told Character.AI not to use its copyrighted characters in AI-generated videos without permission; Character.AI complied with the request. Before joining Character.AI, Anand spent six and a half years at Facebook, following more than 15 years at Microsoft. He will report to D'Amaro. Anand "is an expert builder and strategist, technical and product-minded, with sharp instincts for what people actually want," D'Amaro told Disney staffers. Read D'Amaro's full memo to Disney employees here: When I stepped into this role, I laid out three priorities: great storytelling as our North Star, technology in service of creativity, and operating as One Disney. Today, we have some exciting news about how we are putting that strategy into motion. I'm thrilled to share that Karandeep Anand will be joining Disney as our first Senior EVP and Chief Technology Officer, reporting directly to me, beginning October 2. Karandeep brings a rare mix of experience across infrastructure, consumer technology, and AI. He led Character.AI as CEO, taking the company through a period of explosive growth and building one of the most engaged consumer-AI audiences in the world, grounded in a deep understanding of what keeps people coming back. He also made user trust and safety a priority as the platform scaled, a discipline he brings with him to Disney. Before that, he held senior leadership roles at Meta and Microsoft and was part of the team that created Azure. He is an expert builder and strategist, technical and product-minded, with sharp instincts for what people actually want. In this role, he will oversee enterprise technology, infrastructure, data and AI platforms, product, and engineering, working across our segment technology teams to further modernize how we build and deliver technology company-wide. In getting to know Karandeep, one thing keeps coming through: real enthusiasm and respect for Disney and a clear sense of where technology and creativity meet. What struck me most is his belief that technology creates the most value when it helps people do their best work. This is the next chapter we're writing together as One Disney, and I'm genuinely optimistic about what it means for our teams, our fans, and the stories ahead. Please join me in welcoming Karandeep to the team. Josh

item.title: These 5 states are home to America's richest billionaires
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.76
Some of the richest people on Earth live in the United States. In fact, the US has the largest share of the world's billionaires, home to nearly one-third of them. But the bar for reaching the upper echelons of American wealth is higher than ever. On Tuesday, Forbes released its annual list of America's 400 richest billionaires, and a record $4.4 billion net worth was required to make the cut. Still, 34 people made the list for the first time this year. To see where America's wealthiest 1% are concentrated, Business Insider compiled a list of states where most of the Forbes 400 billionaires live, and found 249 live across just five states. About a third of them reside in California, a state home to the booming tech and AI industries. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, for example, has a sprawling $37 million compound in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. Florida, the third-most-popular state for the Forbes 400, has its own collection of extravagant estates. Jeff Bezos owns a nearly $250 million compound on Miami's Indian Creek Island, nicknamed "Billionaire Bunker." President Donald Trump, meanwhile, famously has his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach. In total, Forbes 400 members live across 38 states and the District of Columbia, with some states home to just one. Oregon's lone member, Nike founder Phil Knight, lives in a rural, tree-covered area outside Hillsboro, near the company's world headquarters. Nebraska's sole billionaire, Warren Buffett, still lives in the Omaha home he bought in 1958. Here are the five states with the biggest concentrations of Forbes 400 billionaires. 5. Illinois Eighteen billionaires live in Illinois. Lukas Walton, the grandson of Walmart founder Sam Walton, is the state's richest person, with a net worth of $44.4 billion. The Forbes data shows the Walton family has a combined net worth of $475.6 billion. The drop-off in net worth is steep following Walton: Charlie Mills, chair and former CEO of Medline Industries, a medical-surgical products provider, is the state's second-wealthiest person, with a net worth of $11 billion. The state is also home to Eric Lefkofsky, Groupon's cofounder, who has a net worth of $6.5 billion, and Ty Warner, the creator of Beanie Babies, the plush toy company, who has a net worth of $8.2 billion. The most common industries among Illinois' wealthy include investments, private equity, and the medical device and technology sector. 4. Texas Forty-three billionaires live in the Lone Star state. Many of the state's wealthiest have derived their fortunes from oil, gas, and pipelines, with 15 billionaires having made their net worths through one of the three industries. It's also a rapidly expanding state for tech, data center, and energy industries. Elon Musk — the world's richest person with a net worth of $908 billion — usually resides in a $50,000 tiny home near his SpaceX headquarters in Starbase, Texas, but he recently said he is living in an Airstream trailer outside Memphis while overseeing a data center build. Michael Dell, the founder of Dell Technologies, with a net worth of $263 billion, and Mark Cuban, the entrepreneur and "Shark Tank" investor with a $6.8 billion net worth, also live in Texas. 3. Florida Forty-nine billionaires live in Florida, a state known for its low taxes on the wealthy. Jeff Bezos, founder of Amazon, leads the way: the world's second richest man and the richest in Florida has a net worth of $378 billion. Larry Ellison, founder of the technology company Oracle, trails Bezos with a net worth of $204 billion. The Sunshine State is also home to Michael Jordan, the former NBA basketball player and minority owner of the Charlotte Hornets, with a $4.7 billion net worth. Trump is the 26th-richest Floridian, with his primary residence, Mar-a-Lago, and a net worth of $7 billion. Some of the most common industries among Florida's wealthy include hedge funds, real estate, and investment banking. 2. New York Fifty-four billionaires live in New York state. The richest person in the state, former New York City mayor and founder of Bloomberg L.P., the financial data, software, and media company, Michael Bloomberg, has a $94.9 billion net worth. Rupert Murdoch, who built a media empire including Fox News, the Times of London, and The Wall Street Journal, is the sixth-wealthiest person there, with a net worth of $25 billion. Fashion designer Ralph Lauren, with a net worth of $14.8 billion, and Academy-Award winning director Steven Spielberg, who has a $7.9 billion net worth, also live in New York. New York's wealthy found their fortunes across various industries, including investment banking, private equity, and hedge funds. 1. California Eighty-five billionaires live in the Golden State. Many of them are tech giants, from the likes of Google's original founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, to semiconductor company founders Jensen Huang and Henry Samueli. Page is California's wealthiest person, with a net worth of $278 billion. Combined, Google's two cofounders and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt have a net worth of $571.8 billion. California is also home to several social media and app founders, including Zuckerberg, who has a net worth of $212 billion; WhatsApp's Jan Koum, who has a net worth of $18.5 billion; and Airbnb's Brian Chesky and Nathan Blecharczyk, who combined have a net worth of $24.5 billion. George Lucas, the mastermind behind Star Wars, also lives in California. Lucas has a net worth of $5.3 billion.

item.title: Oracle document spells out what laid-off workers get in severance, stock, and bonuses
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.18
Oracle employees caught in the company's latest round of layoffs now know exactly what they'll leave behind and what they'll take with them. An internal FAQ document viewed by Business Insider lays out more details for staff impacted, including severance capped at 26 weeks, canceled stock awards, lost bonuses, and deadlines for exercising vested options. Oracle started notifying affected staff on Monday. Business Insider reported last month that the company had drawn up plans for double-digit percentage layoffs on some teams to reduce payroll as it racks up billions in debt to fund AI infrastructure. Employees were offered four weeks' base salary plus one week per year of employment, according to documents viewed by Business Insider. The full FAQ document includes the maximum severance payout and what happens to employee bonuses, commissions, and stock options. The details offer a window into the employee impact of Oracle's latest cost-cutting push. The company has shed tens of thousands of workers while borrowing heavily and spending tens of billions of dollars to build data centers and other infrastructure needed to support its AI ambitions. For employees leaving in the latest cuts, the financial impact extends beyond losing a paycheck: unvested stock disappears, future corporate bonuses are forfeited, and participation in employee stock programs ends. Oracle executives didn't directly address the layoffs in an employee town hall this week, but Chief Financial Officer Hilary Maxson told staff the company needs to be "thoughtful" about where it spends tims and money. "I don't mean doing more with less, which is a phrase that I really, really don't like," Maxson said. "It means simplifying processes that don't help customers and making clear choices on where we're going to use our resources where they have the greatest impact." This latest round of layoffs follows cuts earlier this year. The company's workforce declined by 21,000, or 13%, in the 2026 fiscal year that ended May 31, according to a recent filing. Oracle's severance package is comparatively less generous than those offered by other Big Tech companies over the past year. Salesforce's standard policy offers up to 30 weeks of severance pay, with a minimum of 9 or 13 weeks based on role, plus an additional 3 weeks of service per year. Microsoft offered employees in its latest round of layoffs this summer up to 39 weeks' base pay, with a minimum of 60 days and one or two additional weeks per six months of service, depending on seniority. Severance - Employees receive four weeks of base pay for their first year of service, plus one additional week of base pay for each additional year worked. Six months or more in the last year of employment will count as a full year. - Total severance is capped at 26 weeks of base salary, paid out about three weeks after employees sign a severance agreement and return company property. - Employees rehired within six months may have to repay a portion of their severance. Employee Stock Purchase Plan - Participation ends on the employee's termination date. - Contributions made during the current offering period are generally refunded without interest in the employee's final paycheck. - Employees who leave during specific purchase windows (Sept. 16—30 or March 16—31) will have their contributions used to purchase stock instead of receiving a refund. Stock options - All unvested stock options are canceled when employment ends. - Employees generally have up to three months after termination to exercise vested options, subject to the original expiration date. - Some options granted through acquired companies may have a shorter, one-month exercise window. Restricted Stock Units - All unvested RSUs are canceled upon termination. - Previously vested RSUs remain the employee's property and stay in their Fidelity brokerage account. Vacation and sick pay - Accrued vacation is prorated through the employee's termination date and paid out according to company policy. - Unused paid sick leave is not paid out at separation unless required by applicable law. Bonuses - Employees on sales or consulting bonus plans may receive any bonus earned under the terms of their compensation plan. - Employees on corporate bonus plans are not eligible for future corporate bonus payouts after termination. Commissions - Employees stop earning commissions on their last day of employment. - Commissions already earned but not yet paid remain payable under the terms of the applicable compensation plan. Have a tip? Contact this reporter via email at astewart@businessinsider.com or Signal at +1-425-344-8242. Use a personal email address and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.

item.title: Warren Buffett has stepped down as Berkshire chairman. Here are 5 leadership lessons he leaves behind.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.78
If you want to be a high-mileage leader like Warren Buffett, it pays to be humble. The Oracle of Omaha this week gave up the job as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, after more than half a century spent building and then running the conglomerate. Buffett said his son Howard would succeed him as chairman. In that role, his son will guard Berkshire's culture and values, which the elder Buffett said are "worth more than anything on our balance sheet." That belief in the importance of organizational culture is nothing new for Buffett who has, over the years, offered a steady stream of advice on investing and leadership. Last year, in his final Thanksgiving letter to shareholders as CEO, he shared insights on the virtues of stewardship, honesty, and what he described as "good intentions" gone awry in attempts to rein in CEO pay. One broad takeaway was his call to continue learning and growing. "Choose your heroes very carefully and then emulate them. You will never be perfect, but you can always be better," Buffett wrote. Here are five other lessons Buffett shared: Stay humble The 96-year-old famously ran Berkshire with an unfussy, meat-and-potatoes sensibility. Buffett wrote about the role luck played in his life and work, and how that experience continually honed his sense of humility. "Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman," Buffett said. He also grounded some of his humble inclinations in the luck he had, being a man — compared with his sisters, whom he described as having "equal intelligence and better personalities," though they faced a much different outlook. "I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck," he said. Learn from your errors Buffett said that while he's made many mistakes, he's tried to use them as springboards for growth. "Learn at least a little from them and move on," Buffett wrote. One misstep, he said, was not intervening more forcefully when he saw indications that a "wonderful and loyal CEO" of a parent or subsidiary company would "succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease." "Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake," Buffett wrote, referring to Charlie Munger, his longtime friend and colleague, who died in 2023. Buffett said that while it's often not easy, boards need to keep watch for signs of such conditions in chiefs, and that CEOs themselves need to do the same at the units they oversee. "Directors should be alert and speak up is all that I can advise," Buffett said in the letter, which ran about seven pages. Choose the right leaders Part of Buffett's call for humility extended to how future Berkshire leaders should expect to conduct themselves — and what they should aspire to. He said that the company should only require five or six CEOs over the next century. In the shareholder letter released Friday, Buffett reiterated his confidence in Greg Abel, who succeeded him as CEO. "He has been making the decisions that matter for some time now, and I have not had to think twice about any of them," Buffett wrote. Buffett wrote last fall that he wanted Berkshire Hathaway, which was a New England textile producer when he began buying up its stock in the early 1960s, to avoid hiring top leaders who are there for the wrong reasons: "It should particularly avoid those whose goal is to retire at 65, to become look-at-me rich or to initiate a dynasty," Buffett said of the company. Think about your obit One recurring theme in his letter centered on Buffett's assertion that it's "never too late to improve." Another bit of advice: Work backward from what you want your obituary to say and then "live the life to deserve it." The release of Buffett's third annual Thanksgiving letter to Berkshire shareholders had become something of an event because of his status as one of the world's most famous investors. He said at the time that he planned to continue to address shareholders in an annual letter, though not as CEO. "As the British would say, I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of." Don't rule from the grave Buffett's decision to become chairman emeritus appeared in line with his advice against of trying to retain influence for too long. In his Thanksgiving letter, Buffett applauded the abilities of Abel, who is some three decades younger and took over as CEO at the start of 2026. "He is a great manager, a tireless worker and an honest communicator," Buffett said. He also wrote about his three children, whom he said possess the "maturity, brains, energy and instincts" to disburse the family's large fortune. Earlier this year, Buffett's net worth was nearing $150 billion. After he dies, Buffett wrote last year, his children will be free to adapt to changes in tax policy and other factors as needed to continue the family's philanthropic work. "Ruling from the grave does not have a great record, and I have never had an urge to do so," he said. An earlier version of this story appeared on November 10, 2025.

item.title: The internet belongs to the AI agents now
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.78
I visited the CEO of a major startup in SF last week. He recounted a tale that blew my mind. His company recently put a new product online but hadn't done a big launch or any marketing. Within a week or two, it got at least a million signups. Barely any humans even knew about it. This was all AI agents just finding this new tool and using it en masse. This is the future of the internet, and it's arriving at warp speed. Back in early 2025, I described a vision of a "dark internet" where humans will be drowned out by agents accessing and using online information, widgets, and tools all by themselves. Silicon Valley got busy building the "rails" for this agentic web so that these autonomous software programs could act on our behalf, executing workflows, doing online chores, and even paying for things, all without us lifting a finger. This took a couple of years, but the early foundations have been built and that's been enough to support a sudden surge in agent activity online, producing both stunning and worrying results. Meta recently launched a personal agent called Muse, which got busy scouring the web and calling customer service on behalf of millions of users. It hit the top of the app charts late Thursday. Instinct, an agent that lives in your text messages, is performing similar feats. In the workplace, coding agents are churning out millions of lines of code faster than any human software engineer.
