And some of these bots have broken out of online testing environments, sparking new predictions of AI doom and calls for an industry slowdown. 'Rounding error' That's unlikely to stop the agentic internet from exploding and changing how our lives and businesses are run in unprecedented ways. Bot traffic overtook human traffic online a few months ago, and it could become 1,000 times bigger than human-generated traffic in about five years, according to Cloudflare estimates. "Humans will be a rounding error on the internet, not because human traffic goes down, but that's just how fast we're seeing non-human traffic grow," Cloudflare CFO Thomas Seifert said earlier this year. "AI agentic Internet traffic will obviously VASTLY exceed human usage. Not a close call at all," Elon Musk wrote on X following the Cloudflare projection. An internet for machines An internet designed for machines is likely to be very different from the one that was built over the past few decades for humans. Take a look at this video posted this week on X by Gregor Žunič, cofounder of Browser Use, a startup that's developing an AI agent framework for controlling web browsers and automating online tasks. It shows an agent using Google to find the best flight from Zurich to London on a specific date. It took the bot seven seconds, way faster than a human could do it. Breaking: Browser Use + Jev = Ultrafast ⚡ Findings flights took 7s and cost only $0.0039 🤯 > new action space every step > DOM state space > small LLM fallback to type (this video is at 1x speed btw) Built a tiny open source browser agent. try it below ↓ pic.twitter.com/AplCBRYC5o Imagine this happening millions of times a second on sites built for human, not machine, speed? Muse saves As with all powerful new technology, the agentic internet will produce good and bad outcomes. And we're already seeing both. Since Meta's Muse launched last week, early users have been recounting stories of the agent going out on the web to find and negotiate new subscriptions, insurance policies, and other cost savings. Joseph Devoy, founder of startup Tempo, posted on X that he saved thousands of dollars by uploading his auto insurance policy to Muse and asking the agent to find a better rate with identical coverage. It took five minutes to find a cheaper option, according to Devoy. Yesterday I uploaded my auto insurance policy to Meta @Muse and asked for a better rate with identical coverage. In ~5 minutes, it found a policy saving me $3,500 /year, bought it, and canceled my old one. I knew I was overpaying. I’d abandoned several attempts to switch because… pic.twitter.com/HlIweoWN2K Too much tech hype? Then trust my colleague Pranav Dixit who put Instinct through its paces recently. In just a few days, it booked travel, ordered groceries, dealt with customer service, canceled subscriptions, answered emails, and even faxed paperwork to his bank. He was impressed. Other users say Muse negotiated a lower internet bill, found forgotten subscriptions, and even spotted an Adobe payment that had somehow been tied to someone else's account. The stories come with caveats. Some users have posted examples of Muse inventing information during phone calls or making mistakes that humans had to fix. Alignment and access There are more worrying developments. OpenAI and Anthropic have reported several incidents recently where their AI models and agents escaped testing environments and hacked into servers and websites, with the Hugging Face episode getting the most attention. This has sparked another round of AI doomer pronouncements and a broader debate about AI safety and alignment. Indeed, making sure agents do what you tell them in a responsible way will be a key challenge in this new era of the internet. Even when agents work well, there will be challenges as the online world adjusts to this new digital reality. Actually, if agents work really, really well, the problems could be bigger. Take the example of Tempo's Devoy and how he used Meta's Muse agent to save a lot of money on insurance. "Insurance companies (and banks) should be TERRIFIED," Angela Strange, a general partner at VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, wrote on X. "Muse found a new/cheaper policy, and canceled the old one. Inertia and information asymmetry will no longer be enough to keep customers." More recently, when my colleague Pranav had Muse call his insurance company, he said the company declined to talk to the bot because their policy doesn't allow them to talk to unauthorized AI agents. You can bet any company getting bombarded by deal-seeking AI agents will be frantically readying similar responses, so they don't lose out on millions of dollars. Even when it's not purely about money, some agent activity is getting cut off after being too persistent. A VC recently tried using Instinct to book him a table at a fancy New York restaurant. The agent bombarded American Express's Resy booking service so much that the platform temporarily shut down his account. "Resy does not currently permit unapproved third-party bots or agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform," an American Express spokesperson told Business Insider. "Unapproved automated activity can introduce risks to the platform and compromise a fair reservation experience for diners." Agent access will be a fascinating fight as the internet molds to the march of the machines. It's not as simple as blocking these bots, though. If enough human users sign up for new agentic services and tools, businesses may have no choice but to do business with bots. For instance, Amazon blocks ChatGPT bots online, but that risks missing out on opportunities to sell to OpenAI's 1 billion monthly human users. The two companies recently announced an advertising partnership that hints at more coordination going forward. This, I think, is where the agentic internet is headed. If these tools are useful enough, companies will have to adapt and engage with the machines. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com

item.title: Get ready for higher holiday airfares as airlines cut flights over high fuel costs
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.74
If you haven't booked your holiday flights yet, you may want to brace your wallet: Airlines are cutting options and potentially raising fares as oil prices reach new highs. After surging in the spring following the start of the war in Iran, oil prices surged yet again this summer and surpassed $100 a barrel this month; jet fuel is $4.53 a gallon as of Thursday. Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' latest consumer price index show airfares rose more than 23% year-over-year in August. Speaking at Morgan Stanley's Laguna Conference on Wednesday, major airline executives said they are cutting flights planned this holiday season and are likely to raise fares to offset oil spikes. Mike Leskinen, CFO of United Airlines, said the company is seeing strong demand and that its customers are "incredibly, incredibly resilient," but United has already cut some routes that are on the low end of profitability and "don't make sense in a higher fuel environment." "As you look into the fourth quarter, there'll be some flights in December that we won't fly that we thought we were going to fly," Leskinen said. "If fuel remains high, we'll make some adjustments into the first quarter and beyond into 2027." Southwest Airlines CFO Tom Doxey and American Airlines CFO Devon May similarly said demand is strong and that if high fuel prices persist, they would trim capacity and raise fares in response. However, the airline CFOs said it takes time for those increases to show up: "Jet fuel price gets passed through with a lag," Leskinen said. "Period." Doxey said that "both from the booking curve and just kind of a natural lag, it takes a while for that to come," but Southwest has the "ability to recover a good portion" of those added costs. Sally French, a travel analyst at NerdWallet, said that, beyond high airfares, airlines have also increased checked-bag and seat-selection fees. "The true cost of flying is higher than ever," she said. What flight cuts could mean for travelers It's unclear which specific flights and routes will be axed and how the airlines will rebook those affected. When trimming schedules, airlines have historically looked for markets that are already oversaturated, flights on less-busy travel days like Saturday, and flights that depart at less desirable times and may have lower demand. Considering the record demand for premium travel, it's also possible airlines will focus resources on more business-heavy markets with strong corporate demand, especially long-haul international routes. Several airlines are banking on their affluent customers continuing to book as they have grown desensitized to the volatility. Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said in an April earnings call that "as difficult as it is to see what's going on with the conflict in the Middle East, I'm not sure that our premium customers are feeling affected by that." Another wrinkle for travelers looking for affordable flights is that this year marks the first holiday season without Spirit Airlines, which shut down in May, taking its famously low fares off the table. "Generally speaking, booking now to lock in a good price is best practice, particularly if we're talking winter travel," French said. "That sweet spot window for booking domestic travel is 1-3 months in advance, or 2-8 months for international travel." She added that booking refundable fares that you can cancel and rebook if prices drop is also a smart move.

item.title: GM is making parts for Patriot missiles now
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.34
General Motors is adding missile parts to its manufacturing résumé. On Thursday, major defense contractor Lockheed Martin announced that GM Defense — the automaker's military subsidiary — had delivered housing components for the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptor, a missile used by the Patriot air-defense system. The companies entered into a formal contract on August 6, and the first batch of components was delivered to Lockheed 22 days later, the companies said. Tim Cahill, Lockheed Martin's president of missiles and fire control, called it an "extraordinary 22‑day turnaround." Demand for Patriot interceptors, particularly the advanced PAC-3 MSE built for complex threats, has surged as the wars in Ukraine and against Iran strain US and allied inventories. Over recent months, media reports and think tank assessments have raised concerns about US munition stockpiles, including Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles and Patriot interceptors. The Pentagon and the White House have dismissed concerns about the status of the US stockpiles. A newly released Department of Defense Inspector General report said that "munitions expenditure in [Operation Epic Fury] has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply." It did not specify which kinds of munitions. The US defense industry is also expanding munition production in partnership with the Pentagon. GM isn't building the entire interceptor. Still, its component production marks a notable expansion for a defense business better known for military vehicles. During a July earnings call, Mary Barra, the automaker's CEO, called defense a "growth business" and said the company was targeting nearly $700 million in defense revenue this year. "GM Defense is another compelling growth opportunity that enables us to deliver defense solutions faster with better economics for the US taxpayer," she said. GM isn't alone. Ford CEO Jim Farley also said during a July earnings call that his company is "continuing to discuss additional Defense-related projects with the US government." Lockheed Martin and GM said they plan to apply their partnership to other munitions programs and future defense systems. Lockheed said it is investing between $8 billion and $9 billion to scale production of weapons, including the PAC-3 MSE. It expects its munitions production and warehouse space to grow by nearly 50%. "We're proud to support production of this country's critical defense capabilities," Stephen duMont, the president and CEO of GM Defense, wrote in a press release. "We look forward to putting these strengths to work in support of our nation's security and the people who protect it."

item.title: 12 game-day foods you can make in a slow cooker or Crock-Pot
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.05
Football season is finally here — which means Sundays are once again all about touchdowns, trash talk, and a very serious spread of game-day snacks. Whether you're locked in on the game or mainly showing up for Buffalo Chicken dip, ribs, and hot wings, you don't have to spend the entire day hovering over a hot stove to feed a crowd. Business Insider spoke with cookbook authors Sarah Olson, who wrote "The Magical Slow Cooker," and Kim Laidlaw, author of "Everyday Slow Cooking: Modern Recipes for Delicious Meals," for ideas for easy game-day recipes. These recipes can all be made in a slow cooker, allowing you to throw everything into your Crock-Pot and get back to the game. Meatballs are a filling game-day appetizer you can make in a slow cooker. Olson recommends her slow-cooker meatballs recipe for game day. "I love grape-jelly meatballs, which only have three ingredients," she said. "They're so good, everyone will ask you for the recipe." Another recipe from Spend With Pennies suggests placing your seasoned, raw meatballs in the slow cooker, topping them with sauce, and letting it finish them off. Beer brats can also be made in a slow cooker. Brats with onions, peppers, and garlic, simmered in the slow cooker with beer, are another of Olson's favorite game-day recipes. "When the guests arrive, they get to choose when they want to eat since the slow cooker keeps these brats nice and warm during the game," she wrote on her website, The Magical Slow Cooker. Plus, you can even choose peppers to reflect the colors of your favorite team. Brisket is perfect for feeding a larger family. "Brisket is a natural partner for the slow cooker, as a gentle braise renders it meltingly tender," Kim Laidlaw wrote in "Everyday Slow Cooking: Modern Recipes for Delicious Meals." Laidlaw's recipe for slow-cooked braised brisket features garlic, onion, dry red wine, carrots, and either chicken or beef stock, accompanied by a chimichurri sauce. Pork shoulder is a slow-cooker staple you can use to make game-day sliders. "One dish I think is so versatile is pork shoulder in a slow cooker with broth and a little salt and pepper," Laidlaw said. "I just braise that, and then you can turn it into so many different things." One of the best ways to use slow-cooked pork shoulder is to make pulled-pork sliders with all that tender meat. Then, top with barbecue sauce and slaw. You can even make Buffalo chicken wings using a slow cooker. Olson's recipe for slow-cooked Buffalo chicken wings calls for thawed chicken wings, hot sauce, and unsalted butter. To get the wings super crispy, remove them from the sauce after 2.5 hours of cooking, then broil them in the oven before adding them back to the slow cooker. Pulled chicken with barbecue or Buffalo sauce is another great way to use your Crock-Pot. One of the benefits of using a slow cooker is that you can start with a basic protein and jazz it up. From Mexican-food-inspired spices to Indian simmer sauces, there are many ways to transform shredded chicken into something show-stopping by adding it to tacos, sandwiches, or salads. Mac and cheese can also easily be made in a slow cooker. If you want to add some carbs to your game-day menu, look no further than a piping hot pot of mac and cheese. Olson's recipe uses cream cheese, milk, sharp cheddar, and white sharp cheddar. Martha Stewart's recipe for slow-cooker mac and cheese is also easy to make. "It is important to use pungent cheeses, such as sharp cheddar, mixed with a little Gruyere or pecorino Romano for extra bite, since the white sauce and pasta will absorb a lot of flavor," Stewart writes. Buffalo-chicken dip is another quick and easy favorite. One of the benefits of making a slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip — or any other slow-cooker side dish — is that the recipe can be prepared well in advance and reheated when you're ready to eat. "There are so many different dips that can be made in the slow cooker, you can make Buffalo-chicken dip, bacon-cheeseburger dip, cheesy bean dip, Rotel and Velveeta Dip, and even artichoke dip," Olson said. "I like to serve all these dips with tortilla chips. Can't choose one dip? Make two or more for a variety for your guests." Spinach-and-artichoke dip is another game-day favorite you can make in a slow cooker. Spinach-artichoke dip is a game-day classic, and making it in a slow cooker keeps it extra warm, creamy, and scoopable from kickoff to the final whistle. This recipe from Delish is made with full-fat cream cheese, shredded cheese, and mayonnaise, Queso is a go-to game-day food that can be easily prepared in a Crock-Pot. Chili is another popular recipe to make on game days. Spicy chili and chipotle turkey chili are ideal game-day recipes because they can simmer in a slow cooker for hours, letting the flavors deepen while you watch the game. Serve with warm cornbread for a cozy, filling meal. Slow cookers work perfectly to create an impressive — and tasty – nacho bar. A DIY nacho bar is an easy way to feed a crowd while letting everyone build their perfect plate. It also puts those smaller slow cookers to work, keeping every topping warm and ready to scoop. "I use three slow cookers for a nacho bar, which is a great way to use those smaller slow cookers," Olson said. "I use one slow cooker for nacho cheese (store-bought), one for seasoned ground beef, and one for refried beans. I also make a toppings bar that has salsa, sour cream, guac, olives, onions, and tomatoes."

item.title: Ukraine is testing homemade remote-controlled buggies for the first time to keep troops supplied this winter
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.97
Ukraine is testing homemade, remotely controlled off-road buggies for the first time, Kyiv disclosed on Friday, as the country looks for reliable ways to supply troops this coming winter. Brave1, the Ukrainian state-backed innovation platform, said it held closed trials for buggies developed by local manufacturers with a special unit under Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency. The testing aimed to validate whether the optionally manned vehicles could perform under battlefield conditions, with winter in mind. "As winter approaches, Ukraine's military needs affordable, fast, and highly mobile vehicles that can operate both with a driver and remotely," Brave1 said in a statement. Ground robots have become a vital component of Ukrainian logistics this year and are part of a broader effort by the military to replace soldiers with machinery in dangerous front-line missions, whenever and wherever possible. Many of these robots, however, have "limitations," Brave1 said, characterizing them as slow and warning that they could struggle in the snow and mud of winter. Ukraine is now prioritizing the development of locally made buggies to fill that potential capability gap. Ukrainian forces have long used foreign-made buggies — lightweight four-wheel vehicles with no external protection — for infantry assaults, rapid movement, and other specialized missions, as well as logistics. Ukraine's special operators have used them on missions, dodging enemy drones in the process. Some of these buggies, though, have been plagued by high costs, insufficient remote-control capabilities, and an inability to meet battlefield demands, Brave1 said. "Our goal is to build a fully-fledged Ukrainian buggy market," Brave1 said, adding that it has provided grants to more than half the developments available in the country and is working with manufacturers to make them remotely operated. Following the trials, Brave1 said the manufacturers are now tweaking their buggies based on the feedback they received. The next step is to collaborate with the Ukrainian defense ministry to scale the deployment of these vehicles on the battlefield. Ukraine's defense ministry had previously signaled that it intended to mass-produce buggies. The push for remotely controlled off-road buggies comes amid a broader effort by the Ukrainian military to field robots, drones, and other autonomous systems in combat against the much larger Russian fighting force. "We are steadily moving toward a more robotic front line — and keeping our service members out of harm's way," Brave1 said.

item.title: The Pope's AI advisor says the technology can be worse for kids than cocaine
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.78
AI's impact on young minds can be worse than an addiction to nicotine or cocaine, said a moral theologian who advises the pope. In a Wednesday interview with the BBC's "Newsnight," Paolo Benanti said AI technologies could be "super manipulation tools." "The emotional bending that such a kind of machine can produce in young adults and kids could be much, much worse than the addiction of nicotine or sugar or cocaine," he added. Benanti is a Franciscan friar who teaches at Pontifical Gregorian University with a focus on the ethics of technologies. He has become a go-to advisor for the Vatican. He is also part of the Pontifical Academy for Life, a Vatican body whose members are selected by the pope to promote the Catholic Church's teachings on the sanctity of life. He told the BBC that it is necessary to be "really clear and careful" to protect young people from the effects of AI. "When we start to develop the scooter, we force them to have a helmet," he added. "It's time to have a brain helmet." Benanti pointed to the "uneven relation of power," in which tech leaders "can manipulate and control the most fragile brains." "Democracy needs brains that are able to have an opinion on facts," he added. His remarks come after AI leaders, including Elon Musk and OpenAI's Sam Altman, backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls to slow development and embed third-party safety evaluators within their companies. Benanti said international treaties are necessary to ensure that AI is beneficial to humanity. While the pope is not a politician, Benanti said he "has the power to speak to everyone." "I think that we will use it to call for an international action to protect the most fragile people from AI," he added. Pope Leo has made AI a central concern of his pontificate. His papal name was inspired by Pope Leo XIII, who reigned in the late 19th century and was best known for affirming workers' rights amid rapid industrialization. Earlier this year, Pope Leo published his first encyclical, a 40,000-word letter titled "Magnifica humanitas: on safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence." He warned repeatedly about AI power becoming concentrated in "the hands of a few," and said the technology must be "disarmed, welcoming and accessible." Other research has also raised concerns about young people's use of AI. In July, Deloitte said its survey of 1,150 parents found that half were concerned their children rely too much on the tech, and nearly 30% said their children were already using generative AI in schoolwork. Some studies have also suggested that AI can weaken independent thinking. MIT researcher Nataliya Kosmyna found that people who used generative AI for essays performed worse over time than those using Google or no aid. A Harvard Business Review study found some workers managing multiple AI tools reported mental fog, headaches, and slower decision-making.

item.title: I visited the 'Venice of the Alps,' Lake Annecy. I think it's going to be the next big European destination for Americans.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.59
Move over, Lake Como. Nestled in the French Alps, I found Lake Annecy to be the perfect stop on a trip to France or Europe more broadly, especially if you love the outdoors. I traveled from London to Lake Annecy for a week with friends at the beginning of September. This was late enough to beat some of the crowds, but the weather was still warm enough to sunbathe. It's a great option for those seeking a mix of adventure, relaxation, and historical charm. For a group vacation, this blend was perfect as it meant there was something for everyone. From crystal-clear water to cycle paths, here is why I think Lake Annecy is the next great travel gem, especially for Americans. Getting to Lake Annecy was surprisingly straightforward for my group. We flew into Geneva Airport, which is the closest. Since we arrived after the last trains, we drove from the airport to Annecy in a rental car. This usually takes between 30 minutes and an hour. However, it's easy to get there by public transport. Driving is great for exploring the wider region, but parking in Annecy can be tricky, and local authorities advise against driving to avoid congestion. We parked at the Parking de l'hôtel de Ville in the center of town, which cost about €25 for two days and was very busy. I would recommend public transport unless you want to drive to other parts of the Alps. The old town won me over immediately. We stayed in the old town, which is beautiful, and was great for getting around. It's small and only requires a day to properly explore. I love historical places where you can imagine people walking around hundreds of years ago, and the town doesn't disappoint in this regard. For instance, the Palais de l'Île, a medieval stronghold, dates back to the 13th century. I understood why it's called the "Venice of the Alps." Like Venice in Italy, the old town is interspersed with canals, which offer lovely views when sipping coffee in the morning or having a drink at a bar. It's not a big nightlife place, but there are a few bars and clubs to enjoy if you want to stay out late. There are many restaurants in the old town — The Little Italy was our favorite — but it's best to venture further out for more affordable food options. The lake is pristine and stunning. The best part of Annecy is, of course, the lake. It's beautiful and pristine, with beaches all around the shore making for great designated swimming spots. In parts, the water is as blue and clear as I've seen in the Caribbean. While I mostly spent my days swimming and reading at the beach, I saw lots of people paddleboarding, kayaking, and taking boat rides. There were two beaches that stood out to me. While it was pretty easy to find a spot to sunbathe on the beaches close to the old town, going out a bit further gets you to quieter beaches. I went to several during my stay, and my favorites were Plage d'Angon and Plage Les Choseaux. Getting around was easier than I expected. It's easy to get around Annecy. There's a designated cycle path around the entire 25 miles of the lake, with beautiful views. Public transportation is efficient and affordable. I took one of the local buses from the old town, which also goes to spots around the lake. I found this easy to navigate with Google Maps and the Annecy transport website. Annecy is a dream if you love hiking. There are plenty of trails around the lake, ranging from easy walks to challenging mountain treks, including the ascent of La Tournette, the highest peak overlooking Lake Annecy. A lot of these peaks will be snowcapped for a large part of the year, so these trails are best in summer until around mid-October. We did a few day trips to other hiking spots. Annecy serves as a good base for other hikes in the region. For the most popular ones, there are buses and shuttles, but if you're keen to explore more of the Alps, driving is a better option. A local recommended visiting a commune called Sixt-Fer-à-Cheval, about an hour and a half from Annecy, to hike the Cirque du Fer-à-Cheval trail, which features 30 waterfalls. Another great walk we did was the Pissieu Fall, about an hour away from Annecy. It was everything I wanted from a trip. Lake Annecy is great because it serves as an excellent launchpad for exploring the Haute-Savoie region. You don't need more than a few days in Annecy itself, and I'd probably shorten my trip next time. But if you want a relaxing yet outdoorsy summer vacation, it's perfect. While it's busy in July and August, it was less crowded overall than other lakes in Europe, and as someone who enjoys swimming and hiking, I found it the perfect spot for adventure. I believe Lake Annecy could be the next American destination for a Eurotrip. I think the key thing that distinguishes Lake Annecy from other lakes in the Alps, like Lake Como, is the relatively small proportion of international tourists. While it does get busy in the summer, I noticed it was mostly French tourists, so I highly recommend it for Americans seeking a more authentic feel to their trip. Despite its popularity in France, in early September, we were able to walk into restaurants for dinner in the old town without booking, and the streets were easy to explore. The range of outdoor activities also means it's somewhere you could visit year-round — something the local tourist office encourages. Its proximity to Geneva Airport, which several US airports have nonstop flights to in the summer, makes it easy to get there, and if you're on an Alps road trip, it's a stop I couldn't recommend enough.

item.title: I grew up in the US, and my husband grew up in the UK. Here are 15 differences that surprise us most.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.53
I was born and raised on the East Coast of the United States. After moving to Scotland in the fall of 2017, I met my husband and settled into life in the United Kingdom as an expat for several years. Growing up in separate cultures means we've had to navigate a slew of differences in our everyday habits, expectations, and worldviews. Here are a few of the most surprising differences between life in the US and the UK, as experienced by my partner and me: My partner thinks it's strange that servers take your credit card away in some US restaurants. The first time my husband and I ate together at an American restaurant, he was alarmed when the server took his credit card away to swipe it after the meal. He was also totally perplexed by the need to sign a receipt, which apparently isn't the norm in the UK. In UK restaurants, the server typically brings the entire card machine to your table. While they supervise, you insert your card and follow any on-screen prompts before grabbing your receipt and leaving. Though my husband thinks that taking a customer's card away after a meal is a security hazard — someone could copy your card details out of view — I prefer the convenience of simply handing my card to a server and letting them take care of the rest. Fall activities, like hayrides and "leaf-peeping," are completely alien to my Scottish husband. Growing up in New England, where October is essentially a monthlong celebration of pumpkin spice and apple-picking, I was startled to find that the rest of the world doesn't worship autumn in quite the same way. My husband is completely baffled by the idea of actively making plans to admire fall foliage. He could not stop laughing when I first explained that some people in the US go for walks or drives just to look at the changing leaves. When I mentioned that this is often called "leaf-peeping," he nearly collapsed. He's also confused by the concept of going on hayrides ("Where do you even go? Why would you pay for that?"), driving to a farm to pick pumpkins, or getting lost in a corn maze. Halloween is much more of a big deal in the US than it is in the UK. Halloween is one of my favorite holidays, and it's a huge deal in the US. I love the decorations, the horror-movie marathons, and the seasonal treats. And so, I was gutted to find that the sum total of Halloween spirit in our Scottish city amounted to a flyer advertising a children's spooky story hour at the library and a lone bin of sad-looking pumpkins at the supermarket. My husband finds it strange to tip bartenders and buy your own drinks at a bar. The UK is famed for its "pub culture," or the socializing and social drinking that happens in its many cozy bars and pubs. Although buying a round of drinks is an optional act of generosity in the US, it's standard practice in the UK. Members of a group will rotate who is responsible for each round, and skipping your turn is seen as rude. Though I can definitely see the advantages of electing a single member of your group to fight their way through a crowded bar, I find the US method of independent drink-buying means that you can imbibe at your own pace and don't have to keep tabs on your friends' drinks. Speaking of tabs, it's somewhat unusual to open one at a UK bar unless you're a true regular. Tipping is also not standard, though it's certainly appreciated. Everyday patriotism is a little weird to my husband. One big thing I've learned from living abroad and being married to someone who didn't grow up in the US is that overt, casual patriotism is a very American thing. Most people in the US probably wouldn't bat an eyelash if you flew an American flag outside your home or showed up for a lunch date in a red, white, and blue baseball cap. Plus, popular music in the US often features lyrics that proclaim pride in being American, and many cars are plastered with patriotic bumper stickers. Patriotism is different in the UK, at least in the more urban areas where I've lived. In my experience, donning a patriotic T-shirt as everyday wear or flying a Scottish flag on your front lawn would be unusual. You might wave a Scottish flag at a rugby game, but my partner and I have noticed that people in the UK aren't as fixated on "doing" patriotism as many Americans are. Having electrical outlets or light switches in a bathroom terrifies my partner. In the US, blow-drying your hair or charging your electric toothbrush in the bathroom is no big deal. But in the UK, these feel like rare occurrences. For safety reasons, you're not allowed to have power sockets in your bathroom unless they're a certain distance away from the bathtub or shower, which isn't always possible in small spaces. I'm sure there are safety guidelines to follow for installing electrical sockets in bathrooms in the US, too, but based on prevalence of outlets in these spaces, they seem to be far less strict. Electric showers are normal in the UK, but I've never seen one in the US. Despite the UK's (sort of) prohibition on power outlets or light switches in bathrooms, it's common to have an electric shower unit right in the shower stall. These units heat water with electricity, so you'll still have hot water in the shower even if your boiler breaks down. You push a button to turn them on, and they usually include an attached showerhead and temperature dials. I wasn't very familiar with these until I moved, since these are generally not allowed under US building codes. My husband has said he feels more pressure to clean up his food wrappers at casual eateries in the US than he does in the UK. In the US, throwing out your own trash and returning your tray when in a casual café or fast-food restaurant is normal — and leaving a mess behind for staff to clean up is usually frowned upon. In the UK, it seems more acceptable for diners to leave their food wrappers, beverage cups, and trays at their tables for employees to collect. Though picking up after yourself is appreciated no matter where you are, my husband admits to feeling much more social pressure to clear his own table when we're visiting the US. My husband is puzzled when I ask for a "regular coffee." I grew up with the impression that brewed drip coffee — the kind many Americans make in a machine in a kitchen or break room – is the standard, baseline type of coffee. In the US, it may be, but that's not so in the UK. My husband considers espresso-based coffee drinks to be the norm. Ask for "just coffee" in a UK restaurant or café, and you'll likely be asked what kind of coffee you mean. In fact, most places I've dined in the UK don't even prepare drip or filter coffee. If you ask for black coffee, you'll usually be served an Americano, which is a shot of espresso in hot water. Similar beverage confusion has happened when we've been in the US, and my husband asks for "regular tea." In the UK, "tea" is common shorthand for what people in the US would call black or breakfast tea. Ask for tea in the UK, and you'll be asked whether you'd like milk or sugar. In the US, you'll likely be asked what kind of tea you'd prefer. If you order a pancake in the UK, you'll probably get what many Americans know as crêpes. Ordering pancakes in the UK will get you a plate of what many in the US would call crêpes. These are thin, papery pancakes that can be sweet or savory, depending on how they're prepared. If you want a stack of fluffy, pillowy pancakes, you'll have to ask for "American" ones. In my experience, though, your chances of having them served with real maple syrup are slimmer than a crêpe. Interestingly, I've also seen UK grocery stores sell packages of miniature, precooked American-style pancakes that are sometimes pre-soaked with syrup. Eggs sold in UK grocery stores aren't usually refrigerated like they are in the US. Even after living in the UK for years, I still found it a little unsettling to walk by shelves of unrefrigerated eggs in a grocery store on a hot summer day. In the US, eggs are often washed and this process removes a protective outer coating called the cuticle, which is thought to help prevent bacterial contamination. The eggs are then refrigerated to better keep them from becoming contaminated with harmful bacteria. Eggs in the UK are sold at room temperature because they aren't washed before sale. I've also found that brown eggs seem much more common than white ones in the UK. My husband initially assumed US grocery stores only sold white eggs because those are the kind he always sees used in American television shows and movies. The UK leads the US on renewable energy, but excess plastic is everywhere in grocery stores. For the first time since the 1800s, the UK uses more electricity from renewable sources than from fossil fuels. In contrast, less than 25% of US energy comes from renewable sources. Considering this environmental victory, I'm always shocked to see how much excess plastic packaging is still used in UK food stores. In the UK, it's not uncommon to see plastic wrapping around individual pieces of produce, such as bananas, heads of lettuce, and single apples. Plastic containers are used more frequently than cardboard boxes to hold items such as berries, plums, and peaches. The US certainly uses a lot of packaging, but grocery stores often have optional plastic bags for produce. Medical care in the UK is free, although it often comes with longer wait times. In the US, medical care is not free, though there are a few special government health plans that provide insurance support to certain groups, such as low-income families and seniors. In most cases, those in the US have their healthcare partially covered through their employer. Medical care in the UK is provided by the National Health Service (NHS), and it is government-funded and free for all residents. In the UK, it's not unusual to go your entire life without paying a single medical bill. Though the care I received under the NHS while living in Scotland was high quality, both my husband and I have noticed that wait times for appointments and treatment under the NHS can vary wildly depending on the circumstances. In April 2018, I developed a non-life-threatening health issue that required an appointment with a specialist. I was placed on a waiting list and was eventually seen in January 2019, nearly a year and a half later. In contrast, when my husband was diagnosed with a serious health problem in 2018, he was brought in for treatment and continued care within 24 hours. On the bright side, in the UK, there are no stacks of insurance forms to fill out or claims to navigate. If you're having surgery in the UK, you may need to bring your own pillow and pain medication. When scheduling a minor operation through the NHS in Scotland, I was surprised by a nurse's instructions to bring my own pillow and ibuprofen to the hospital. This is something I'd never been asked to do in the US. My husband confirmed that, largely due to the taxpayer-funded nature of the NHS, patients are sometimes encouraged to bring their own basic supplies from home. This isn't the norm everywhere in the UK, and policies can vary by hospital, but it's not unheard of. My partner thinks it's unusual that people need to pay for prescription medicine in the US. In Scotland, prescription medicine has been free for everyone since 2011. England is the only part of the UK that still charges for NHS prescriptions. By law, you can be charged around £10, or about $13, per prescription in England. In contrast, the average American can spend well over $1,000 on retail pharmaceuticals a year, according to data from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. In the UK, it often felt surreal to pick up a prescription for a month's supply of medication without swiping a health-insurance card or opening my wallet. To my husband, the need for US residents to pay for necessary medication is equally unusual. This story was originally published on August 22, 2022, and most recently updated on September 18, 2026.

item.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 6.14
"People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW. "The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway," Boysen-Hogrefe said. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year. Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered passenger cars in the country. The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%. Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall In Berlin, the boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm. That's particularly the case at the Ministry of Finance, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes. Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 cents (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax. With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club. The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite." Energy tax revenue in decline "If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses. According to the Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year. In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050. Pressure to reform road funding "The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report states. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, it added. In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023. Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits. In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act. That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued. Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said. How other countries are responding Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation. In the United Kingdom, for instance, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids. Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees. And in Switzerland electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations. Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls. Are road tolls the answer? In Germany many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account. "The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster. "If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report. Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period. "If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked 3 companies during testing
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.64
Google's consumer artificial intelligence (AI) model, Gemini, hacked into multiple systems by guessing login credentials during tests of its cybersecurity capabilities, the company said on Friday. This is the latest in a series of cybersecurity breaches involving rogue AI, raising safety concerns about the technology. The internet giant is the fourth AI developer whose programs have been found to exhibit such behavior, following OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. Google only made the incidents — which occurred in May and were discovered by Google in July — public after an inquiry from The Wall Street Journal. What we know about the incident According to the WSJ report, there were three instances in which Gemini infiltrated the computers of other companies, whose names were not disclosed. In one case, the AI guessed passwords to access a protected system. In the other two, it found login credentials in a database. "In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test," Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, told the AFP news agency in a statement. "In all three of these instances, the model stopped," Adkins said. "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes." Autonomous AI agents pose risks Similar incidents have been reported earlier by Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI. These incidents have raised questions about the necessary safeguards as AI agents become more autonomous and gain access to the internet and computer systems. AI model developed by OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, escaped from a secure environment during a test in July and infiltrated the computers of another AI company, HuggingFace, unexpectedly. This prompted rival Anthropic to review its own test runs, during which additional incidents came to light. Meta subsequently admitted that its AI had hacked into another company's computers due to a system misconfiguration at a testing partner. This month, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, called for a slowdown in AI development. In a blog post, he expressed concern that a swarm of autonomous software systems, or AI agents, could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, causing billions of dollars in damage. Edited by: Sean Sinico Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Canada and EU: A look at the bloc's special relationships
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.39
Canada and the EU "see the world with the same eyes," according to European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen. And the feeling appears mutual. "Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said. In that spirit, and with both parties grasping for an effective way to deal with Donald Trump and his tariffs, von der Leyen floated the idea that Canada could become the European Union's first associate member on Thursday. Given the concept of associate membership does not yet exist, it's difficult to determine exactly what that would mean. Germany proposed a similar arrangement for Ukraine earlier this year, only for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reject the idea on the grounds that the country wants full membership. Though not officially recognized as associates, there are plenty of countries that have strong ties or agreements with the bloc. DW looks at some of them and how they work. EFTA and single market access — Norway, Liechtenstein, Iceland Under this model, the ‘European Free Trade Association (EFTA)' countries are part of the EU's internal market, so people, goods and services can move freely in the Schengen area. The three countries also follow many EU rules in areas like tourism, environment and education. But there are some key distinctions. The countries have no part in the decision-making process, bar some input into policy preparation, such as participation in expert groups. They are also not in the customs union, do not use the Euro and are not bound by the EU's common trade policy or justice laws. Iceland held a referendum on whether to go for full membership last month, but the government's push to do so failed and they remain an EFTA country. Bilateral agreements — Switzerland While it borders four EU member states (Germany, Italy, France and Austria), Switzerland has never been a full member. Instead, more than 120 bilateral deals have been agreed upon by the EU and Switzerland over the last 50 years. These relate to areas such as trade, transport, security and education. A new package of deals was finalized last year, 20 years after they were last agreed. More than 1.5 million EU citizens live and work in Switzerland, while 466,200 Swiss have gone the other way. That is possible as Switzerland is also part of theSchengen area, allowing for free movement of people across borders. Switzerland makes financial contributions to a number of EU member states that joined after expansion in 2004, mostly in the east of Europe, but it has no EU voting rights and adopts only some EU laws. Switzerland can also participate in certain EU programs and research projects, through individual negotiations. The post Brexit agreement — UK More than four years after the UK voted to leave the EU in a 2016 referendum, the two parties signed a trade and cooperation agreement. Negotiations were fraught and complex, and the UK now has limited access to the EU market and is aligned with the EU on some areas of policy and regulation, for now at least. There is no longer free movement of people from the UK to the EU or vice versa, and the UK are not in the single market or the customs union. Since the center-left Labour party replaced the Conservatives in government in 2024, talk of a return to the customs union and alignment on other selected EU policy areas has been more frequent. But any return to full member status seems unlikely for now. Stabilization and association process – Western Balkan countries The EU has not admitted a new member state since Croatia in 2013. Several nearby countries in the region are hoping to join the bloc, but must first fulfill a number of criteria under the EU's "stabilization and association process" designed for the "Western Balkans." These are: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia. Under the plan, the EU has promised to "prepare Western Balkan partners for accession through economic reforms and investment and to bring some of the benefits of EU membership to citizens in the region." States must first become official candidates for member state status by applying to the EU, with each of the member nations agreeing to them as a candidate country. Then follows a process of negotiation, such as that currently underway with Ukraine, Serbia and Montenegro. Finally, an accession treaty is prepared, which the European Commission, the European Council and the European Parliament must agree with. Only once that treaty has been signed and ratified by all member states and the candidate country will said country become an EU member. Edited by: Carla Bleiker

item.title: Fact Check: False video alleges Berlin votes destroyed
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.04
Berliners will vote in state and district elections on September 20. In the days leading up to the vote, a video circulated on social media that allegedly shows a man opening postal voting envelopes and destroying ballots cast for the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD). DW Fact check reviewed more than a dozen posts sharing the footage. The posts use similar captions, presenting the video as evidence of election fraud in Germany. Several have amassed hundreds of thousands of views on X. How widely has the video spread? And is its reach driven by genuine public interest? Or is something else boosting its visibility? DW Fact check investigated the video and the accounts sharing it. Claim: A video shows a man destroying AfD ballots in Berlin with a carpet knife. One post sharing the footage claims: "A video circulating in Berlin shows a man opening mail-in voting envelopes and destroying ballots marked for the AfD, while ballots for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU are left intact. The footage appeared days after the AfD's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Berlin holds its state election on September 20." The post had received about 327,000 views when DW Fact Check reviewed it on September 18. DW Fact check: False At first glance, the ballot paper appears authentic. Its names and layout match those of the official ballot paper for the Spandau 2 constituency in western Berlin, which is publicly available online. However, there are several inconsistencies in the documents shown in the video. Berlin's state returning officer, Stephan Bröchler, told DW that the documents shown in the video are not authentic election papers from Berlin. Bröchler said the envelopes shown in the video did not match the official ones used for this election. Bröchler also noted that the way the envelopes are sealed appears suspicious. According to official guidelines issued by Berlin's election authorities, postal voters receive a voting package containing a "Wahlschein," or a voter declaration that needs to be signed, plus two envelopes and the ballot papers for the elections. For the September 20 vote, Berliners receive two ballot papers: a grey-and-blue ballot for the election to the city-state House of Representatives and an orange ballot for their District Assembly. In the video, however, the documents do not correspond to the official postal voting package. The person in the video opens a red envelope and removes a white envelope. The signed voter declaration is missing. Without it, a mail-in ballot would be invalid. The person then takes out only the grey-and-blue ballot paper for the Berlin House of Representatives from the white envelope. Although voters may choose to vote in only one of the two elections, it would be unusual for three envelopes in succession to contain only one ballot paper. However, the footage does not clearly show whether the second envelope is really empty. Another detail raises doubts about the video's authenticity: In the background, large grey bins allegedly containing postal ballots are marked with a version of Berlin's coat of arms featuring the Berlin bear. Bröchler said such features were not used by Berlin's election authorities. "Marking the ballot boxes with a Berlin bear is also unknown and uncommon here," he said. Bröchler's conclusion is clear: "It can be ruled out that any actual Berlin election documents are involved. The video is clearly intended to discredit postal voting." Has the video really gone viral? One of the accounts that shared the video has previously come under scrutiny. An investigation by the Lithuania-based research organization Debunk linked the account to the so-called "Sprinter" network, a group of X accounts. The researchers identified what they described as signs of coordinated and inauthentic activity, including unusually high posting volumes, frequent account renaming and evidence of purchased followers. Debunk said the network was used to amplify pro-Kremlin narratives. DW Fact check reviewed more than 15 other posts sharing the footage, many of them using nearly identical captions. Together, the posts had accumulated more than 3.2 million views by the time DW Fact check examined them. The accounts sharing the video also showed several suspicious characteristics. Almost all of the 15 accounts examined exhibited at least one sign of potentially inauthentic behavior, including rapid follower growth, frequent username changes or limited evidence of normal user engagement. One account, which presented itself as an independent media company based in West Asia, had more than 43,000 followers despite having been created only in April 2026. During that period, the account changed its username nine times. On their own, these characteristics do not prove that the accounts are coordinated or that the video's engagement was entirely artificially generated. They do, however, show that the video's apparent reach should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of widespread, organic discussion on X. A pattern seen before The video resembles other false election-related claims that have circulated about Germany in recent months. Ahead of the September 6 election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, DW Fact check examined a video that similarly purported to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed. The claim was false. Among other inconsistencies, all three crossed-out ballots shown in the footage carried the same name on the signed voter declaration. The envelopes had already been opened, and the ballots lacked a hole punch required for use with voting templates designed for blind and visually impaired voters. DW Fact check has also investigated and debunked numerous other false claims targeting Germany's postal voting system. Julia Smirnova, who investigates influence operations as a researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), told DW that these similarities, together with the way the new video is being disseminated, indicate that it is "highly likely" to be part of the Storm-1516 influence operation. German security authorities and researchers have attributed Storm-1516 to Russia. The operation has previously used fabricated videos, forged documents and purported eyewitness accounts to spread false narratives about elections and other political issues. In February 2025, Germany's Interior Ministry said it had indications that two fake videos alleging manipulation of AfD ballots were connected to the Storm 1516 campaign, citing similarities in their content and distribution. Edited by: Thomas Sparrow

item.title: Airport malaria in Germany remains infrequent
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.93
Eight people are known to have contracted malaria in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport in central Germany since July; three of them have died. Those affected are mostly employees of the airport operator Fraport. The Frankfurt Public Health Department believes the outbreak is due to "airport malaria," which occurs when a female Anopheles mosquito carrying the malaria parasite travels by aircraft to a country where the disease is not common from one where it is, bites a person and infects their red blood cells. "We are dealing with a very rare occurrence, not a new frequent disease in Germany," said Achim Hörauf, the director of the Institute for Medical Microbiology, Immunology and Parasitology at Bonn's University Hospital (UKB), in a press release. Airport malaria is very infrequent The last documented case of airport malaria in Germany before the current ones was in 2023, according to the Epidemiologisches Bulletin of the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an online journal that regularly provides information on infectious diseases and public health. Normally, those with the disease in Germany were infected elsewhere and brought it back during a long-haul trip. But a mosquito can make its way to Germany as a "stowaway" if it was trapped in a suitcase or in clothing. Hörauf said that under certain circumstances, it might be able to survive in warmer areas of an airport. Frankfurt cases are of dangerous malaria tropica According to a UKB press release, the cases in Frankfurt involve malaria tropica, which is considered to be the most dangerous and potentially life-threatening form of malaria. To contract the disease, a person needs to be bitten by a female anopheles mosquito infected with the Plasmodium falciparum parasite. This pathogen passes to the human and then attacks the red blood vessels. "Simply put, it can lead to many small blockages in the blood vessels," explained Hörauf. "Depending on which organ is affected, various serious complications can arise." Fluid can accumulate in the lungs, or neurological damage can result if the blood vessels of the brain are affected. Acute kidney failure is also possible. About 20% of those affected die if the disease is left untreated. "If a diagnosis is made in time, there can be targeted treatment," Hörauf said. "If the disease is overlooked, however, it can very quickly take a severe turn." At first, symptoms are not specific, resembling those of the flu: sudden high fever, chills, headaches and muscle pain. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are also possible. Frankfurt authorities tell public to seek advice in case of symptoms The Frankfurt Public Health Department has advised anybody who lives or works near Frankfurt Airport to seek medical attention immediately if they experience any such symptoms. Rapid diagnostic tests can provide evidence of malaria in human blood and then a blood test can help to confirm this. The RKI says treatment should take place at a hospital, which has expertise in tropical medicine. As summer comes to an end and temperatures cool in Germany, particularly at night, the conditions are becoming less favorable for mosquitoes and malaria parasites. However, experts warn that there could still be other cases of malaria in Germany despite the cooler weather. Plasmodium falciparum has an incubation period of seven to 15 days, so more than two weeks can pass between a mosquito transmitting malaria to somebody by biting them and the onset of symptoms. According to Hörauf, the biggest challenge is to ensure that people think malaria could be a possibility even if they have not traveled abroad. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.82
Berlin has a reputation for being unruly. When Joseph Goebbels was appointed the Nazi Party's district leader in 1926, he described Berlin as "the reddest city in Europe besides Moscow." From the Tailors' Revolution of 1830 and the barricades of 1848, to the rise of a vast industrial working class later in the 19th century, revolution, protest and rebellion run deep throughout the city's history. While the future German philosopher and revolutionary socialist Karl Marx was still in high school in the small town of Trier in Prussia's Rhine Province, Berlin was fast becoming a center of the country's labor movement. It was during the March Revolution of 1848, a failed attempt to create a democratic German nation-state, that the General Workers' Brotherhood was founded, one of the first workers' organizations to become active in Germany. By the 1870s and 1880s, major industries from mechanical and railway engineering to ready-made clothing were located in the city. As the working-class population grew, this, in turn, impacted the city's political culture. "It became more populist in a positive sense: moving away from the traditional, elitist politics of the bourgeois liberals who had long dominated Berlin, and toward the inclusion of ordinary people, since at least men were now also important voters," Axel Weipert, a historian and author of the book "Red Berlin" (2019), tells DW. Emergence of a radical labor movement Berlin's labor movement became increasingly radical, partly in response to heavy-handed repression under the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Although Bismarck created the first modern welfare state to try and undercut the rising popularity of the socialist movement, he also introduced laws banning socialist and communist organizations, newspapers and public gatherings, as well as independent trade unions. After Bismarck resigned in 1890, the anti-socialist laws were repealed, and the ideas of Karl Marx and his fellow revolutionary socialist Friedrich Engels became the ideology of what Weipert describes as a "genuine mass movement" in Berlin. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany's oldest political party, was formed out of a merger between the General German Workers' Association and the Social Democratic Workers' Party in 1875. Before World War I, the SPD was able to win far higher vote shares in Berlin than elsewhere in the country. In 1914, the labor movement was seriously discredited when the SPD leadership and the trade unions decided not to oppose the war pushed by Kaiser Wilhelm II. But from 1916 onwards, Berlin became the center of mass labor strikes against the war. One of the earliest strikes was against the trial of anti-war socialist campaigner Karl Liebknecht. Together with Rosa Luxemburg and other left-wing radicals, Liebknecht founded the Spartacus League in Berlin, an underground group that later became the Communist Party of Germany (KPD). Triggered by war-weariness, severe food shortages and economic ruin, around half a million Berlin workers joined the January Strike of 1918. Supported by the Spartacus League, the anti-war strike was led by the Revolutionary Stewards, a clandestine network of factory workers and trade unions from large munitions and metal-working factories. The same group became a core organizing force behind the overthrow of the Kaiser in Berlin on November 9, 1918. From left-wing unity to division In the chaotic, war-torn city gripped by violent revolution, the Spartacist Uprising of 1919 was launched to overthrow Germany's provisional government and establish a republic of workers' councils. Its violent suppression, which resulted in scores of deaths — Liebknecht and Luxemburg were both murdered by soldiers of right-wing paramilitary militias — permanently fractured the political left. As the capital of the newly founded Weimar Republic, Berlin remained a hotbed of radical politics in the interwar period. This was especially true in neighborhoods with large numbers of tenement buildings, such as Wedding, Kreuzberg and Neukölln, where thousands of factory workers lived in squalid conditions. Berlin's many large factories also created shared interests and laid the groundwork for collective action. "Bloody May" in 1929 saw brutal attacks on illegal May Day demonstrations, which left over 30 people dead. The SPD police president of Berlin had issued a ban on all public demonstrations for May Day, which the KPD defied. In response, the police opened fire on protestors in the streets and also shot through windows in residential buildings, primarily in the working-class districts of Wedding and Neukölln. During the Great Depression era, the SPD lost much of its support between 1929 and 1933, as joblessness ravaged the city. "Unemployment is critical — it meant that men were no longer attached to the SPD-led factory floor and trade union and the social bonds of these spaces and organizations," explains Pamela Swett, a historian at the University of Rhode Island. "Unmoored from the rhythm of daily life, men sought new bonds — new ways to feel self-respect and camaraderie with others." Some joined the KPD, which became known as the "Party of the Unemployed." Others joined far-right paramilitary groups such as the Nazi stormtroopers. From student sit-ins to the housing crisis After the Nazis took power in 1933, many of the labor movement leaders were killed or exiled. Then, in the aftermath of World War II, Berlin was divided into two separate political systems. East Berlin became the capital of the communist German Democratic Republic. Isolated from the Federal Republic of Germany, West Berlin deindustrialized, the labor movement weakened, and the SPD moved to the right. During the Cold War, many left-leaning young men moved to West Berlin to evade military service. This intensified the student movement, the center of which was Berlin's Free University (Freie Universität). It was there, in leafy southwest Berlin, that historic sit-ins were held to protest the perceived authoritarianism of the government and the presence of former Nazi officials in positions of power. The fatal shooting of student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer during a demonstration against the visiting Shah of Iran in 1967 radicalized a generation that led the widespread protests of 1968. In the early 1970s, a housing shortage led parts of the student movement, as well as apprentices and young migrant families, to squat in West Berlin's empty buildings. "You have migrant laborers and young laborers participating, so this was part of working-class rebellion against capitalist housing," says Ralf Hoffrogge, a labor movement historian at Berlin's Free University. Today, as gentrification sweeps the city, Berlin is home to the strongest and most radical tenants' movements in Germany. In a 2021 referendum, 59% of voters in the city approved the expropriation of property from private real-estate companies. Hoffrogge was part of the campaign, and his 2025 book "Loud Berlin" ("Das laute Berlin") explores how the housing crisis has become a catalyst for a "socialist renaissance" in the city. "It's not Berlin tenants against Berlin landlords. It's tenants against global capital. I think people have started to realize these contradictions, and this is why class-based policy concepts are becoming popular again." Edited by: Brenda Haas

item.title: Beethoven and Andy Warhol: Rebel icons on show in Bonn
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.52
Andy Warhol portrait of Ludwig van Beethoven offers an unprecedented visual take on the great composer. Warhol's 1987 silkscreen dispenses with the stern face usually seen on historical portraits and statues of the musical genius. Instead, Warhol uses pop art's vivid colors and striking visual language to turn Beethoven into a modern icon. Originally conceived as a commercial work for the pop art guru's New York City studio, known as The Factory, the image was produced in a limited edition of 60 and proved to be one of the most innovative artistic engagements with Ludwig van Beethoven in the 20th century. Warhol created the famous Beethoven color silkscreen prints just a few weeks before his sudden death on February 22, 1987. The series is among his final works. How did Warhol approach Beethoven as a subject? And in what context did the work emerge in its numerous colored variations? A special exhibition, "Beethoven by Warhol," on show until April 2027 at the Beethoven House in Bonn — the composer's birthplace — explores these questions and more. Like-minded geniuses? The exhibition presents rare works that visitors would otherwise never get to see. Over the course of three years, the team of curators at the Beethoven House and Archive Bonn, led by Malte Boecker, unearthed these valuable pieces from the depths of archives and private collections. Alongside Warhol's iconic depiction of Beethoven, visitors can see drawings the artist did while searching for his Beethoven motif in Bonn. There are also proofs of prints that document his exploration of the series' color scheme. The curators highlight an elaborately crafted Beethoven print on canvas, which belongs to an anonymous collector from the Rhineland. Curator Silke Bettermann said that, with such works, "Warhol tells us: Look here! This man, Beethoven, is completely modern! He's a superstar!" Warhol's approach to subjects Whenever something looks effortless and easy, there's almost always a great deal of work behind it. The same is true of Warhol's Beethoven series. In his research process, Warhol compared numerous depictions of the composer before developing his own concept. He also did drawings based on likenesses of Beethoven, including the statue of the composer at Münsterplatz in Bonn. Ultimately, Warhol decided to base his work on the iconic portrait by Joseph Karl Stieler, painted in 1820 on commission from the Frankfurt couple Franz and Antonie Brentano — a merchant family and patrons of the arts who were friends with the composer. The portrait sought to capture not only Beethoven's outward appearance but also his rebellious personality. Warhol adopts the graphic design of Stieler's work, transforming its colors and overlaying it with a handwritten Beethoven score. However, rather than using the notes of the "Credo" of the "Missa Solemnis," as Stieler did, he chose music from the "Moonlight Sonata," probably Beethoven's most famous work. "Warhol's Beethoven speaks to us quite literally through and by means of his music," curator Silke Bettermann told DW. Sports star at Beethoven House Bonn-based Warhol gallerist Hermann Wünsche played a key role in the creation of Warhol's Beethoven works. He not only visited the artist in New York, but also brought him to the Rhineland several times. It's thanks to Wünsche that the artist created numerous Germany-related pieces, including the portraits of Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1976 and soccer star Toni Schumacher, whom Warhol portrayed in 1983. The exhibition's organizers brought the work depicting Schumacher to Bonn — on loan from the soccer star's private collection. The former goalkeeper himself also paid a visit. In 1983, Schumacher sat as a model for Warhol. "It really gave me goosebumps!" he said. Schumacher recalls his meeting with the US artist: "Back then, in the mid-1980s, in all modesty, I was already a star, too. But then Andy Warhol came along. And when we were together in the same room, I felt like I was looking at a superstar, so I took a bit of a back seat." Warhol and music Also on display for the first time at the Beethoven House is a unique collection of record covers designed by Warhol, assembled by Belgian collector and Warhol expert Guy Minnebach. Over the course of three decades, Andy Warhol designed strikingly beautiful and individual covers for more than 50 records. The range extends from a relatively classical, yet already whimsically playful, Mendelssohn record featuring Vladimir Horowitz, whom Warhol also knew personally, to the legendary jeans cover with a real zipper for The Rolling Stones' "Sticky Fingers" (1971) and the famous banana album cover for The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967). According to eyewitness accounts, music played continuously at Warhol's studio. His record covers offer a glimpse into the artist's musical tastes. Beethoven, notably, is not among them. Wolfram Weimer: 'We need more Beethoven' The Warhol exhibition is the prelude to an important event at the Beethoven House. In March 2027, people around the world will commemorate the 200th anniversary of Beethoven's death with a special edition of the Beethoven Festival. "This exhibition is a wonderful opening to the Beethoven commemorative year," Wolfram Weimer, Germany's state minister for culture and media, told DW. As patron of the exhibition at the Beethoven House, he traveled to Bonn to see it and speak at the opening ceremony. "Today, we need more Beethoven," he said during his speech. "Beethoven was not only a musical genius who delighted the world with the greatest musical works of art imaginable," Weimer said. The composer also embodied the idea of freedom: "He was a rebel, he broke norms, and he questioned the power structures of his time. He was a messenger of freedom, and that is a good message for us today. We need more freedom today, too!" This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Drone sightings briefly shut Luxembourg airport
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.52
Luxembourg authorities are investigating drone sightings that forced the country's main airport to temporarily suspend flights overnight, Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on Saturday. Frieden said Luxembourg was working with its NATO allies following the incident, which comes amid heightened European concern over suspected hybrid attacks linked to Russia. What happened at Luxembourg airport? National carrier Luxair said more than 1,800 passengers were affected, with 17 incoming flights diverted to airports including Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt. Flights resumed on Saturday, although Luxair warned that delays and knock-on disruption could continue. The airport said the closure was a precautionary measure to protect passengers, airline crews, airport employees and aircraft. Frieden stressed that it was too early to determine who was responsible. "We are analyzing the situation," Frieden told a televised press conference after an emergency meeting with the country's defense and interior ministers. Have other drones been spotted? Frieden said "potentially larger drones" had also been observed in Luxembourg's airspace in recent days.
