"This is new for Luxembourg, but it is not completely new for our neighboring countries," he said. Unauthorized drones have previously been detected near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark. "We will ensure, together with our partners, that we can guarantee the security of our populations," Frieden said. European governments have repeatedly warned of Russian-linked hybrid activities since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such incidents have included suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and unauthorized drone flights. There is currently no evidence establishing who was responsible for the Luxembourg sightings. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Dual citizenship means Germany now in competition for talent
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.33
When Jürgen Klopp named his oversize squad for Germany for the upcoming international break, a number of other national team coaches will have taken notice. Among them was Mohamed Ouahbi, of Morocco, who lamented that he had already had Eintracht Frankfurt striker Younes on his radar since last season. "He had a profile that interested us. I spoke to him on the phone and explained the Morocco project to him — without making any promises," Ouahbi said. If the 23-year-old Ebnoutalib sees any action in the UEFA Nations League over the next couple of weeks, as expected, he will be cap-tied to Germany — and ineligible to play for Morocco in the future. Several players with multiple options This is by no means a unique situation. A growing number of Germany players in recent years have held another citizenship through their parents and thus have other options for their international careers. This applies to several members of Klopp's 44-man squad. Vitaly Janelt, whose father moved to Germany to play professional ice hockey, is also eligible to represent Czechia. Bambase Conte's father is from Guinea, and Josha Vagnoman has an Ivorian father. Finn Dahmen has an English mother, while fellow goalkeeper Noah Atubolu has Nigerian roots. Said El Mala's father hails from Lebanon, and Brajan Gruda's father was an Albania international. All of them were all born and raised in Germany and have represented the country at youth levels. Vagnoman has even made two senior international appearances for Germany, though he has yet to play a competitive match. High number of dual nationals There are also numerous established Germany players who could have chosen another nation. These include Felix Nmecha (England), Kevin Schade (Nigeria), Jamal Musiala (Nigeria, England), Karim Adeyemi (Nigeria, Romania), Jonathan Tah and Serge Gnabry (Ivory Coast), Malick Thiaw (Senegal, Finland), Nathaniel Brown (USA), Nadiem Amiri (Afghanistan), Aleksandar Pavlovic (Serbia), Waldemar Anton (Russia), Yann Aurel Bisseck (Cameroon), and Ridle Baku (DR Congo). The men's national team reflects German society as a whole: According to the Federal Statistical Office, 21.8 million of the country's approximately 83 million inhabitants have an immigrant background. "More than 40% of children in Germany under the age of 5 have a migration background. This means they will later have the option to play for one country or the other," Andreas Rettig, the managing director for sport for Germany's DFB football association, told DW prior to the 2026 World Cup. This forces the DFB to compete with other countries for talent for its national teams — and it hasn't always been successful. A prime example is Ibrahim Maza of Bayer Leverkusen. Born and raised in Berlin to an Algerian father and a Vietnamese mother, he holds not just German but also Algerian and Vietnamese citizenship. The midfielder possesses many qualities that could help Germany, yet two years ago he opted to play for Algeria and represented the "Desert Foxes" at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and the 2026 World Cup. Germany also missed out on Paul Wanner and Can Uzun. Wanner, a top prospect developed at Bayern Munich, chose Austria—his mother's home country. Can Uzun of Eintracht Frankfurt has been playing for Turkey since September 2024. Both took part in last summer's World Cup. International break a cap-tying opportunity Had Maza, Wanner and Uzun chosen Germany instead, each of them would have stood a good chance of being named to Klopp's first squad as national team coach. With this international break featuring four instead of the previous customary two matches — and to see as many players as possible, Klopp named two squads for this break — every player selected has a strong chance of getting playing time. The upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures — away against the Netherlands, home and away against Greece, and at home against Serbia — are all competitive matches. This means that, even if it wasn't the primary factor in his selection process, over the next couple of weeks, Klopp could wind up cap-tying a few more players for Germany. This article was adapted from German.

item.title: Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.19
The 191st Munich Oktoberfest officially opened at noon on Saturday, with the city's new mayor tapping the festival's first barrel of beer. The annual ceremony, which takes place at midday, is always an eagerly awaited event, with no beer served until it has taken place. Relief for Munich's new mayor Green Party politician Dominik Krause needed just two strikes of the mallet for his first ceremonial tapping before handing the first liter mug of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). Krause had practiced for the occasion with a personal tapping coach. The 36-year-old had said he hoped to open the barrel with two or three strikes. His predecessor, Dieter Reiter of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), had set a high standard by regularly opening the first barrel with two strikes. After the tapping, Krause then presented the first liter of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). It's the first time Söder has received the ceremonial drink from a Green mayor. Cannon fire then signalled that beer may be served throughout the festival grounds. Revelers race to grab drinking spots Crowds had earlier rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened at 9 a.m on Saturday. Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets. Organizers briefly held back sections of the crowd at the entrance, allowing people onto the grounds in stages and preventing a more concentrated rush. How big is Oktoberfest? More than 6 million people are expected to attend the 191st Oktoberfest, which runs for 16 days until October 4. The festival, known locally as the Wiesn, features beer tents, fairground rides, traditional Bavarian food and live music. Opening day was expected to bring blue skies and temperatures of up to 24 degrees Celsius (75 degrees Fahrenheit). How much is an Oktoberfest beer? A 1-liter (1.8-pint) beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17–$18.27) this year. The average price has risen by 2.38% compared with last year to €15.61. An analysis found that the average price has almost quintupled since 1985, when a liter of beer cost about 6.25 deutschmarks — equivalent to €3.20 at the fixed conversion rate. Consumer prices have risen by about 120% over the same period. Edited by: Karl Sexton If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.97
Billionaire investor and philanthropist Warren Buffett is stepping down as the chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, the holding company said Friday. Buffett is 96 years old. His son, 71-year-old Howard Buffett, will succeed him in the role as chairman. 'I have never felt better about what comes next' "I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett told shareholders in a message. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. This is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next." This comes after Buffett stepped down as the firm's CEO last year, with Greg Abel succeeding him in that position. "Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values — both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," Buffett said. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against." In a statement of his own, Abel said "the culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian." How did Buffett lead Berkshire Hathaway? Buffett purchased textile firm Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 and transformed it into a multinational conglomerate holding company with a worth of over $1 trillion (€871 billion) in terms of market capitalization. Most of the companies worth more than $1 trillion are in the tech sector. Buffett's investment prowess has led to Berkshire beating the S&P market index in 40 out of the past 60 years. Berkshire owns whole businesses in sectors such as insurance and energy; the firm also owns restaurant chain Dairy Queen. Moreover, Berkshire invests in companies such as Apple, Coca-Cola, Chevron and Bank of America. According to Forbes, Buffett is the 10th-richest person in the world today with a net worth of $144.7 billion. Buffett grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, where Berkshire is also headquartered. Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett has embraced a folksy public persona and is enamored with American staples such as McDonald's breakfasts, Dairy Queen sundaes and Coca Cola. Edited by: Zac Crellin Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: German-Russian relations at freezing point
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.60
For many years, Germany and Russia had a perfect partnership. Russia supplied cheap energy, which helped German industry succeed in exporting its goods worldwide. This partnership began in the early 2000s. On the German side was Chancellor Gerhard Schröder from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), followed later by Chancellor Angela Merkel of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Their counterpart was Vladimir Putin. Even when Russia annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in 2014, business continued as usual. It was then that the agreement to build Nord Stream 2, a direct gas pipeline between Russia and Germany designed to bypass Ukraine was signed. At the time, other European countries and the US warned that the pipeline would provide Russia with powerful leverage. The warnings proved to be correct. On February 24, 2022, Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. German hopes for a stable European order, the democratization of Russia, and the continuation of its lucrative business model were shattered. How could so many German politicians be so wrong? "Shortly before the invasion, the widespread view was that there were no rational grounds for an attack on Ukraine, because the economic, military, and political costs to Russia of starting a war would be far too high," Russia expert Mario Baumann of the German Council on Foreign Relations told DW. "People [in Germany] had projected their own rationality onto Russia. They underestimated the regime's imperialist and revisionist ambitions." After that, nothing in the bilateral relationship was ever the same again. Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) spoke of a Zeitenwende (epochal shift) in foreign and security policy, in the days after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine began. Since then, the German armed forces have expanded. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the following year, "We must become capable of waging war," a statement that critics still say was an escalation of tensions. Germany ended its decades-long energy dependence on Russia and shut down Nord Stream 2. In September 2022, the pipeline was blown up. The Federal Prosecutor's Office suspects a Ukrainian group was responsible. A series of EU sanctions have long since reduced Russian-German trade relations to a minimum. Government cooperation in culture, science, and education has also practically ceased to exist. A new low point While the German government under Scholz initially hesitated to take dramatic steps on military aid to Ukraine, Friedrich Merz, then the leader of the opposition, stepped up his rhetoric. "Ukraine must win the war. Russia must lose the war," he said in 2024 as leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in parliament. In 2025, as chancellor, he then spoke of Russia's "economic exhaustion," which the West must "help bring about." But that has yet to materialize. To this day, Russia has shown no serious willingness to compromise. Meanwhile, Germany is feeling the consequences of its military support for Ukraine. The German government has long suspected Russia of being behind cyberattacks on government agencies and critical infrastructure. So when an armed drone was discovered and defused in August 2026 at Leipzig Airport close to Ukrainian transport aircraft — which transport a large portion of the military aid to Ukraine — the government was certain: For the first time, it publicly blamed the Kremlin. A Russian cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn were closed, which the German government said were being used as espionage centers. Moscow responded by closing the Goethe Institutes and the German consulate in St. Petersburg. Putin has denied Russian responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling it a "serious mistake" to blame Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov even described the accusations as the "beginning of a real war." But Baumann says: "We shouldn't give in to the fears being stoked, because they are part of Russia's strategy to weaken Germany and Europe." AfD wants to resume relations with Russia The German government is also facing domestic pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) has made gains in regional elections and is rising in the national polls. The AfD would prefer to end support for Ukraine and normalize relations with Russia, including deals on oil and gas. High fuel prices in Germany have only made the issue more explosive. "German support for Ukraine worries many people," said Sven Leunig, political scientist at the University of Jena in Thuringia, following the election in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won the September 6 election by a landslide. However, he noted, "it is less a fundamental rejection of the support itself than a reaction born of fear. People want to 'stay out' of the conflict so as not to be drawn into it more deeply themselves." In the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, 42% of respondents believe military aid to Ukraine has gone too far. "If public support weakens over the long term, the government will eventually have to respond," says Leunig. Carry on or change course? So far, the German government is sticking to its course, as Merz made clear once again following the AfD's election victory. But opinions on how to deal with Russia and the war in Ukraine differ not only among politicians but also among political scientists and experts. Johannes Varwick of Halle University in Saxony-Anhalt believes it is long past time for a change of course: "German and European policy toward Ukraine resembles a mix of platitudes and wishful thinking," Varwick told DW. "It is high time for a course correction, and Germany should exert pressure on Ukraine to move closer to the latest American proposals, which aim for a compromise and could thus possibly bring about a political solution." Baumann, on the other hand, argues: "Supporting Ukraine remains the best investment for safeguarding German and European interests. The government has recognized this and should stick to this course and continue to communicate it as such." However, it is important that Berlin act in concert with its European partners. The war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than World War I. And there is no end in sight. Hopes that Russian-German relations will return to the way they used to be seem illusory for the foreseeable future. This article was translated from German.

item.title: France: Macron orders defense against Russian hybrid attacks
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.45
French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday highlighted the threat of Russian hybrid attacks and called for measures to protect key infrastructure. "The Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," Macron said, adding that he had asked "the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure." The plan would also involve protecting the "most sensitive" defense industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks. What else did Macron say? Macron said that France would continue supporting Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 and vowed to respond to Russia's shadow attacks. "This will not go unanswered," Macron said, without elaborating. "The intention behind it is to intimidate us and to derail the effort to support the Ukrainians. The consequence will be the opposite," he added. "We are not intimidated, because we know that what is at stake today in Ukraine is our security." EU states concerned over Russian hybrid threat The comments come amid increasing concern from European states that Russia is ramping up hybrid threats that include acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and possible drone incursions. Poland, Germany and Denmark have in recent weeks accused Russia of being being a series of drone incursions as well as instances of sabotage, arson, and surveillance of defense facilities. Moscow has also been accused of planning to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport. On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU needed a mechanism similar to NATO that would allow for a better response to hybrid attacks blamed on Russia. The EU chief cited incidents such as an attempted drone attack on Leipzig last month that German authorities have attributed to Russia. Von der Leyen said the EU needed to develop "a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents ... that fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security." Edited by: Zac Crellin Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Iran's 'new Hezbollah:' How powerful are the Houthis now?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.39
After recent events in Yemen, a small crowd marched down an Iraqi street holding signs that were almost identical. The signs said, "death to America" and insulted Saudi Arabia and Israel, with slogans very similar to those used by the Houthi rebel group in Yemen. The men in the Iraqi video are members of one of Iraq's Shiite Muslim paramilitary groups. Both the Iraqi paramilitaries and the Houthi group in Yemen are part of what is known as the "axis of resistance" in the Middle East, groups supported by Iran that often act at Iran's behest. Other members are Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza. After the US and Israel began attacking Iran in late February 2026, "axis of resistance" members responded by targeting sites associated with the US or Israel. But up until recently, the Houthi group had remained more or less on the sidelines. However their latest military campaign, which has seen Houthi fighters take further control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea, "sets up conditions to establish… an axis of resistance-controlled body of water as part of [an] effort to assert control over regional oil exports," US-based research organization the Institute for the Study of War explained last week. Iran and the US are already fighting for control over the Strait of Hormuz, another important waterway for oil exports and trade. In Iran, hardline regime-supporting newspapers published laudatory articles about the Houthis' territorial gains. The gains "greatly increased the weight of Sanaa [the Yemeni capital, under Houthi control] as a branch of resistance in the ongoing regional war," one of Iran's most conservative newspapers, Kayhan, wrote. Supporters of the Iranian government have been holding nightly gatherings in major cities across the country since the US-Iran war began and this week, at the 200th such event, crowds chanted "you are my soul, O Yemen!" The 'new Hezbollah?' This was the kind of praise previously lavished on another "axis of resistance" group, Hezbollah. But Hezbollah's armed faction, degraded by recent Israeli attacks and the loss of their base in Syria, looks less intimidating these days. And the Houthis now appear to be doing things that Hezbollah couldn't — for example, bringing down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet this week using a missile the group said it modified itself. Hezbollah has managed to shoot down large Israeli drones and has targeted fighter jets but never hit any. Could the Houthis be taking Hezbollah's place as the potentially most important and possibly even more dangerous force in the "axis of resistance?" The Houthis haven't had to fight Israel — they are too far away geographically. "But I think they [the Houthis] have become more valuable than Hezbollah could ever be," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House. "Of course, Hezbollah had decades of experience and was the one who built the Houthis' capacity over years. But the Houthis have now exceeded them." The Houthis are "increasingly performing a similar strategic function for Iran [as Hezbollah] and in some respects a more useful one," confirms Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London. "Hezbollah gave Tehran deterrence against Israel from Lebanon. The Houthis give Iran leverage over Saudi Arabia, Israel and global shipping," he told DW. "So I think their strategic importance to Tehran has risen sharply as Hezbollah has come under much greater pressure." Al-Muslimi notes that Houthi leaders, including current chief Abdul Malik al-Houthi, were devoted fans of Hezbollah leader Nassan Hasrallah, killed by Israel in 2024 and seen as a hero because of his organization's part in forcing Israel to withdraw from Lebanon in 2000. "You can see how he even tries to imitate Nasrallah in his speeches," al-Muslimi, who co-founded the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told DW. "And now Abdul Malik al-Houthi has more leverage than Nasrallah ever had." Nasrallah was once seen as "the fixer" for the "axis of resistance," he notes, a leader who acted as a conduit between the different factions, giving orders to Iran-supported fighters in Lebanon, Yemen and Syria. Al-Houthi is likely moving into that role now, al-Muslimi believes, pointing to the fact that one recent attack on Saudi pipelines actually came from Iraqi axis members. Iranian proxy or ally? Unlike with Hezbollah though, there's still disagreement over exactly how much control Iran has over the Houthis. A review of press by the Iraq-based outlet Amwaj showed that while Iranian media celebrated Houthi gains as a victory for Iran's "axis of resistance," Houthi-run channels were more focused on their own fight against Saudi Arabia, which has set up a blockade on Houthi-controlled territories. Krieg believes the biggest difference between the Houthis and Hezbollah is autonomy. "The Houthis… have their own leadership, ideology, domestic constituency and territorial project," he pointed out. "Tehran can enable them, arm them and benefit from their actions, but it cannot necessarily switch them on and off at will." Other observers note that in the past, the Houthis moved ahead with certain military plans despite objections from Iran. Tehran has also denied having anything to do with this latest campaign. But al-Muslimi isn't so sure. He says that over the past two years, the Houthis have come a lot closer to Iran. There are regular reports of Iran sending sophisticated weaponry to the Houthis. In July, sources inside Iran told Reuters news agency that Iranian leadership had discussed with the Houthis having them close off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. "Even as Houthi leaders frame their actions in local terms, their alignment with Tehran appears to have tightened," Allison Minor, previously the US deputy special envoy for Yemen, said in Foreign Affairs magazine last week. Can the Houthis be beaten? The one thing everyone does agree on is that the Houthis will be hard to rein in. Past military campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the US and other countries have failed. Sanctions and economic pressure tend not to impact either because the Houthis don't operate within the international financial system. The Houthis take a "zero sum approach," al-Muslimi explains. They collect taxes but don't pay salaries or provide public services; everything goes towards fighting. The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test. That's very different from Hezbollah: The Lebanese group also has a political branch at home, and offers social welfare services. It must also carefully balance relationships with other demographic groups in Lebanon. The Houthis have none of those restraints. "They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," al-Muslimi says. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice." Which, he suggests, makes them potentially more dangerous than Hezbollah, especially for Yemeni civilians. "They are a major international threat," he agrees, "but they're the biggest threat ever to the idea of a republic and citizenship in Yemen's history." Edited by: Carla Bleiker

item.title: Ebola: DR Congo outbreak not slowing, MSF warns
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.26
Medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Friday that "the race to contain the Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is far from over." MSF issued the comments after DRC's government and the World Health Organization (WHO) had both spoken of signs of slowing transmission in some places earlier this week, prompting some relatively upbeat headlines and coverage. The outbreak, which was first declared in mid-May but likely started spreading several months earlier, is the largest in DRC's national history and the fastest-spreading on record anywhere. What did MSF say about the outbreak and its spread? MSF — which has around 1,700 staff in the DRC, most of them Congolese — warned that while the observed spread was slowing in the initial epicenter of Ituri province, the number of new cases being recorded had not fallen on a national level. "Assuming the outbreak is under control because some Ebola treatment centers are admitting fewer patients would be a mistake," MSF's emergency coordinator in DRC Anthony Kergosien said. "The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving: South Ubangi has become the seventh affected province, while North Kivu now accounts for nearly half of all newly confirmed cases, with test positivity rising sharply in recent days," Kergosien said. He added that undetected chains of transmission had already taken hold in the worst-hit areas, and said "the spread of the outbreak into new areas with even weaker preparedness and response capacities poses a serious risk." Which factors helped DRC's worst Ebola outbreak spread so fast? The deadly virus has killed more than 3,500 people from more than 7,200 confirmed cases since the outbreak was declared in May, according to WHO figures. Based on the recorded data, the quality of which is gradually improving with the passage of time, the 2026 outbreak is the fastest-spreading in history. It's also the largest in the DRC's history, second in overall size only to the West African outbreak of 2013-2016. The West African outbreak needed around two and a half years to reach a caseload of more than 28,000, not four months to pass 7,000. Many of the cases have been concentrated in hard-to-reach areas in DRC's north and east long plagued by instability, poor health infrastructure and a series of armed groups. Medical staff strikes have also contributed to problems fighting the spread, as have dearly-held funeral and burial traditions that pose the risk of post-mortem transmission as people bid their loved ones farewell. The outbreak also involves a rare Ebolavirus strain, Bundibugyo, meaning that existing treatments and vaccines — several of which are prohibitively expensive by the standards of the region anyway — were untested and of uncertain value against it. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.21
Recent months have seen a rise in Russian drone attacks on locomotives, stations, and infrastructure. More than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026, according to Oleh Holovashchenko from Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator. On September 16, a train traveling between the capital Kyiv and Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine was struck by a Russian drone. The day before, another train in the Volhynia region was attacked near the Polish border. Two days earlier, a drone had struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn border crossing, just two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Polish territory. Nobody was injured, as Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring system had previously detected the drone and the train had been evacuated about 15 minutes before the attack. At the time, CIA Director David Petraeus was on another train at the same station. A separate train carrying several former European leaders, including ex-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers had stopped at the station earlier the same day. The Ukrainian authorities believe that this diplomatic train was the drone's actual target, but the train departed earlier than scheduled. 'Putin's terror' against Ukrainian logistics Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives since its full-scale invasion of Ukrainebegan in 2022. More than half of these attacks happened this year, according to a post on the social media platform X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. He said that part of "Putin's terror" was to destabilize Ukraine's logistics system. The minister called on international partners to tighten sanctions against Russia further and to provide financial assistance to the Ukrainian government so that it can procure more locomotives that are compatible with Ukraine's Soviet-era broad-gauge (1,520 millimeters or almost 5 feet). "Ukraine's railway keeps the country moving," Sybiha said. "It enables the rapid evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, transports essential cargo, and keeps grain and other critical goods moving across the country." Russia was specifically targeting locomotives because they were ideal from a technical point of view, said Vasyl Shevchenko, a former Ukrainian deputy transport minister. "A locomotive's thermal signature is very large, and almost impossible to miss," he told DW. "The impact of a strike can be devastating, because 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of explosives in a diesel locomotive can cause several metric tons of fuel to detonate and completely destroy it. A strike on an electric locomotive will cause a fire that can paralyze an entire stretch of track. That's why they are targeting areas where the loss of a single train can bring traffic to a standstill." Shevchenko also pointed out that locomotives could not be replaced immediately but had to be ordered in advance and this could take years. Ukrzaliznytsia says that negotiations are underway with various international partners and a contract has already been signed with the French company Alstom. These locomotives are scheduled to start arriving next year. In the meantime, trains are also being repaired. "While our top priorities used to be saving on costs, providing comfort to the train crew and making sure the trains were attractive, these have changed," Holovashchenko said. "What is most important today is that the locomotive is technically sound and ready to transport passengers and freight." But he added that it was difficult to protect trains against Russia's weapons. Zelenskyy intensifies protection of critical infrastructure On September 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief to discuss strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and logistics. The key issues were contracts for the production of protection systems for critical infrastructure and logistics, but he added that there were plans to expand the electronic warfare component and reorganize the operation of designated mobile fire teams, as well as strengthening air defense lines. Zelenskyy said that decisions on backup logistics routes in frontline regions were also being made, and he had instructed Ukraine's Finance Ministry of to find additional funding for the logistics sector. Ukrzaliznytsia sets up monitoring centers According to Holovashchenko, Ukrzaliznytsia is also seeking its own answers to the new challenges and there are plans to develop early detection systems. He said that a monitoring center had been established to track the movement of drones and trains all over Ukraine. The fact that Russia has started to use jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are much faster than previous models, has made it more difficult and given less time to respond. "We used to wait longer to stop trains so we could evacuate passengers," Holovashchenko said. "Now, there are more precautionary stops. But in general, we try not to go into areas where there is a potential danger." Buses are deployed in areas of particularly high risk and the "train plus bus" concept is being expanded in cooperation with military authorities. Passengers are also being given instructions on how to respond in the event of an alarm and advised to try to get further away from a station than previously. The most difficult question remains where they should be evacuated to. Holovashchenko said that the monitoring centers had access to maps showing all the shelters along train routes and that dispatchers always tried to stop trains near them, but this was not always possible. He said that train personnel were receiving special psychological support to help passengers. Ukrzaliznytsia is currently preparing for winter, while working with foundations and other donors to ensure that trains will be heated. Evacuations will be even more difficult as temperatures drop. "This is no easy task. We're providing blankets, rain jackets, and equipment so that train staff can supply passengers with at least the bare necessities if their train comes to a standstill in the middle of nowhere because of a snowstorm, Holovashchenko said. This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

item.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.60
Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing. The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26. "This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone." How the disaster unfolded The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years. The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow. Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours. How did this happen? It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events. Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades. Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it. Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable. In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean. An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater. Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure. A disaster beyond adaptation Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one. Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation. The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in. "When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said. "Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come." Edited by: Sarah Steffen

item.title: Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.25
Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland. After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat. "Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday. "Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war. Poland prepares response Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details. "Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening. On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe. "There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security. Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time. Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack. Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train. "Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do." "The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said. Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster. Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine. Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest. But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion. In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up." Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment." "In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added. Polish media sound alarm The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm. "Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line." "These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote. Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door." "The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski. Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat. "We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.05
Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media. A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK. She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain. What did Greer's husband say about her death? Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life." Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness. He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together. "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated. Who was Bonnie Greer? Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers. Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings. She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career. Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer. Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities. She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play. Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time". Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time. She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School. item.title: The Emerging U.S.-China Détente
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 5.29
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump met in Beijing, in May, they agreed that their two countries should build a constructive relationship of strategic stability. Although many observers in Washington responded skeptically to this new framework, dismissing it as empty words, it marks the first time in more than a decade that China and the United States established a consensus about how to define the relationship that leaders on both sides broadly recognize. Strategic stability does not refer to nuclear détente; rather, it suggests a new equilibrium in which both sides can avoid further deterioration of the relationship and even expand cooperation where interests align. Leaders in Beijing do not expect that this new framework can resolve most of the differences between China and the United States or that it can stop new frictions from emerging. In June, for example, the U.S. Department of Defense placed more Chinese companies—including private-sector giants Alibaba, Baidu, and BYD—on its list of firms involved in civil-military fusion activities, barring the Pentagon from contracting with them. In retaliation, China placed ten U.S. entities on its dual-use export control list, which prevents any company from supplying them with items that have the potential for both military and civilian use. But Beijing hopes that a consensus built around strategic stability can help China and the United States manage their differences more effectively and that it will prevent the worst outcomes: military conflict or a new cold war. So far, ongoing friction has not derailed the overarching consensus established in May. By keeping sanctions and countermeasures relatively limited, Beijing and Washington have avoided dangerous escalation and kept the relationship moving forward. The goal of the new diplomatic framework between Beijing and Washington is a pragmatic one. It aims to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations rather than try to achieve an unlikely grand bargain that would resolve all conflict. It also represents a changing approach in Beijing to dealing with the United States. Unlike in the past, when China rejected U.S. frameworks focused on competition, it is now willing to recognize that the fundamental nature of U.S.-Chinese relations is competitive. Allies or partners, after all, would not set strategic stability as the overarching goal of their relationship; only competitors, or even adversaries, need to do so. Beijing’s willingness to accept a formulation to manage, rather than exclude, competition shows that it is gaining confidence and seeing itself more as an equal to Washington. Adopting this confident mindset could lead China to act with more restraint in its dealings with the United States—which could in turn bring a further degree of calm to the relationship. It now appears plausible that bilateral relations have turned a corner and entered a more stable phase. Although fundamental challenges remain that could cause new turbulence, the peak tensions of the past eight years may well be receding. The upcoming leaders’ summit in late September, when Xi and Trump are scheduled to meet in Washington, is a chance to further move the relationship forward. The two leaders can now add more concrete measures to support this new framework of strategic stability, including taking steps to reduce economic friction, increase military-to-military communications, improve crisis management mechanisms, expand citizen exchanges, and offer reassurances about Taiwan, thereby defusing tensions that could escalate into potentially catastrophic military conflict. With Xi and Trump likely to meet again multiple times in the next few months, the new framework is the first chance in years to lay the groundwork for enduring stability in bilateral ties. BEYOND STRATEGIC COMPETITION For a long time, leaders in both Beijing and Washington sought to define the bilateral relationship in terms of some kind of partnership. In 1997, when Chinese leader Jiang Zemin visited the United States, Beijing and Washington announced aims of “a constructive strategic partnership oriented toward the twenty-first century.” In 2005, the George W. Bush administration urged China “to become a responsible stakeholder” in the international system; Chinese leader Hu Jintao responded in 2006 that the two countries were not only stakeholders but “should also be constructive partners.” But between 2009, when President Barack Obama and Hu agreed to “steadily grow a partnership” to address common challenges, and the Trump-Xi summit earlier this year, the countries’ leaders were unable to reach a new consensus on how to position the relationship. The United States moved away from seeing the relationship as a partnership earlier than China did. During Trump’s first term, the United States began to define U.S.-Chinese relations in terms of “strategic competition.” At first, China tried to accept the competitive element in bilateral relations. Beijing acknowledged that some competition was inevitable while hoping that the relationship could remain positive overall. But as U.S.-Chinese relations deteriorated sharply in the final year of Trump’s first term and continued to worsen into the Biden administration, Beijing began to see “strategic competition” as a narrative designed to foreclose China’s rise. It felt that the U.S. approach threatened its development prospects, leading Beijing to push back more forcefully against the concept. In July 2022, during a phone call with President Joe Biden, Xi told his counterpart that it was a mistake to make competition the defining feature of the relationship. To policymakers and analysts in China, the framework of strategic competition turned all U.S.-Chinese interactions into something akin to the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. They saw the United States’ actions such as export controls on semiconductors as concrete manifestations that the United States was trying to suppress China, to undercut its political system, and to constrain its development. Although official statements from Washington discussed bilateral ties in terms of cooperation, competition, and confrontation, in practice competition and confrontation snuffed out any potential for cooperation. After almost a decade in which China rejected and criticized strategic competition, transitioning to a relationship of constructive strategic stability reflects Beijing’s recalibrated assessment of both countries’ positions and roles in the international system, as well as the new realities of U.S.-Chinese relations. China is looking at bilateral relations from a position of greater equality and with more confidence, and it is less anxious that competition will undermine its national development prospects. Instead, Beijing believes that competition can be effectively managed without presenting an existential threat. MORE THAN ONE MAN Whether strategic stability succeeds as the basis of a new phase in U.S.-Chinese relations depends on whether it is rooted in the personal wills and agendas of Trump and Xi or it arises from structural forces that are more powerful than any individual leader. Many observers in both Beijing and Washington view the emerging consensus as a contingent result of the interests of the two men currently in charge. Trump, for instance, has taken it upon himself to change the direction of U.S. policy. His unexpected turn toward embracing a more stable relationship with China coincides with other unexpected turns in his second-term agenda, including adopting a cold and even hostile attitude toward European allies and launching a war against Iran despite frequently decrying U.S. military involvement overseas. But these shifts also obscure more durable structural factors in the U.S.-Chinese relationship that have pushed the two countries toward more stability, and which make it more likely that the new diplomatic framework can survive. The current rapprochement is the fourth time in the past eight years that a period of tension between China and the United States has given way to an announcement of some kind of stable state. Ongoing friction has not derailed the consensus established in May. After China and the United States first aggressively confronted each other on trade and technology, culminating in the trade war in 2018, the two countries reached the Phase One trade agreement, in January 2020, which stabilized ties. The COVID-19 pandemic, which broke out soon afterward, severely inflamed tensions, sending the relationship to its lowest point since before U.S. President Richard Nixon first visited China, in 1972. In November 2022, Biden and Xi met in Bali and announced that they wanted to restabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, but just months later, in February 2023, recriminations over a Chinese object floating over the United States—described by Beijing as a civilian meteorological airship and by Washington as a spy balloon—interrupted such efforts. That November, Biden and Xi smoothed over ties for a third time at their San Francisco summit. This set the tenor of relations until April 2025, when Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs spawned a new trade war. Across this period, the United States went through three different presidential terms under both Democratic and Republican administrations, yet U.S.-Chinese relations repeatedly swung back to a stable state. Structural factors independent of any individual leader’s views encourage stability in the relationship. This includes the prohibitive cost of total economic decoupling and the catastrophic consequences of potential military conflict. Put differently, since the beginning of Trump’s second term, it has become clear to both sides that the bilateral relationship is simply too big to fail. The two sides occupy such important positions in global and international affairs, each with enough power to cause enormous damage, that neither wants to see the other become an enemy. The intense clashes between China and the United States over tariffs and rare earths in 2025 revealed that each side could exploit the other’s vulnerabilities, reminding them both that the two countries are highly interdependent and need to act prudently in an economic confrontation. Moreover, as nuclear powers, Beijing and Washington are aware that they cannot afford the prospect of a steadily deteriorating relationship that increases the risk of military conflict. If U.S.-Chinese relations again become more volatile after the next U.S. president takes office, it will test the resilience of the relationship. Yet the structural forces at play are unlikely to have changed. Even if future American leaders announce a new approach to the U.S.-Chinese relationship, therefore, in the end it is likely that they will come to the same realizations as their predecessors and seek stability. TANGLED UP IN RED Other critics argue that the consensus on strategic stability is, at most, a temporary truce. In their view, both sides will use this time to shore up their weaknesses, seek new sources of leverage, and prepare for a future confrontation. The United States could find alternate suppliers for the rare-earth elements it needs, for instance, and China could find new sources of semiconductors or develop its own advanced chips. But despite intense trade and geopolitical frictions, global supply chains have proved more resilient—and more deeply intertwined—than most observers anticipated. U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology have fragmented global supply chains, but they have not severed them. Attempts to route production away from China have merely dispersed Chinese enterprises across a wider array of countries and partners while retaining their irreplaceable role in most supply chains. In 2023, for instance, as the Biden administration sought to limit U.S. battery supply chains’ reliance on China, Chinese firms such as CATL actually expanded their market share by increasing production and supply networks in Asia and Europe, and CATL licensed its technology to Ford to produce batteries on U.S. soil. Even if China and the United States patch up their vulnerabilities in chips and rare earths, respectively, the two countries’ broader connections ensure that other areas of interdependence will remain. The rapid development of technologies such as artificial intelligence will make it particularly difficult for either the United States or China to eliminate the other’s sources of leverage. New technologies create new vulnerabilities. With the possibility of artificial general intelligence on the horizon, the frictions in the U.S.-Chinese relationship are unlikely to be concentrated in the same fields and to manifest themselves in the same ways as today. The likelihood of either China or the United States creating what Chinese martial arts novels call an “iron shirt”—a training regimen that makes someone impervious to blades and bullets—is very low. As both countries acquire more powerful, faster, and less predictable technological capabilities, what is needed to preserve stability is likely to change. Attempts by either side to achieve an overwhelming advantage or to ensure absolute security could instead heighten the other’s insecurity and intensify bilateral competition, ultimately forcing both countries to accept some mutual vulnerability and a different strategic equilibrium. The two countries are already realizing that they will have to manage the enormous challenges that AI presents, especially safety risks, whether through joint action or parallel efforts. U.S.-Chinese relations have stabilized four times over the past eight years; this also means that, viewed from the opposite perspective, the relationship has repeatedly devolved into confrontation. With each successive clash producing renewed grievances and hostility, a palpable fatigue has set in on both sides. Lowering their ambitions to the limited goal of stability makes it possible to dampen volatility, achieve tangible progress, and work with the reality of interdependence in more productive ways. THE EAST IS RISING One of the most significant changes underlying the acceptance of strategic stability is China’s growing confidence. When the first Trump administration began pushing for more decoupling, in 2018, many Chinese policymakers and citizens alike worried that escalating tensions with the United States would harm China’s progress and end the prospect of China developing into a stronger and wealthier country. In contemporary China, development is linked to openness: the more international cooperation there is, the faster technological development proceeds. The United States’ embrace of strategic competition challenged this basic premise. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which further drove countries apart and into blocs, made decision-makers and ordinary citizens worry even more. But after eight years of on-and-off trade and technology wars with the United States, China’s economic fundamentals have remained stable. Real estate markets are struggling and traditional industries are mired in distress, but high-tech industries have advanced by leaps and bounds and the manufacturing sector, particularly advanced manufacturing, has become stronger. China’s inability to obtain semiconductors from the United States has forced it to strengthen its own chip industry. The mainstream view in China now is that U.S. government restrictions on high-tech sectors have forced China onto a better path toward more self-reliance and innovation, rendering Washington’s containment policies ineffective and ultimately counterproductive. Structural factors have pushed the two countries toward more stability. China’s successes are mounting. In early 2025, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released a large language model that achieved near-parity with U.S. frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost. In April of that year, China successfully retaliated against Trump’s tariffs, forcing Washington back to the negotiating table. In those negotiations and later talks, China’s rare-earth dominance gave the country a chokepoint over U.S. supply chains. These episodes have increased China’s confidence and made its policymakers and strategists less worried about discussing competition as part of China’s relationship with the United States. Western commentators often believe that a confident China will become more assertive. The opposite is true. When China’s leaders believe that they can manage their external environment and that the country’s core interests and development prospects are not threatened, they are more willing to show restraint, engage in consultation, and focus on solving problems at home. In the 1990s and the first decade of the twenty-first century, for example, as China’s economy grew rapidly, it shelved disputes in the South China Sea with its neighbors. It was only after the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia,” when Beijing felt that the United States was uniting countries in the region against China, that it adopted a tougher approach to resolving disputes in the South China Sea. In 2026, a more confident China did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran, but instead quietly promoted peace talks behind the scenes. Likewise, now that China is less worried that the United States has either the intention or the ability to block China’s development prospects, it is more willing to accept a bounded competition with the United States. From a position of confidence, Beijing can engage the United States pragmatically on an issue-by-issue basis, looking to find specific policies to manage an inevitable amount of competition. A NEW BALLAST The fundamental requirement of the new framework of strategic stability is maintaining peace. That requires that the Chinese and U.S. militaries establish more mature measures for crisis avoidance, crisis management, and confidence building. The two sides can reduce the likelihood of conflict at low cost by setting up regularized military-to-military exchanges and fleshing out and expanding existing maritime and air encounter protocols. They can also coordinate on issues related to outer space, such as preventing near-earth-orbit collisions, regulating space traffic, and building trust around their respective strategic intentions. Addressing concerns in more politically sensitive domains, such as nuclear weapons and the military application of artificial intelligence, will require a more gradual approach. Although the Trump administration has shown heightened interest in discussing nuclear arms control with China, Beijing believes that formal negotiations are premature because of the vast disparity between U.S. and Chinese nuclear capabilities. Progress does not need to be confined to top leaders. More exchanges at all levels between China and the United States are another low-cost way of solidifying a framework of strategic stability. The United States and China could increase opportunities for engagement by easing visa restrictions and reviewing and reducing sanctions, removing entry or exit bans, and limiting other travel restrictions on institutions and citizens, as well as allowing more of the other side’s news media to operate there. Trump could take the opportunity to explicitly remind Chinese students that they are welcome to study in the United States, and Beijing could formulate clearer policies to guide scholars and students about the boundaries of acceptable research in China and guarantee openness, safety, and academic freedom for any scholarship falling outside those boundaries. Taiwan remains a dangerous flash point that could set back progress toward a relationship of strategic stability. Taiwan is the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict between China and the United States, and pressure is increasing. Continued rule of the island by the more pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, combined with Beijing’s strong desire to advance national unification and uncertainty about what kind of Taiwan policy the United States is going to pursue, has inflamed tensions on all sides. A new equilibrium can emerge only through an arrangement in which no party is completely satisfied yet each can live with the result. The goal is to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations. As long as Beijing believes that cross-strait integration remains achievable, it has no reason to resort to military force. The United States could shift its declared policy to align more closely with Beijing by recognizing Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan or by explicitly opposing Taiwan’s independence, which would reassure Beijing that the prospect of “peaceful reunification” remains viable. This would allow China and the United States to reach a consensus that realizes the U.S. objective of a peaceful resolution to the dispute yet also maintains the ability of the people in Taiwan to preserve their political and social systems. By keeping the prospect of peaceful reunification alive, the core concerns of all three parties can be accommodated as much as possible. Washington’s decision to pause $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, reached during Trump’s May summit with Xi, defused a rapidly escalating flash point in U.S.-Chinese relations. But it presents a new challenge to the nascent framework of strategic stability. Although Beijing certainly welcomed the delay, the pause has also raised expectations for future U.S. policy regarding Taiwan. Should the Trump administration eventually resume arms transfers—an outcome deemed likely by most Washington observers—Beijing will fiercely oppose the move, potentially jeopardizing the strategic stability framework. This scenario represents a concrete and salient threat that both countries must manage in the period ahead. A relationship of strategic stability is not a concept that one side imposed on the other or that will benefit Beijing but hurt Washington. It is the result of joint efforts by both countries, which makes it a rare opportunity. The next step is to build out this basic framework, breathe life into it, and make it sustainable. The September summit and additional scheduled leaders’ meetings this year offer a timely window of opportunity to make further small steps toward solidifying this baseline of stability. Some believe that this goal is too modest. But if two major powers such as China and the United States can keep fluctuations in the relationship within a manageable range and avoid any kind of war, it would be far more than a modest achievement.
