item.title: The Case for Letting China In
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.40
Industrial policy is back in fashion in the United States. As fragile global supply chains and a weakened industrial base present growing economic and national security risks, policymakers in both parties have embraced energetic efforts to rebuild the country’s industrial capacity. With interventions such as the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, Washington has made historic commitments to strengthening the United States’ technology and manufacturing base, which is becoming increasingly important to the country’s economic success and ability to defend itself. As director of U.S. President Joe Biden’s National Economic Council, I helped to design and drive this shift. Initiatives to revive domestic capacity are a necessary response to real dangers. But more and more, American leaders are seeking to support industry at home in ways that are counterproductive. In particular, they are growing hostile to foreign investment. Many policymakers fear that foreign investors could steal sensitive data or gain dangerous leverage over U.S. companies or critical infrastructure. Their aversion is most pronounced with respect to China but has been trained on allies and partners as well. It applies not only to cases of foreign ownership of U.S. companies but also to joint ventures, the licensing of foreign intellectual property, and other arrangements in which a foreign company shares its knowledge or resources. Stephen Miran, the chair of the president’s Council of Economic Advisers, has suggested imposing fees on foreign holdings of U.S. assets, including those owned by allies. Senators Tammy Baldwin and Josh Hawley have introduced bipartisan legislation in the U.S. Congress that would tax foreign capital inflows outright. At the federal, state, and local level, those in power are taking steps to shut global capital out of the United States and prevent American enterprises from harnessing the latest advances in data storage, critical mineral processing, and chip-making. This is a troubling and ultimately self-defeating strategy. Of course, the U.S. government should mitigate the risks of foreign investment. But today, its screening regime is overzealous. The United States is undermining its own industrial policy by denying itself the tools to become competitive globally in crucial sectors. What the country needs is a new framework for selectively encouraging investment from abroad to match its industrial ambitions. The U.S. government’s existing policy toolkit isn’t designed to take on this task. Washington has an elaborate apparatus for saying no to inbound investment but few ways of getting to yes. An improved system would welcome foreign capital and know-how while maintaining transparency, protecting U.S. data, and ensuring that Americans have control of companies when it matters. The fact is, the frontier of knowledge for many industries lies outside the United States. The federal government must get better at weighing the risks and rewards of foreign investment to take advantage of that expertise. THE HIGHEST FORM OF FLATTERY Throughout its history, the United States has used foreign knowledge and tools for its own gain. At the turn of the nineteenth century, for example, the country’s military readiness depended on a fledgling domestic gunpowder industry. Washington could no longer rely on its single foreign supplier, Britain, against which it had just fought a revolution. Supported by a significant French investment, the chemist Éleuthère Irénée du Pont brought French expertise in advanced manufacturing techniques to the United States, establishing a company in 1802 that would quickly become the biggest purveyor of explosives to the U.S. government. The firm, DuPont, remained at the center of innovation in U.S. chemical and materials production for centuries. Foreign knowledge has proved invaluable in more recent cases, too. In the early 1980s, when U.S. car companies were lagging behind their Japanese competitors, General Motors and Toyota jointly reopened a shuttered GM plant in Fremont, California. By bringing in state-of-the-art Japanese manufacturing systems, the companies transformed a failed factory into the most productive auto assembly plant in the United States within two years—while largely retaining the same American workforce. The methods GM picked up from Toyota are now standard across U.S. auto manufacturing. The CHIPS and Science Act was designed to replicate these and other successes, but with semiconductors. American lawmakers understood that creating a domestic chips industry would require investment and expertise from companies such as South Korea’s Samsung and the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Under the 2022 law, Washington issued grants and loan guarantees to firms, domestic and foreign, to build semiconductor fabrication plants in the United States and to train American workers in chip making, which is notoriously difficult to master. The act also funded the National Semiconductor Technology Center, which facilitates technology transfers and shared research and development between domestic chipmakers and foreign ones operating in the United States. Companies that accepted money from the U.S. government were barred from expanding advanced chip capacity in China. The United States is undermining its own industrial policy. If efforts to encourage foreign investment from U.S. allies and partners have proved contentious at times, deciding how to treat investment from the United States’ biggest rival, China, has been downright incendiary. More than any other government in history, Beijing has aggressively wielded the tools of economic statecraft. Its theft of intellectual property and enormous subsidization of domestic industry, combined with Washington’s longtime complacency, have hollowed out manufacturing capacity in much of the world and created dependencies on China for many critical technologies. It is easy in this context to conclude that the United States must keep out Chinese investment. The analyst Oren Cass, for instance, recently argued that allowing Chinese companies to invest in the United States would be “an unforced error of world-historic proportions” because it would cede dangerous economic influence to Beijing. But if the United States wants to produce more advanced goods, it needs to remain open to foreign investment, including from China. Indeed, China itself followed the same playbook beginning in the 1980s, luring U.S. companies to its shores with cheap labor, low taxes, and access to its vast domestic market. Much of China’s expertise can be linked back to foreign companies that set up factories in the country—expertise that Chinese firms later used to outcompete their foreign counterparts. In 2018, for example, China convinced Tesla to establish manufacturing facilities in Shanghai by offering cheap land, low-interest state loans, tax breaks, and permission to fully own its plant. Chinese automakers absorbed what they needed from Tesla and applied those lessons to propel the domestic electric vehicle sector forward. China is now at the forefront of many critical technologies, including electric vehicles and energy storage. Gaining access to that knowledge via foreign investment is, in many cases, the only way for the United States to catch up. BRAIN GAIN Chinese companies are already doing business in the United States in limited cases. In 2023, Ford announced a multibillion dollar plant in Marshall, Michigan, that will manufacture batteries for electric cars with technology and know-how licensed from China’s largest battery maker, CATL. Ford fully owns the facility but has a long-term agreement that enables it to train its workers on CATL’s core technological processes. Eventually, Ford could use the expertise learned from CATL to design and produce its own batteries without Chinese licenses. What Ford is doing in Michigan provides a model for an ambitious industrial strategy: encourage investment, work with foreign firms when necessary, and learn by doing. The partnership was possible because of a novel intellectual property-sharing arrangement with CATL that entailed licensing but not foreign ownership of the facility. In many other cases, however, presidential directives and onerous regulations get in the way of deals that have similar potential to strengthen the U.S. industrial base. U.S. presidents from both parties have used their authority under the Defense Production Act to block major foreign direct investments out of fear that sensitive American technology and data will fall into the wrong hands. The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), the government body that reviews deals that could threaten national security, has become backlogged, difficult to navigate, and overly cautious. When the committee identifies a concern with a foreign company’s proposed investment, the firms involved frequently cannot negotiate a resolution within the statutory deadline and end up starting the process from the beginning. In 2024, applicants withdrew and refiled nearly a quarter of all notices. Filings have declined because the lengthy process discourages companies from even trying. In other cases, the problem is a lack of regulation altogether. CFIUS, for example, generally screens only those transactions in which foreign entities seek to acquire an interest in an American business. If a foreign company, say, wants to license out the use of its equipment, there is no formal review process through which it can receive approval. Such an arrangement falls into a gray zone, vulnerable to a political attack. Congress spent years threatening to disqualify Ford’s electric vehicle plant in Michigan from receiving a tax credit and investigated it for national security risks, in part, because the plant was not subject to any review process. DUE DILIGENCE To encourage American companies to pursue strategic foreign partnerships, the U.S. government must cut red tape and stop reflexively rejecting investment. It should treat capital from close allies as different from capital from countries of concern such as China, Iran, and Russia. It should also develop new systems to review and greenlight new models of foreign investment and partnership. When it comes to allies and partners, CFIUS should simplify its process. To reduce the number of U.S. companies and foreign investors that need to apply for approval, it ought to expand its list of countries whose firms are exempt from this requirement—currently just Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to include Japan, South Korea, and countries in Europe. Low-risk deals, such as investments in software companies whose only critical technology is routine encryption, should be exempt from filing, and there should be more rapid approval for pre-vetted investors. Most important, CFIUS should change how it judges the deals it does review. It should, for instance, analyze transactions on the basis of whether a foreign adversary could plausibly exploit the investment to harm the United States, instead of fixating on the investor’s nationality and business affiliations. The committee must also change its risk calculus. Today, the body can approve foreign investments in U.S. companies only by certifying that there are no unresolved security concerns. That means even a deal that would benefit national security overall cannot be approved if doubts linger about any single component of the arrangement. If resolving those doubts is impractical, the deal dies altogether. In other words, CFIUS only takes risk into account, not opportunity. Congress should replace this standard with one that lets the committee approve investment deals that are, on balance, in the national security interest. U.S. companies need more options for entering partnerships with foreign firms. For more risky investments, such as those by Chinese companies, the U.S. government should adopt a model similar to the Defense Department’s Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence program, which polices foreign control over defense contractors. The framework allows critical U.S. industries to benefit from foreign investment while guarding against foreign access to American secrets and foreign influence over key industries. Consider BAE Systems. The defense firm is wholly owned by a British parent company, yet it employs roughly 35,000 Americans, generates close to $13.6 billion in annual sales, is among the Pentagon’s largest suppliers, and is deeply involved in classified projects. This arrangement is possible because, under FOCI, a special agreement restricts the parent entity’s control over BAE Systems. The company has a separate U.S. board dominated by American directors with security clearances, and firewalls shielding technology, products, and programs from the foreign parent company. The arrangement gives the United States another major contractor competing for Pentagon work, tens of thousands of domestic manufacturing jobs, and access to British technology and capital. The British parent company, for its part, gets to profit from the world’s largest defense market. Meanwhile, the risk of leaks remains relatively low. Today, the FOCI regime applies only to companies that do business with the U.S. government on classified contracts. A system based on this program, however, should also be used to assess the risk and opportunity of foreign investments in companies that don’t need security clearances but could pose national security risks, such as those that make advanced chips, batteries, drones, or critical software. The Department of Commerce, which has already started negotiating arrangements with semiconductor companies that resemble those the Pentagon reaches with defense contractors under FOCI, could oversee an expanded system immediately under existing authorities (some of which were granted by the CHIPS Act). But Congress should codify the department’s authority to review and request adjustments to deals involving foreign adversaries. In practice, a firm contemplating an acquisition, joint venture, or licensing arrangement would submit a proposal to the Department of Commerce, which could add safeguards to the deal before issuing its approval. The goal is to give American companies more options for entering partnerships with foreign firms, with safety measures tuned to the specific risk presented by the investment. When the risk is that sensitive information may be leaked, a new FOCI-based system might allow foreign ownership as long as the parent company’s access to sensitive technology, data, and day-to-day decisions is severed through proxy boards, security agreements, and cleared American directors. When the foreign firm holds expertise the United States needs but is based in China or another country of concern, the right template may look like the Ford plant in Michigan, where an American company retains operating control but benefits from foreign ingenuity. Under such a system, the government would no longer default to rejecting deals but act as a creative problem solver. NAYSAYER NO MORE Establishing new pathways to approve foreign investment will not be easy. The politics of blocking these transactions are well entrenched in both parties. Regulators are so afraid of approving a deal that leaks sensitive technology or hands adversaries control over a key company that they err on the side of restricting access to knowledge, money, and production capability from abroad. The way to calm those fears and bring in productive foreign investment is to execute foreign deals competently. The Trump administration has treated announcements of major foreign investments as ends unto themselves but has shown little appetite for building a process to encourage safe deals with foreign companies. Democrats should embrace openness to foreign investment but improve on the practical application of that philosophy by championing legislation that institutionalizes a better and more transparent method for vetting agreements. With a system that approves the right kind of partnerships, the United States can gain the experience it desperately needs to revitalize its industrial capacity. From du Pont’s gunpowder to Arizona’s semiconductor factories, the United States has always become stronger not by walling itself off from the world’s know-how, but by making that knowledge its own. item.title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.18
Separated from China by a roughly 100-mile-wide strait, Taiwan relies on its navy as the first line of defense against a potential invasion. It must be able to prevent an assault by a Chinese force carried across the Taiwan Strait in large amphibious ships. Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet, both as visible symbols of state power and as tools for signaling resolve in the face of Chinese coercion, and Taiwan’s current shipbuilding plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large and expensive new ships. Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack. China has invested in cutting-edge intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (collectively known as ISR), as well as electronic warfare systems, drones, and missiles. Taiwan’s large surface ships are now a liability. But Taiwan has an advantage: these same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives. Taipei can take advantage of this mismatch by replacing its destroyers and frigates with a greater number of smaller surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial wave of Chinese strikes and remain capable of attacking a Chinese invasion fleet. The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates. These large ships are impediments to the radical transformation of the Taiwanese navy that the Chinese threat requires. Building ships of this size with stealth features and defense systems to survive a battle in the Taiwan Strait would be prohibitively costly; without these features, they would be too vulnerable to play a major role in the navy’s primary wartime mission of denying a Chinese invasion force the use of the Taiwan Strait. Efforts elsewhere to build similarly capable ships have proved costly and difficult. The U.S. Navy’s Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capabilities needed to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters. In comparison, the spending on Taiwan’s entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually. Rather than spend resources on large ships, Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait. Combined with current plans to build shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with antiship missiles, and eight submarines, Taiwan can create a dispersed and hard-to-destroy defense system that can withstand Chinese attacks and repel a potential amphibious assault. SITTING DUCKS Large ships may be potent signals of national power, but they are relatively easy to target and politically costly to lose. When ships are fighting in narrow waterways under heavy surveillance, visibility quickly becomes a deadly liability. The sinking of a large ship can also have consequences beyond an immediate military setback. A highly visible and costly loss may make political and military leaders more cautious about risking additional warships as conflict continues. Major naval engagements over more than the last four decades suggest that any navy expecting to fight near an enemy’s coast should be wary of building its force structure around expensive, irreplaceable hulls. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, for example, showed how a single successful strike on a warship can constrain an entire surface fleet. Argentina entered the Falklands conflict with powerful ships, including the cruiser General Belgrano and the aircraft carrier Veinticinco de Mayo. But after a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war. In the Persian Gulf six years later, the U.S. Navy’s ability to combine surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons devastated Iranian naval forces during Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates. Whereas the Falklands War illustrated the political consequences of losing a major warship, Praying Mantis highlighted the danger for ships facing an adversary with a much more effective “kill chain”—the sensors and communications to detect, identify, track, target, and attack an opponent’s fleet. For Taiwan, the lesson is that the combat power of large warships is irrelevant if they cannot survive long enough to fight, and an early loss could have cascading effects on the navy’s sustained combat operations. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. Losing a smaller ship is less costly politically and militarily than losing a larger warship. In 2006, for instance, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit, which was operating in the waters off Lebanon. The ship had not been warned of the threat and had little time to detect and respond to a missile launched from shore 12 miles away, and some of its defensive systems were not fully activated. The missile killed four sailors and damaged the ship’s equipment, but the crew contained the damage and the Hanit limped home. The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes. Most important for Taiwan, Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign after Russia’s invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet. The campaign combined land-based antiship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones, and external intelligence to impose heavy costs on Russian naval operations in the Black Sea. These attacks helped push much of Russia’s fleet farther from Ukraine’s shores. The sinking of the flagship Moskva, for example, showed that even a ship equipped with layered air defenses was vulnerable to an adversary’s kill chain. The ongoing war in Iran reinforces this pattern: the United States and Israel severely damaged Iran’s surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats. The result is that Iran, despite losing much of its conventional naval power, has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz. SMALL IS BEAUTIFUL As these examples show, a less powerful navy does not need to control its coastal waters to deny a stronger adversary the ability to use them. In the Taiwan Strait, therefore, the goal should be “sea denial”: preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion. Achieving sea denial does not require Taiwan to abandon its surface navy. But it must build a different kind of fleet—one based on a greater number of smaller ships that can operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks, making the fleet more likely to survive an initial assault and repel an invasion force. Finland and Sweden are good models. Both countries must deter and defend against a larger, more powerful adversary—Russia—and they are simultaneously contesting sovereignty challenges to areas they control and preparing for potential amphibious attacks on their coasts. With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas. They have escorted away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodged diplomatic protests with Moscow. Both countries have extensive, sophisticated, and steadily improving surveillance, communications, and decision-support networks. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. In July, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te attended the commissioning ceremony of the navy’s eighth and newest missile patrol ship—a lightweight but heavily armed corvette built in Taiwan with an innovative catamaran hull that makes the ship faster and more stable—and four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan’s shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become. Sustained production would bring costs down, and each successive batch of vessels can incorporate new weapons, sensors, and uncrewed systems as they develop. Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion. These changes should be combined with a broader upgrading of Taiwan’s armed forces’ network of sensors, communications tools, drones, and missiles. Taiwan is already making some of these investments. Its most recent special budget and the next round of its naval plans strengthen the kill chain with maritime surveillance drones, upgraded command-and-control networks to direct and coordinate military forces, and artificial intelligence–assisted combat decision support systems. These are the essential building blocks of an effective system to deny China the ability to freely navigate the Taiwan Strait. But the same technologies that make Taiwan’s kill chain more effective also make its large surface ships susceptible to attacks. Only by restructuring and upgrading its surface fleet can Taiwan be ready for a potential invasion. A restructured Taiwanese surface fleet would also support plans to build eight new submarines, the first of which is already in sea trials. Submarines are slower but stealthier than corvettes. Missiles and drones launched from corvettes can disable ships by hitting them above the surface, and torpedoes launched from submarines can sink them. Changing its approach to its surface fleet is a key part of how Taiwan can make its other naval investments more effective. RIGHTING THE SHIP The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical. Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement, and visible proof of the government’s commitment to national security. By contrast, the public cannot see a warehouse full of drones or a mobile missile launcher hidden in the mountains. For navy leadership, too, the status quo is easier than pushing for major change. Taiwan’s destroyers and frigates, many of which are based on 50-year-old American designs, are well understood and therefore institutionally safe choices. But rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs. Moving away from familiar platforms will require political and military leaders to take risks and overcome the setbacks and criticism that accompany any institutional change. Production of Taiwan’s first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule. But such challenges are inevitable when dealing with complex vessels and should not derail necessary investments. Government and defense leaders need to sustain support for these programs and justify their importance to the public, even when opposition politicians criticize them. After years of stagnation and decline, Taiwan’s defense spending is finally increasing. Taiwan’s proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May (a significant sum, albeit down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch). But Taiwan will not be more secure if these resources are spent on outdated defense concepts and a small number of vulnerable large warships. The country needs a dispersed, agile, and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait. Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion. item.title: China’s Purges Are Working as Designed
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.94
For two decades, scholars believed that the main reason Chinese communist rule endured into the twenty-first century—whereas every communist regime in Europe collapsed—was that it had built sturdy, long-lasting institutions. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had moved away from the unpredictable personalist dictatorship of the Mao Zedong era and established the foundations of a modern state. It set term limits on its leaders, embraced collective leadership, and increasingly promoted officials based on merit, which made it resilient enough to bounce back from the external and internal shocks that had felled other socialist systems. Chinese leader Xi Jinping, however, has spent the past decade demolishing nearly every institution that supposedly kept the party strong. He abolished presidential term limits in 2018, hollowed out collective leadership, and has declined to designate a successor. Xi has also purged high-level officials at will, especially in the most sensitive domain: the military. In January, only months after party leaders expelled nine senior military officers, the country’s Ministry of National Defense announced that General Zhang Youxia and General Liu Zhenli—until that point the People’s Liberation Army’s most senior uniformed officer and top operational commander, respectively—had been placed under investigation. Since 2022, according to data compiled by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, the party has formally purged three dozen generals and lieutenant generals, and many more are conspicuously missing. In Washington, many observers see these purges as evidence of China’s weakness. They see a powerful leader consumed by suspicion and obsessed with maintaining his own grip on power. If the party’s strength were indeed based on the freestanding institutions that China had built in the post-Mao era, then Xi’s purges would be a warning sign of fragility and even a potential crackup. But the party has not shown any signs of falling apart. If anything, as these purges have continued, Xi and the party appear to have only gotten stronger. Far from weakening its rule, the way the CCP cleans its ranks can explain part of what makes it durable. A purge is not an event but a process—one that the party has run in nearly identical form for a century. It regularly targets, evaluates, and forces cadres to seek clemency to retain their standing within the system. The goal is to reform them rather than get rid of them entirely, which strengthens the party by encouraging obedience and dedication to the party’s cause. CCP leaders believe it’s working, too: Xi has embraced “self-revolution,” or continuous and permanent rectification, as the means by which China will escape the unhappy fate of the Soviet Union and other socialist regimes now residing in the dustbin of history. What could threaten the party’s longevity, then, is not the count of how many officials have been purged but the one problem that such a strategy cannot solve and can even make worse: how to handle succession. A regime of self-revolution will rise and fall on that question, no matter how hard it tries to avoid internal decay. CURE THE SICKNESS, SAVE THE PATIENT China’s history of purges predates the founding of the People’s Republic, in 1949. In some cases, as has been true in similar regimes, the CCP launches violent purges to remove cadres from its ranks. The type of purge now synonymous with the actions of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union aims at eliminating someone from the party, whether through incarceration, exile, or death. The victim of such a purge does not come back. Mao employed this tactic as early as 1930, when he executed more than 700 army officers in a show of total control. But what the CCP has also done, and what is unique to its continued rule, is not a purge in the traditional sense. CCP leaders often turn to a different method of discipline: rectification. Rectification aims to keep a person inside the party, even if sometimes at a greatly diminished status. Whereas the traditional idea of a purge seeks to eliminate enemies in the ranks (the Chinese term qingdang means to “cleanse the party”), rectification aims to retain and remold cadres while keeping them in the party’s orbit. Throughout its history, the CCP has sought to rectify cadres far more frequently than it has sought to eliminate them. In December 1929, in the village of Gutian, in Fujian province, Mao put forward a resolution called “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party” that asserted the party’s control of the military. The resolution also included clues as to how the party understood internal discipline: it described its targets not as enemies but as people who had deviations in their thinking. Cadres might suffer from ailments such as having a “purely military viewpoint” (a perspective untethered from politics), promoting ultrademocracy (a political system lacking party authority), and supporting individualism. Mao’s resolution treated each of these as a sickness that could sometimes be cured through a regimen of criticism and self-criticism in front of peers. And it attached a promise to the cure: if party members submitted to the process, the CCP would retain them rather than destroy them. In the northern Chinese area of Yan’an, where Mao and his followers set up a wartime base camp starting in the mid-1930s, leaders turned rectification into doctrine. Party membership exploded from roughly 40,000 in 1937 to 800,000 by 1940, which meant that almost everyone in the organization was new and not yet trustworthy in the eyes of party leaders. The Rectification Movement of 1942–45 was the solution. Every cadre wrote an autobiography, measured his or her life against printed self-examination outlines, confessed before his or her party branch or work unit, and was examined, graded, and sorted by the party’s personnel department. In February 1942, Mao summarized the approach in a famous line: “Cure the sickness, save the patient.” Rectification aims to retain and remold cadres. None of this was gentle. The Yan’an campaign was brutal: many were tortured, and thousands died. Subsequent campaigns were often even harsher. But Mao’s approach separated Chinese communism from its nearest relatives. Stalin quickly executed unreliable cadres, and Pol Pot sent them to mass graves. In China, in many cases, the strategy was to keep cadres and try to remold them while also building permanent files detailing their every mistake. The basic procedure remains nearly identical today. A person is singled out for deviating in some way and made to write an account of his or her shortcomings. The account is checked against what his colleagues say about him and against what the organization’s records (in that individual’s personal file) already hold. The cadre is placed on a graded scale of possible sanctions, ranging from no action at one end to expulsion from the party at the other. (Most sanctions fall in the middle, including issuing a serious warning or putting someone on probation.) When a verdict on how to deal with a cadre, official, or campaign target is issued, that person, if deemed to have confessed sufficiently, is kept in the party but on terms that are revocable and conditional on the political winds. And every piece of paper the process generates goes into the cadre’s official file, permanently. It is the process used in 1952 against a village storekeeper who skimmed off the top of procured grain. It is also the process used today for China’s Politburo, whose members—the country’s most powerful men—read self-criticisms aloud to one another once a year and have their confessions written down and permanently attached to their files following the same template that was used in Yan’an. Even as Xi has expanded the scope of who can be targeted, the machinery has not changed. The ongoing case of the purged military officers under Xi likely fits this model, too. Zhang and Liu have been placed under investigation, not shot, and there is a chance that they remain on the party’s books, even if they are saddled with a thicker personal dossier and given a meaningless post or sidelined from public life altogether. In 2023, the diplomat Qin Gang, for instance, was removed from his position as foreign minister; news investigations reported that he had kept his party membership but had been reassigned to a low-level desk job at the foreign ministry’s publishing house. And even if Zhang and Liu are expelled from the party, purging remains the exception rather than the norm, as has been the party’s long-standing practice. Of the 101 generals and lieutenant generals that the Center for Strategic and International Studies identified as purged or potentially purged, only 14 had been officially kicked out of the party as of February. SINGLE FILE Rectification rarely, if ever, changes cadres’ beliefs. Eighty years of evidence, much of it the party’s own, shows cadres parroting the scripts given to them, performing the required contrition, and then reverting to their earlier behaviors the moment the campaign ends. It is a process so ritualized that participants learn to say exactly what examiners want to hear. Yet the main goal of the process is not to reform belief but to create a document to put into a dossier on file. Such a file contains objective personnel data as well as observable assessments of a cadre’s political shortcomings. It is this paper trail that enables the regime to maintain discipline even if no cadres change how they act or think. For cadres and others subject to rectification, the process sorts who is in and who has fallen out of the good graces of party leaders. As cadres constantly jockey for status, a purge is exceptional and devastating. For most party members, surviving a rectification process with minimal punishment is grounds for relief (and often accompanied by a desire to recommit to a forgiving regime) combined with a sliver of fear that the next campaign is always just around the corner. Expanded to 100 million party members, this process produces an internalized discipline in each person that strengthens the organization’s grip on power. Each cadre wakes up every day knowing the dossier exists and that it can be used against them at any time. The permanent, standardized, reopenable record of every party member’s history, associations, and vulnerabilities is also an information system that gives party leaders immense power. Autocratic rulers need information to head off threats to their power; the CCP’s personnel file system, filled with information about the party’s cadres, is an irreplaceable channel of information for China’s rulers. Most cadres are willing to go along with the party’s wishes, but for the small minority that does not express the proper attitude in the face of a discipline campaign, the party can expel them or put them in jail, heading off any threat of revolt from within. High-level defection and dissent sometimes occur, but when they do they are rarely organized and quickly fizzle out. Such record-keeping might be expected to generate resentment among party cadres, but the process is designed to spread the blame and thus insulate Beijing from any backlash. There is no single person or entity that issues a rectification verdict. Instead, party task forces (known as work teams) are mobilized to draft the verdict, colleagues from their workplace endorse it, and then a committee at a higher level of administration ratifies it. It passes through enough hands in the process that authorship is aggregated and spread so that no individual leader or party entity can be said to be responsible. Even the cadre, through his or her own self-criticism, is a co-author in the verdict. Disciplining cadres with rectification is also a coordination device. The Chinese party-state is a sprawling network of bureaucratic agencies, regional power bases, and administrative offices that have their own interests and frequently have to bargain with one another. A rectification campaign is one of the few instruments that transcends these fissures. As with the party’s other massive campaigns, such as the one-child policy, cadres understand that compliance with rectification is mandatory and a high priority for leaders. Discipline campaigns offer unambiguous carrots and sticks, including leniency for cadres who show the right attitude and professional purgatory, even exile, for those who do not. Many cadres who normally benefit from taking advantage of the fragmentation in China’s political system know to drop everything else and go along with discipline campaigns, providing Beijing with a highly visible way to impose unified priorities and strengthen party control. WHAT DISCIPLINE CANNOT SOLVE Chinese history is rife with examples of once powerful dynasties weakening and eventually falling apart. To avoid this outcome, Mao’s solution was mass mobilization: only by letting the people supervise the government, he believed, would it not slacken. Xi’s answer, offered in 2021 and elaborated since, is the party’s self-revolution. In this framework, the cure for the party’s ills can only come from inside the party, not from any external force. Ongoing party rectification campaigns require all officials to discipline themselves, and the occasional outright purge of some cadres provides undeniable proof that failure to comply has consequences. It is the first time the party has explicitly located the mechanism of its own survival inside itself. The choreography has been equally explicit. In the fall of 2014, with investigations that felled two senior military leaders underway, Xi summoned some 400 senior officers to the same hall in the village of Gutian where Mao had issued “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party.” State media called it the “new Gutian conference.” In 2024, Xi convened the military to discuss political work (that is, ideological loyalty) at Yan’an—a clear reminder that the party sees a direct line from past rectification campaigns to its present strength. Beneath the symbolism is Xi’s fear that China could end up like the Soviet Union, whose own Communist Party, Xi believes, let its internal disciplinary mechanisms atrophy and thus was the architect of its own demise. Beijing believes that the purges and rectification must continue permanently if the party is to remain in power. Whether or not the analysis of Soviet collapse is accurate, the CCP’s continued strength suggests that the party’s method of disciplining cadres may indeed explain its durability. Xi’s purges should not be measured by how many cadres they ensnared but whether they continue to produce files, verdicts, and party retention that keep the party firmly in control. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. But what strengthens the party also weakens some of China’s instruments of power. Senior military commands sit vacant or are staffed by less experienced officers, and future officers learn that the safest career record is a thin one. When forced to choose, political control is always more important to the party than operational effectiveness. This is a tradeoff that the party has been willing to make for a century and will continue to make. And China’s method of purges cannot solve the danger of succession. Rectification produces no mechanism for choosing the next ruler—if anything, by ensuring that no subordinate accumulates independent standing, it makes the emergence of a credible successor even harder. Succession, not discipline, is where the system is weak. The older generation of CCP leaders, including Mao and Deng Xiaoping, overcame the challenge of succession by drawing on their unassailable authority as revolutionaries who had fought for the party’s survival, and subsequent leaders relied on the institutions—term limits, collective leadership, and regularized succession rules—that Xi has summarily destroyed. Xi has neither, which makes the succession problem especially acute. The moment to worry about Chinese stability is not when generals disappear amid an investigation, but when the man who reads their files begins to age out of the role without an answer as to who will follow. The CCP is not going to collapse: the file system exists precisely to prevent elite fracture, and it has worked. What is likely to emerge instead is a state that is militarily weaker and politically stronger than most assessments suggest. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. Beijing’s own theorists are watching this, too, because they know that even a well-engineered system of rectification that has kept the party strong for a century has no answer for an elite power struggle over who comes next. item.title: What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.58
What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree Ahead of January elections, Bola Tinubu is pulling out all the stops to stem insecurity. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Spending Spree Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has appointed Maj. Gen. Ibikunle Ajose as the new top army commander for the northeast, the epicenter of the country’s Islamist insurgency, after the previous leader spent less than two years in the role. The move is the latest in a series of military reforms ahead of January’s general elections, in which insecurity will be high on the list of voters’ concerns. Ajose’s appointment was part of a bigger reshuffling last week that involved 15 top generals. These redeployments, along with a major hike in military spending, are key to the government’s wider plan to stabilize bellwether regions before Nigerians head to the polls. Tinubu is seeking a second term as the candidate for the All Progressives Congress party and will face the same main challengers he came up against in 2023: former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, who is running under the African Democratic Congress (ADC), and former Anambra state Gov. Peter Obi, with the Nigeria Democratic Congress. This year, Abubakar and Obi initially joined forces to unseat Tinubu under an ADC-led opposition coalition, but the alliance fractured due to their competing ambitions. Observers are looking to see whether Obi in particular, who came in third in 2023, can translate the unprecedented backing he garnered from young Nigerian urbanites in the last election into rural support. Importantly, the public is paying close attention to how candidates intend to address widespread violence and kidnappings for ransom. A mass kidnapping of schoolchildren in Tinubu’s political heartland in the southwestern state of Oyo in May magnified the issue. More than 7,800 people were kidnapped in Nigeria between July 2025 and June 2026—a 66 percent increase from the previous year, according to a new report from risk advisory firm SBM Intelligence. Over that period, kidnappers received some $5.8 million in ransom money, three times that of the previous year. Boko Haram collected 90 percent of those payments, mainly from mass abductions. The insecurity has ripple effects across the country. For instance, many farmers have been unable to access their lands due to the threat of kidnappings, leading to food shortages and hunger, especially in the north. The “security question in Nigeria is closely connected to the economic one: An attack that closes a road, displaces farmers, or shuts a market very quickly becomes an issue of household income and food prices,” said Sekinat Ojeniyi of Africa Practice, a global risk advisory firm. On the campaign trail, Abubakar has pledged to end insecurity within one year if elected. His plan centers on cross-border military collaboration with Sahel nations and providing jobs for young people drawn to extremism. Obi has also promised to fix insecurity in one term through youth poverty alleviation and education. “You cannot create widespread poverty and expect peace,” Obi told Nigerian broadcaster Channels Television. Tinubu’s government, meanwhile, is injecting unprecedented amounts of money into defense in an attempt to address the issue. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Nigeria’s military expenditure surged 55 percent year-on-year to $2.1 billion in 2025. That figure is expected to double this year. With this money, Tinubu approved salary increases for members of the military last month. The massive investment also supports the largest expansion of the Nigerian military since the country’s civil war in the late 1960s. In July, Tinubu approved the creation of four new army divisions with a planned recruitment of 28,000 additional personnel by December. A new bill passed by Nigeria’s National Assembly in June would also allow states to establish their own police forces, putting less pressure on the federal police to secure dense forested communities that have become hideouts for extremists. “The government’s emphasis on manpower and personnel welfare makes sense, but more personnel and better pay do not automatically translate into greater security,” Ojeniyi said. “Kidnapping networks are highly adaptive and operate across state and local government boundaries, while the police, military, and intelligence agencies do not always have the same visibility or operational reach.” Meanwhile, many Nigerian and U.S. political observers have commended Tinubu for his handling of tensions with Washington, which has transformed the Trump administration’s divisive rhetoric about supposed Christian persecution in Nigeria into security cooperation. Beginning late last year, the United States deployed troops to assist with counterterrorism operations. (Most U.S. troops withdrew in July.) Although U.S. strikes in northeastern Nigeria in May killed a senior Islamic State leader, the mass abductions have continued. More than 600 people were taken from Nigeria’s north-central Niger state last month in an attack on a mosque. Although many Nigerians welcome his new security reforms, Tinubu will likely be judged on whether these last-gasp efforts a few months ahead of elections can stem the violence. The Week Ahead Wednesday, Sept. 16: The U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee holds a nomination hearing on ambassadors to Benin, Gabon, Kenya, and Togo. Wednesday, Sept. 16, to Thursday, Sept. 17: Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo meet in Geneva to discuss monitoring their cease-fire. Wednesday, Sept. 23: Morocco holds general elections. What We’re Watching Historic IPO. Africa’s richest person, Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote, launched the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering on Monday, floating 4.1 billion shares in his $20 billion oil refinery on the outskirts of Lagos on the Nigerian Exchange. The rush to buy shares briefly crashed many Nigerian investment apps. The move is expected to raise about $1.6 billion, which will fund Dangote’s expansion projects across Africa. Dangote Industries said it will use the investment to double production capacity, deliver refined products across the continent, and build another refinery in Kenya. The public offer closes on Oct. 13, and Dangote is reportedly eyeing a secondary New York listing in the future. Sahrawi citizenship. The Spanish parliament’s lower house approved a bill granting citizenship to Sahrawis born before 1977, when Madrid administered Western Sahara. The legislation will now go to Spain’s Senate. It marks the latest escalation of tensions with Morocco after thousands of migrants entered Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta from Morocco in late July. Rabat claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Western Sahara, and it has occupied about 80 percent of the latter’s territory since the 1970s. More than 170,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps in Algeria, which hosts the Polisario Front, a group fighting for Sahrawi independence. U.S. tech bid. The United States will lend nearly $100 million to Africell, the only mainstream U.S.-owned mobile network operator in Africa, as part of broader strategic investments to counter China in the region. Africell operates in Angola, Congo, Gambia, and Sierra Leone. The loan from the U.S. Export-Import Bank is part of Washington’s efforts to counter the expansion of China’s Huawei company in Africa. But the United States has a long way to go: Chinese firms are now baked into the continent’s tech infrastructure. For example, the three major smartphone brands in Africa—Tecno, Itel, and Infinix—are manufactured by China’s Transsion and have dominated the market for nearly two decades. Congo-Israel ties. Congo has revived plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem following President Felix Tshisekedi’s visit to the country earlier this month. Analysts consider the move an attempt to both court Israeli security support and get the United States to exert more pressure on Rwanda to stop backing the M23 rebel group in eastern Congo. Tshisekedi previously told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2023 that Congo would move the embassy, three years after Tshisekedi announced that he would appoint its first ambassador to Israel in more than two decades. Meanwhile, Tshisekedi faces mounting calls in Congo to resign over his attempts to implement constitutional reforms that could pave the way for a third term in office. This Week in Health The United States has announced that it will no longer fund Namibia’s HIV program after a final $45 million disbursement for the 2027 fiscal year, ending more than two decades of aid through the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, which has provided around $1.1 billion to Namibia since it was launched under President George W. Bush in 2003. The withdrawal follows Namibia’s refusal to give the United States unrestricted access to genetic data and pathogens, which it could then share with private companies and organizations without oversight from the Namibian government as part of Trump’s America First Global Health Strategy. Namibian officials cited concerns over sovereignty, national law, and patient privacy. Since pulling out of the World Health Organization in January, the Trump administration has pursued deals that would provide commercial access to African nations’ health data. So far, Ghana, Zambia, and Zimbabwe have rejected such deals, while at least 19 nations, including Nigeria and Ethiopia, have agreed to them. “We need to reserve our data, and no one has the right to get a sovereign state to be used for other things, except for the World Health Organization cabinet,” former Namibian Health Minister Richard Kamwi said in August. FP’s Most Read This Week - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan What We’re Reading Al-Shabab’s win. In Foreign Policy, Mohamed Gabobe reports from Mogadishu on how the U.S. withdrawal of support for the African Union peacekeeping mission in the country has severely jeopardized the remaining forces’ capacity to counter the Islamist group al-Shabab. The two-decade military intervention’s failure to quash al-Shabab—which has “has retaken nearly all the territory that it lost in a 2022-2023 Somali army campaign,” Gabobe writes—partly informed Washington’s decision. There “is no one other nation that can fill the United States’ void,” he adds. What’s in a map? On Sept. 4, the United Nations General Assembly voted to adopt a Togo-sponsored resolution to replace the traditional Mercator map with one that better represents Africa’s true size. Only the United States voted against it. In Foreign Policy, Howard W. French argues that this is just the latest example of the West being behind in understanding not just Africa’s geographic size but also its demographic weight. “Just as drawing up maps in ways that graphically diminish Africa does nothing to reduce Africa’s true dimensions, actively shunning African migrants will do nothing to change the hard demographic realities that will radically shape our collective future,” he writes. Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. item.title: What the BRICS Summit Meant for Brazil
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.01
What the BRICS Summit Meant for Brazil One year after hosting the event, is the country still shaping the bloc? Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Brazil sends its foreign minister to a BRICS summit in New Delhi, Guatemalans protest fuel price hikes, and Chile remembers a renowned documentarian. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Brazil sends its foreign minister to a BRICS summit in New Delhi, Guatemalans protest fuel price hikes, and Chile remembers a renowned documentarian. Brazil’s Balancing Acts at BRICS The BRICS leaders’ summit in New Delhi last weekend underscored how as the global order unravels, cooperation among the grouping deepens. Many long-standing BRICS demands, such as expanding the United Nations Security Council, haven’t materialized. But the bloc has steadily increased economic ties, including by launching its own development bank. BRICS members have long sought to reform the Western-dominated order, making their joint positions particularly relevant today. This year, the warring parties of Iran and the United Arab Emirates sent their president and crown prince of Abu Dhabi, respectively—marking the furthest international trip for Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian since the Iran war began in February. Brazil, a founding member of BRICS and the host of last year’s summit, has had a more difficult time steering the grouping’s priorities since it expanded from five to nine members in 2024. (Indonesia, the newest member, joined in 2025.) Brazil opposed the expansion, fearing a loss of cohesion with the addition of avowedly anti-West Iran. Like India, Brazil wants BRICS to be reformist, not revolutionary. Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira attended in place of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is in the midst of a reelection campaign. Last week, Vieira said Brazil believes “a multipolar world that promises peace and prosperity must not be confused with a world of spheres of influence.” In other words, Brazil wants a system of rules—not rule by the strongest. Brazil managed to keep some of its priorities alive in this year’s summit declaration. Notably, in the joint statement BRICS reaffirmed its support for the U.N. system and the Paris climate agreement—going further than the G-7, whose most recent declarations did not mention the climate pact. The summit’s endorsements are words, not actions, and some of the group’s members—most notably Russia—have flagrantly violated the U.N. Charter in recent years. But words still matter when both the U.N. system and climate action are under attack—and when the leadership of the U.N. itself is up for grabs. Russia may have only begrudgingly endorsed U.N. principles, but the fact that it agreed to acknowledge the legitimacy of the U.N. system at the BRICS summit bodes better for the world body’s future functioning than if Russia had blocked any mention of it. Brazil’s window to continue shaping BRICS in this direction may be closing as its general elections approach on Oct. 4. Far-right Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro—whose political camp has a record of U.N.-bashing and climate change denialism—has as strong a chance of winning as Lula, polls say. Upcoming Events Saturday, Sept. 19: Chile marks its Independence Day with a military parade. Sunday, Oct. 4: Brazil holds presidential and legislative elections. What We’re Following Support for democracy on the rise. In its latest polling, AmericasBarometer at Vanderbilt University has found increased public support for democracy in Latin America. The share of respondents across the region who agreed that “democracy may have problems, but it is better than any other form of government” rose to 65 percent, up from 59 percent in 2023. The report attributed this rebound in part to “positive changes in individuals’ lived experiences with crime, corruption, and economic well-being.” Support for democracy was higher among respondents who said their household income had risen in the last two years, who had not run out of food recently, and who had not been victims of crime. The survey also touched on geopolitics, echoing a recent Pew Research Center survey in finding that views of China in the region are improving relative to the United States. Washington has historically cast itself as Latin America’s partner in democracy. But under U.S. President Donald Trump, democracy promotion has largely fallen off the agenda. Panama Canal restrictions. A drought worsened by El Niño has Panamanian authorities planning to again reduce the number of daily ship transits through the Panama Canal. Starting in October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed each day, down 18 percent from August, according to a draft plan submitted to the legislature. Transit prices through the canal, meanwhile, are climbing to record highs. Prices shift with demand, and some Asian energy importers that typically source supplies from the Persian Gulf are now buying from the U.S. Gulf Coast instead, amid the Iran war—and those shipments must pass through Panama. Star filmmaker remembered. One of Latin America’s most celebrated documentary filmmakers, Chile’s Patricio Guzmán, died on Tuesday at 85. His three-part series The Battle of Chile chronicled the 1973 coup against Salvador Allende’s government and won international acclaim. Guzmán was already filming in Santiago when the coup occurred, having originally set out to document the implementation of socialism through the ballot box. His cameras captured the range of opinions on the street about that process—and the military intervention that brought it to a halt. Guzmán fled Chile immediately after the coup and managed to smuggle the film negatives abroad for processing, but the film’s cinematographer, Jorge Müller, was detained and disappeared during the dictatorship. Guzmán eventually settled in Paris, where he died, though he returned to Chile over the years to make several more films. “A country that does not have documentary films is like a family without a photo album,” he once said. Question of the Week Panama’s government is planning to create a new reservoir to ensure higher water levels in the canal. What is its estimated completion date? FP’s Most Read This Week - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - Trump Is Killing ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Over Taiwan by James Crabtree In Focus: Unrest in Guatemala Guatemala has joined the ranks of countries where economic fallout from the Iran war has spilled into political unrest. For more than a week, demonstrators angry over high gasoline prices have blocked highways across the country. Some gas prices topped $6 per gallon this week, Bloomberg Línea reported. Guatemalan President Bernardo Arévalo has tried to cap gas prices by decree, but the measure—which requires congressional approval—has been blocked by an opposition lawmaker. Arévalo says organized crime groups are encouraging demonstrations and has sent security forces to clear some roads. The protests are only the latest governance challenge for Arévalo, who was elected in 2023 on an anti-corruption platform but lacks majority support in Congress. Reformers had high hopes that Arévalo could reshape the political environment this year, when a complex process to elect a new attorney general and judges came due. But Guatemala’s moneyed establishment lobbied Trump to oppose Arévalo’s anti-corruption agenda and achieved some success. The Trump administration has worked to boost the candidacies of some would-be judges in Guatemala who had themselves been accused of corruption, the Washington Post reported in June. A U.S. State Department spokesperson denied meddling, saying U.S. policy is to respect “Guatemalan sovereignty.” After the election this year of a top judge who Arévalo has publicly said “lacks integrity” and amid the ongoing fuel price protests, public opinion of Arévalo has nosedived. He had the lowest approval rating among Latin American leaders in a regional CB Global Data poll taken last week. Correction, Sept. 18, 2026: A previous version of this newsletter misstated the rank of the official leading the Emirati delegation to the BRICS summit. item.title: The EU’s 28th State?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.82
The EU’s 28th State? European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floats making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca. The EU Looks Across the Pond Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca. The EU Looks Across the Pond Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. “We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seated on her left, von der Leyen outlined what such a future might look like, starting with an expansion of their existing free-trade agreement. Carney has been pitching such an arrangement to European officials for months. A Canadian official told The Associated Press last week that the two sides are discussing potential ties that stop just short of full membership. This could include allowing Canadian citizens to live and work in EU member states without needing a visa. An expanded partnership might also bolster collaboration in defense production, critical minerals procurement, economic security, and the development of artificial intelligence, among others. Canada wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc, Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said on Wednesday, adding that further discussions are expected to take place at the Canada-EU summit in October. Under EU regulations, the bloc requires unanimous approval to welcome new members. Although von der Leyen insisted on Wednesday that the Canada proposal is “not a partnership against anyone else,” the gesture comes at a time when both Canada’s and Europe’s relations with the United States under President Donald Trump are greatly strained. Last month, the White House imposed sweeping tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting “dollar for dollar” retaliatory duties on around 700 U.S. products. This was in spite of Canada being one of the United States’ largest trading partners; bilateral trade accounted for around $872.3 billion in 2025. Alongside a recent war of words between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford as well as the U.S. president’s repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state, Ottawa has begun to prioritize its relationship with the EU over what it once considered its closest partner. But not everyone in Europe appears thrilled with von der Leyen’s proposal. “Of all the third countries, Canada is one of the few that we all want to get closer to right now,” an EU diplomat told the Financial Times. “But even with them, we all know we have to be careful when you start talking about trade access and preferential treatment.” Notably, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify the bloc’s 2017 free-trade deal with Canada, citing several provisions that they argue favor Canadian investors. Whether the idea ever materializes, the fact that it’s being talked about at such high levels is a sign of what Carney called the “rupture in the world order.” The Canadian premier will take the stage on Thursday to address the European Parliament. Today’s Most Read - Trump Is Killing ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Over Taiwan by James Crabtree - Why My Kyiv Visit Worried Me So Much by Ravi Agrawal - Only China, India, and Russia Can End the Iran War by Amir Handjani What We’re Following Guilty of war crimes. Former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Wednesday after being found guilty of orchestrating war crimes during the country’s brutal fight for independence against Serbia in the late 1990s. He continues to deny any wrongdoing and is expected to appeal the ruling. The sentence was handed down by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a special tribunal at The Hague. According to the tribunal, Thaci oversaw the murder, torture, arbitrary detention, and abuse of alleged opponents, including ethnic minorities and perceived collaborators, while serving as the top commander of the since-disbanded Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA). “The vast majority of them were innocent civilians,” the tribunal said of Thaci’s victims. Thaci was sentenced alongside three other senior members of the ethnic Albanian KLA. Wednesday’s ruling is expected to heighten divisions between Serbians and Kosovar Albanians, the latter of whom often regard Thaci as a hero for his contribution to Kosovo’s independence. Clashes broke out between Thaci supporters and security at The Hague when protesters tried to walk to the tribunal. Incumbent Kosovar Prime Minister Albin Kurti condemned Wednesday’s ruling, saying, “While the verdict may have been formally pronounced in the name of the people of Kosovo, this hollow formula must not be conflated with the will of the people.” Mecca is under fire. Saudi forces claimed on Wednesday local time to have intercepted a Houthi drone targeting the holy Muslim city of Mecca the day before. According to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, the attempted attack crossed a “red line,” as it was “intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims.” The Organization of Islamic Cooperation similarly denounced the operation as a “heinous” assault. This is the first alleged Houthi strike aimed at Mecca since fighting erupted between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in July. The Houthis denied Riyadh’s allegations, with rebel spokesperson Hazem al-Assad saying, “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.” Both sides have escalated their assaults in recent days. On Wednesday, Saudi warplanes struck Yemeni territory, and Houthi troops attacked Red Sea port cities and Saudi military bases. Such assaults have exacerbated the already tenuous global energy crisis and injected further insecurity into the war-embroiled Middle East. Seeking peace. Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo resumed peace talks in Geneva on Wednesday, alongside mediators from Qatar, Togo, and the United States. The two-day session—the seventh meeting since the two countries signed a U.S.-brokered peace accord last year—aims to address continued fighting in eastern Congo between Congolese forces and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels. Less than a year ago, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame signed an agreement in Washington to end the deadly conflict. However, without M23 representatives in attendance—and Kigali maintaining that it does not support the rebel group despite U.N. evidence to the contrary—Trump’s self-proclaimed “historic” peace deal did little to actually quell the fighting; just days after the December 2025 signing, around 200,000 people fled renewed violence in the region. Since then, the situation in eastern Congo has continued to deteriorate despite repeated cease-fire attempts. During this week’s talks, Kigali is expected to seek assurances that armed groups will not be allowed to operate in Congolese territory, while Kinshasa asserts that foreign security forces have no right to Congolese soil. Odds and Ends A Paris court awarded Kim Kardashian 1 euro (or $1.15) on Tuesday as compensation for being the victim of an armed robbery in 2016. Kardashian was at the Hôtel de Pourtalès for Paris Fashion Week when a gang of eight thieves, six of whom are currently in their 60s or 70s, bound the media personality with zip ties and stole more than $6 million in jewelry; the so-called grandpa robbers were found guilty of armed robbery and kidnapping, among other charges, last year. Kardashian has since described the incident as “the most terrifying experience of my life” but only requested a symbolic 1 euro in restitution.
