item.title: Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.79
Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente Despite the thaw, India-China rivalry remains inevitable. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Modi, Xi Meet on BRICS Sideline Over the weekend, Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to India for the first time in seven years. Xi was in New Delhi for 24 hours to attend this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, where he held a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. An Indian Foreign Ministry statement said the two leaders pledged to strengthen commercial and cultural cooperation. A more striking readout came from Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who said that the bilateral meeting covered long-term, strategic issues and that Modi and Xi reached “the most important consensus” to be partners, not rivals. Beijing hopes the meeting will advance bilateral ties “without stagnation or backsliding,” Wang added. These are positive words for a relationship between major competitors—and one that was plunged into deep crisis after a deadly 2020 border clash in the Ladakh region. But an India-China rapprochement has been playing out for nearly two years. Xi’s visit marked the culmination, not the commencement, of India-China detente. Still, the extent of the thaw shouldn’t be overstated. Historically, India-China ties have had their moments, with ample heady talk and good optics. Invariably, fresh tensions have spoiled them; the two are destined to remain rivals by history, geography, and geopolitics. In October 2024, the post-Ladakh tensions began to ease with the inking of a new border agreement. India and China subsequently made pledges to resume direct air flights and bolster commercial cooperation. In March 2025, Modi said on a podcast that cooperation with China was “essential” for global stability. Contrary to some commentary, the detente began before U.S. President Donald Trump was elected to a second term and wasn’t sparked by his policies. But Trump’s tariffs, which have hit both India and China hard, and concerns about access to U.S. markets gave both sides a strong incentive to accelerate their rapprochement and especially to deepen trade ties. However, the reality is that continued India-China rivalry is all but inevitable. Both countries are both proud civilizational states and dispute claims to around 15,000 square miles of territory—equal to the size of Greece—along their shared border. They disagree on many other major issues, from Taiwan and Tibet to surveillance. Perhaps most significantly, China is a close ally of India’s bitter rival Pakistan. Last year, the Pakistani military used Chinese weaponry in air combat operations against India for the first time. Such challenges may seem surmountable, given what the India-China relationship has going for it. This includes their rock-solid trade partnership, shared interests, and considerable cooperation in global forums (including BRICS, but also the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.) Not surprisingly, India-China ties have often enjoyed periods of warmth—but ultimately a trigger, often a border provocation, has shattered that calm. In 2017, a few years after Xi and Modi were photographed smiling on a swing together, a 73-day military standoff on the Doklam Plateau plunged relations into crisis. The Ladakh clash came just months after another Modi-Xi summit in India. Though border tensions have subsided, territorial disputes still fester and occasionally flare. To be sure, there are plenty of reasons for New Delhi and Beijing to bury the hatchet. They want to ease tensions along their fraught border, create space for deeper commercial cooperation, hedge against Trump’s unpredictability, and remove a diplomatic headache from the BRICS grouping, which both capitals badly want to succeed. Ultimately, however, so many divergences and sources of lingering mistrust preempt the possibility of full-on rapprochement. Though an extended period of cooperation is possible, it’s likely only a matter of time before the very “stagnation and backsliding” that Beijing says it wants to avoid. What We’re Following Bangladesh passes 1,000 measles deaths. More than 1,000 people in Bangladesh have now died from the measles virus since March 15, according to the latest government figures, released on Sept. 9. The country is suffering the world’s worst measles outbreak; it has logged thousands of new cases this year, including nearly 60,000 between January and June alone. Nearly 20 million children have been vaccinated in Bangladesh since a new national inoculation campaign was launched in April. Health experts attribute the ongoing crisis to underestimations of how many children needed to be vaccinated—the target figure was 18 million, but experts say that a more accurate estimate is 22.6 million. The number of measles vaccinations in Bangladesh—both first and second doses—fell between 2019 and 2023, and this year’s national campaign was the first since one from December 2020 to January 2021, during the disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. A sudden change of government in August 2024 caused further vaccine interruptions. The current government, which took office in February, is working hard to ease the crisis. But it must grapple with not only the large number of children who still need to be vaccinated, but also economic stress and energy shortages that further complicate inoculation efforts. Thousands still missing in Nepal. Three weeks after a glacial collapse precipitated catastrophic floods in Nepal, more than 5,000 people remain missing. Authorities say they continue to search and are trying to provide information to families as soon as possible. But massive destruction—including 2.2 million tons of—has made search and rescue difficult. Authorities are now transitioning from search and rescue to relief and reconstruction efforts, with an eye toward the large number of people who lost their homes. The disaster leveled entire villages, submerged tunnels, and swept away hydropower facilities. Damage to roads and bridges has created additional complications. Nepal’s government said that the total estimated cost for reconstruction efforts will be $4.8 billion—around one-tenth of the country’s total nominal GDP. Sri Lanka signs labor accords with Thailand. This week, Sri Lanka and Thailand signed agreements to enable 10,000 Sri Lankans to work in the Southeast Asian country, with a focus on young workers and sectors including information technology and tourism. The Sri Lankan workers will receive equal rights and protections under Thai labor laws. The agreements address a key need for both countries: Thailand has a labor shortage, and Sri Lanka is looking to tap into a wider array of foreign labor markets. But the deal goes against a common pattern in Sri Lanka—and elsewhere in South Asia—in which young people go to the Middle East, Europe, or the United States for work. There appears to be a cultural factor at play. The Sri Lankan government believes cultural similarities between Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia will make for a smoother adjustment process—putting them in a strong position to be productive and send home remittances that are critical for the Sri Lankan economy. FP’s Most Read This Week How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan Under the Radar Last week, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said that it was not contemplating the use of military force against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Middle East. The statement came in response to speculation, fueled by a Turkish news report, that Pakistan was considering invoking the Mecca Agreement—the new mutual defense pact among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey—and joining a military operation with the Saudis against the Houthis. Houthi attacks against Saudi targets have escalated in recent days. Pakistan’s statement gives ammunition to critics of the Mecca Agreement—as well as a similar bilateral deal between Islamabad and Riyadh—who dismiss the accord as a paper tiger. In the last year, Taliban military operations have hit Pakistan has been hit multiple times; Saudi Arabia has been assaulted by the Houthis as well as direct Iranian strikes. At no time has Pakistan or Saudi Arabia intervened militarily to assist the other, though Pakistan has sent some arms and troops to Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Still, the two mutual defense pacts are mainly meant to focus on deterrence, which the signatories say the United States cannot provide sufficiently in the Middle East. In Pakistan’s case, the accords are meant to help advance key foreign-policy priorities, including playing a larger role in the security architecture of the region. Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. item.title: Emily Wilson Chooses Her Words Carefully
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.80
Emily Wilson Chooses Her Words Carefully The Homeric scholar’s new book on translation is bitingly smart. Is there a scholar better at promoting a book launch than Emily Wilson? Almost a decade ago she revolutionized the promotion of literary translation after the release of her first Odyssey translation. While literary media outlets were breathlessly heralding the arrival of the first-ever translation of the Odyssey into English by a woman, Wilson took to Twitter and showed everyone in granular detail how a translator works, with lengthy threads (still available here, even though Wilson has since deleted her Twitter account) detailing how the choices she’d made differed from earlier renditions. The threads combined transparency, accessibility, and humor, and they were hugely popular. Whether you came to them as a trained classicist trying to figure out which translation you wanted to teach, or as a newcomer to Homer wondering why another translation was needed at all, Wilson had something to teach you. Is there a scholar better at promoting a book launch than Emily Wilson? Almost a decade ago she revolutionized the promotion of literary translation after the release of her first Odyssey translation. While literary media outlets were breathlessly heralding the arrival of the first-ever translation of the Odyssey into English by a woman, Wilson took to Twitter and showed everyone in granular detail how a translator works, with lengthy threads (still available here, even though Wilson has since deleted her Twitter account) detailing how the choices she’d made differed from earlier renditions. The threads combined transparency, accessibility, and humor, and they were hugely popular. Whether you came to them as a trained classicist trying to figure out which translation you wanted to teach, or as a newcomer to Homer wondering why another translation was needed at all, Wilson had something to teach you. Those threads form the basis of the final, largest essay in Wilson’s essay collection, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea: Journeys Through Ancient Literature, released earlier this month. It’s a wide-ranging and compulsively readable book, comprising mostly revised and reworked review essays that she’s previously published but to which she added substantial new material. And once again, Wilson’s promotion strategy has been impeccable, intentionally or not, with her scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of the Odyssey, which begins by calling the movie “an entertaining way to hide from the high temperatures for a few hours” at which “[m]y teenagers had a good time.” That perhaps was the nicest thing she had to say. Wilson’s review briefly crashed the London Review of Books website and sparked a debate about whether she had been overly or inappropriately harsh with the film. Joyce Carol Oates may not have approved, but if you enjoy Wilson’s shade, you’re in for a treat, because that reviewer voice is the one that you hear in Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea. Readers might expect a book from one of our most prominent public intellectuals to sound like one of those large, endowed lectures universities host to show their commitment to educating the broader public—edifying, learned, entertaining, occasionally funny. Wilson’s book reads more like the kind of jokes scholars make to each other over mediocre wine at the reception after such events. You’ll learn a great deal about ancient literature from this book, and even more about the complexity of translation. But you’ll also learn a whole lot about what academics sound like when the (polite, erudite) knives come out with surgical precision. Wilson’s harshest critiques are reserved for translators who embellish or expand on the original text without adding anything useful or interesting, and she’s especially tough on those whose translations add length without bothering to sound like actual English. The most illustrative example, perhaps, is Wilson’s assessment of the opening of Daniel Mendelsohn’s 2025 translation of the Odyssey. Her analysis of Richmond Lattimore’s opening—“Tell me, Muse, of the man of many ways, who was driven far journeys”—is absolutely withering; by comparison, when she shifts gears to Mendelsohn, she is relatively brief and neutral. Mendelsohn’s Odyssey has many well-deserved fans, but two Odyssey translations coming so close together are bound to jostle for space like kids in the backseat of a car. Wilson ends her book with a set of 20 rules that guide her translation practice, and her second is that a retranslation (that is, a translation of a book that’s already been translated) is “fundamentally pointless” if it doesn’t bring something new to the text. It seems to be in this spirit that she chides Mendelsohn: “Fourteen words in Greek have become twenty-four in English, through the addition of words and phrases that correspond to nothing specific in the Greek, though they often draw on the phrasing of earlier English translations: ‘the tale’ is an addition also found in the 1929 translation by Herbert Bates; ‘off course’ is a nautical phrase, not corresponding to anything in the Greek but also found in Robert Fagles’ version.” She concludes with the most damning of praise, saying that Mendelsohn is “[f]ollowing Lattimore in his courageous defiance of contemporary English idiom.” Ouch, but you can’t say she doesn’t have the receipts. Whether or not you agree with her, Wilson is consistent and has a clear point of view, necessary ingredients for a critic (as I suspect Mendelsohn, a fine critic himself, would cede). Wilson’s rule no. 16 is, “Don’t try to please everyone. If nobody objects to any choice you make, your choices are too timid.” Nobody could claim that Wilson doesn’t live by that rule in any of her writing, including here. In the first essay of the book, “Tongue Breaks,” about the translation and reception of Sappho, Wilson is perhaps especially harsh on women writers whose only connection with Sappho is a shared gender. In the margins of a paragraph where Wilson wrote, Mary “Robinson aspires to sublimity, but, sadly, her writing sounds like this,” I scribbled to myself, “Is EW best when bitchy?” But I could almost hear Wilson’s own voice in my ear, scolding me, because that isn’t the right word. Wilson herself points out the dangers of importing entirely unnecessary misogyny into our interpretations, as generations of translators did with editorializing editions calling the 12 slave girls executed by Telemachus for sleeping with the suitors “sluts” or “whores”—a judgmental gloss completely missing in the original. So when I revisited my note, I considered crossing out my word choice and replacing it with something like “tart”—but no, that’s too archaic. Her critique is often too direct to be rightly called shade; saying her teenagers enjoyed a film is shade, but calling someone’s writing “turgid” is not. So what, exactly, should I call this voice? As I considered, I realized just how much reading this book had conditioned my eye to look for careful word choice—which, actually, feels like the bigger project of Wine-Dark Sea. Wilson sometimes seems to long for a slightly higher caliber of critics and readers of her translations. The seemingly most-quoted and argued-about part of her review of Nolan’s Odyssey is her claim that she “would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.” Harsh, yes, but consider what came right before it: “In at least one interview, he cited my version of the first line of the poem, ‘Tell me about a complicated man.’” My sense, reading this, was that Wilson was especially aggrieved by how an offhand comment by the director got twisted in the media to make it sound like Nolan had substantially based his script on Wilson’s translation. One can only imagine how infuriating it would feel for a translator as careful and considered as Wilson to have her name incorrectly attached to a film she thought was merely entertaining. If only the broader public had a better understanding of what goes into producing a translation and what makes different translations distinct! The answer to this lack of education is to read this volume. Throughout the essays in Wine-Dark Sea, Wilson walks the reader through the infinite number of tiny choices translators must make to try to produce a text that transmits not only the original’s meaning but also its tone, its pace, and its poetic effects into something that will mean something to readers. In her final essay, “Translating the Odyssey,” she delves into minute grammar questions, like the effect of replacing a Greek purpose clause with a participle. Elsewhere she goes further into broader questions of translating texts into very different cultures, especially in back-to-back essays about the challenges of translating ancient comedy, “Punishment by Radish” (a reference to the often-threatened ancient Greek punishment of sodomizing criminals with root vegetables) and “Ave, Jeeves.” In the first, she argues that the spirit of Aristophanes’ comedy is best expressed by the obscene lyrical fluidity of Cardi B and Megan Thee Stallion’s “WAP.” But some tropes may be harder or even impossible to bring to contemporary readers, like the brilliant slaves of Roman comedy, of whom Wodehouse’s Jeeves was the last accessible avatar. Wilson is entirely unafraid of a modern comparison—in one of my favorite passages in the book, she writes approvingly of the resonance between her “complicated man” and Avril Lavigne’s “Complicated.” Other modern parallels didn’t work as well for me. Several of the essays veer, in their final paragraph, into the briefest possible parable for modern times. In an essay about Demosthenes’ rhetoric against Philip, she concludes with a gesture toward Brexit and the election of Donald Trump to show how voters can still be swayed by an “enticing lie,” and an essay about Aeschylus’ Oresteia ends with a claim that it has something to teach us “[a]s we turn our attention to the angry voices of those who feel themselves marginalised in modern life.” Sure, but to my eye the continued relevance of Wilson’s analysis in our world was obvious without making such explicit nods. I wondered if she didn’t entirely trust the reader to get the point, which felt at odds with the confidence she displays elsewhere. But this minor quibble doesn’t detract overall from how much Wilson teaches readers about how to be educated readers of translations—lessons that, one hopes, some will absorb before Wilson’s newly announced retranslation of the Odyssey is released. It is difficult to overstate what an unprecedented literary event this is: Wilson has decided to retranslate from the ground up her bestselling 2017 translation, further iterating on her work along the guidelines she sets for herself in those final 20 rules. Wine-Dark Sea holds some clues for what that new translation might broadly look like; she notes that the translations she uses in the final essay don’t quite match her 2017 text. But it seems she’s also motivated by a desire for more nuance than she originally felt was possible. Her spare 2017 text matches Homer line for line but cuts Homer’s dactylic hexameter into English iambic pentameter, which often meant turning a 17-syllable line into a 10-syllable one, a choice that keeps that translation lean and swift. The new one, she says, will be longer, which will give more room to explore the ancient world. Wilson told the Associated Press that she feels she overused “slave” as a general term—including in the passage I mentioned earlier, the hanging of the slave girls—where she could have given more specificity that would shed light on the broad array of social roles held by slaves in the epic. Ironic, considering that nearly a decade ago her original translation was much-lauded for its willingness to call a slave a slave, where even other recent translations used euphemisms like servant. As always, Wilson is pushing us to be better readers of Homer—and of her. Donna Zuckerberg is the author of Not All Dead White Men: Classics and Misogyny in the Digital Age and the forthcoming memoir Antiquated. She founded and ran the award-winning online publication Eidolon from 2015 to 2020. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: How Americanness Overcomes Islamophobia
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.61
How Americanness Overcomes Islamophobia In Rozina Ali’s new book, four families grapple with the post-9/11 shift. In 1965, as the United States began to ramp up its war in Vietnam, President Lyndon B. Johnson authorized a massive increase of draft numbers. Ron Amen, the son of Lebanese immigrants in Dearborn, Michigan, was one of the young men called up to serve that year. When he received his dog tags before being deployed, he was surprised to find that, even though he had spelled out “Islam” for the bemused official in the recruitment office, his religion was listed as “none.” Amen’s dog tags offer an early glimpse of what would grow into the widespread anti-Muslim sentiment that journalist Rozina Ali traces in her new book, Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America. For generations, Muslims occupied a small and largely overlooked place in U.S. life, even if the country rarely accepted or acknowledged their identity. But after 9/11, a small group of politicians and activists seized on the tragedy to scrutinize Muslims and openly question whether they should be in the United States at all. In 1965, as the United States began to ramp up its war in Vietnam, President Lyndon B. Johnson authorized a massive increase of draft numbers. Ron Amen, the son of Lebanese immigrants in Dearborn, Michigan, was one of the young men called up to serve that year. When he received his dog tags before being deployed, he was surprised to find that, even though he had spelled out “Islam” for the bemused official in the recruitment office, his religion was listed as “none.” Amen’s dog tags offer an early glimpse of what would grow into the widespread anti-Muslim sentiment that journalist Rozina Ali traces in her new book, Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America. For generations, Muslims occupied a small and largely overlooked place in U.S. life, even if the country rarely accepted or acknowledged their identity. But after 9/11, a small group of politicians and activists seized on the tragedy to scrutinize Muslims and openly question whether they should be in the United States at all. Ali’s book documents that shift, illuminating the policies and practices that shaped Americans’ suspicion of Muslims decades both before and after 9/11. Unlike much of the literature on the attacks and their aftermath, Ali does not ask whether the so-called war on terror succeeded or failed. Instead, she examines what it did to Muslims in the United States—and, in turn, to the country itself—through the stories of four families, all of whom experienced Islamophobia in different ways yet refused to relinquish their claims to American life. Seasons of Fury begins with Abdeen Jabara, an attorney whose parents emigrated to the Midwest in the early 20th century from what was then called Greater Syria. Jabara recounts one striking moment in 1967, when he was watching the race riots that rocked Detroit from the city’s Cadillac Tower. He was there for a gathering of the local chapter of the National Lawyers Guild. Yet rather than focusing on the chaos taking place just below, the chapter’s leader called for the condemnation of the Soviet Union for arming Arab states against Israel, which had recently captured more territory in the Six-Day War, leading to its occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza. Jabara pushed back, saying that the situation was more complicated—to no avail. Soon after the guild meeting, a friend who was a professor called Jabara to invite him to a dinner with fellow Arabs to discuss how to better inform Americans about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. There, along with other attendees, Jabara formed the Association of Arab American University Graduates, an organization that sought, in Ali’s words, to “win over American minds.” For a time, the group’s vice president was Columbia University scholar Edward Said. In doing so, Jabara caught the attention of the FBI, which admitted in 1974 that it had been monitoring him since 1967 and sharing his information with Zionist organizations and foreign governments. Under J. Edgar Hoover in 1956, the FBI had launched a covert surveillance program called COINTELPRO to monitor “radical” groups—or at least what the agency deemed radical. It initially targeted communists but expanded to civil rights leaders and anti-war activists. Organizing around Palestine—and against Israel—eventually landed on its radar, even as the government’s own intelligence assessments found “little evidence that Arab groups were plotting attacks against the United States,” Ali notes. Jabara’s experience was not isolated. By the 1970s, Arabs in the United States increasingly came under surveillance, including by the National Security Agency, which Ali writes was “then a little-known part of the Defense Department.” Two decades later, laws helped institutionalize government suspicion and surveillance. President Bill Clinton approved two pieces of legislation in 1996 that, as Ali describes, “would forever shape the country’s criminal and immigration landscape.” One was the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, which “gave the government power to deport more immigrants, by expanding the list of deportable offenses.” The other, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act, stretched the definition of who could be implicated in terrorism under a new “Foreign Terrorist Organization” list. Anyone providing “material support” to any of the listed groups, including Hamas and Hezbollah, could be found guilty of abetting terrorism. Furthermore, the government could offer classified evidence in court that the defendant could not see. Ali notes that “Congressman David Bonior, from Michigan, called it ‘one of the most pernicious laws I’ve seen in my 28-year profession.’” He would see just how pernicious shortly after 9/11, when Congress passed the Patriot Act, which broadened the definition of “material support” to include those who offered “advice or assistance” to a supposed terrorist, effectively allowing the government to investigate and prosecute anyone it deemed vaguely suspicious. The law sparked widespread fear that Muslims would become targets, not just of the government but of an angry public eager for revenge. Indeed, in the aftermath of 9/11, Ali’s own father told her not to tell anyone that she is Muslim. “If a stranger asked, we were Hindu,” she recalls him saying. For good reason. The FBI reported that anti-Islamic incidents grew by more than 1,600 percent between 2000 and 2001. Official suspicion validated public fear, and public fear enabled aggressive government action. Ali gives a human face to these statistics through Jabara and three other families, whose stories before and after 9/11 are the heart of Seasons of Fury. Like a descent into Dante’s inferno, each family history reveals a particular layer of Islamophobia. In an effort to separate the terrorists from Muslims, six days after the attacks, President George W. Bush visited the Islamic Center in Washington, where he spoke about how Islam was a religion of peace. That gave Mohammad “Ali” Chaudry—a Pakistani immigrant who was elected to New Jersey’s Bernards Township council in 2001—hope. His election to mayor in 2004—which made him the first Pakistani-born Muslim mayor in the United States—seemed to indicate to Chaudry that despite 9/11, Americans were heeding the president’s call for tolerance. But the Bush administration’s actions spoke louder than his words. In an effort to identify threats, whether credible or not, the White House shifted counterterrorism efforts into overdrive. By the end of 2002, it had championed the Patriot Act, which expanded mass surveillance and curtailed civil liberties; formed the Department of Homeland Security; and rolled out both a “no fly list” and the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System, more commonly known as the Muslim registry, which required visa holders from specific countries—almost all of which were predominantly Muslim—to register with law enforcement. All of this ensured that the mood in the country locked into vigilance, something Chaudry witnessed a decade later when he moved to build a mosque in Basking Ridge. His neighbors subjected the proposal to years of review and 39 public hearings, repeatedly invoking zoning and planning objections to block the project. (Construction of the mosque was eventually allowed to move forward in 2017.) While Chaudry’s neighbors did not want a mosque in their midst, the Omars—a pseudonym Ali uses for a family of five due to concerns over their safety—came across a neighbor who did not want them, period. Shortly after 9/11, they moved to an unnamed U.S. suburb, where a neighbor began a relentless campaign of harassment: stalking, vandalism, and intimidation. He placed nails on the Omars’ walkway and a lawn ornament of a pig between his house and theirs. When the family sought help, with a meticulously documented record of incidents, local authorities repeatedly dismissed the harassment as an ordinary dispute between neighbors—not a sustained campaign directed at a Muslim family. Racial bias, authorities told the Omars, requires proof beyond a few claims. It took many years for the family to get a protective order in place. As Ali documents, that is the exact opposite problem that the Siraj family encountered from a national-security apparatus determined to find a threat from Muslims. Shahawar Matin Siraj, a 20-something Pakistani American, became entangled with a government informant who encouraged him to follow through with the idea of bombing a subway station—a bombing that never took place. He went to trial, believing that he would be found innocent, but was sentenced in 2007 to 30 years in prison. A day later, U.S. immigration officials detained his mother, father, and sister, who were later released. Siraj’s mother continues to maintain her son’s innocence. If authorities were reluctant to recognize the menace facing the Omars, in Siraj’s case they were willing to go extraordinary lengths to identify, cultivate, and prosecute a potential danger—even if they had to manufacture it themselves. Manufacturing fear against Muslims was not only ideological, but profitable. Tens of millions of dollars went into endeavors claiming to educate Americans about the supposedly dangerous nature of Islam. The Clarion Fund, which helped distribute Raphael Shore’s 2005 documentary Obsession: Radical Islam’s War Against the West, received $17 million from a single donor in 2008 alone. Right-wing commentator David Horowitz received more than $8 million for his eponymous Freedom Center, which housed Robert Spencer’s Jihad Watch blog and hosted Islamofascism Awareness Week on college campuses. Other conservative donors joined in. Banking and oil-fortune heir Richard Mellon Scaife was among several who put more than $42 million into anti-Muslim efforts in the years following 9/11. By the end of the Bush administration in 2008, Islamophobia no longer needed a terrorist attack to sustain it. Individuals and institutions with a financial interest in anti-Muslim sentiment kept it alive. Perhaps that, along with the massive bureaucracy that sustained Islamophobia, is what made it difficult for Bush’s successor to fight it. Ali points out that although President Barack Obama spoke about civilization’s debt to Islam in a 2009 speech in Cairo in an attempt to reset relations between the United States and the Muslim world, his administration did little to correct Bush’s overreach. In fact, she writes, during the first two years of his presidency, “the number of Islamic terrorism-related prosecutions ticked upward.” A Democratic president may speak more acceptingly of Islam, but anti-Muslim bias had already become ingrained in U.S. politics. Despite the racism and fearmongering on display in Seasons of Fury, Ali’s subjects do not reject the United States or the institutions that have failed to protect them. They turned to courts, free speech, activism, and public service to insist on the rights the United States promises its citizens. As Ali notes, the country may not deem Islam compatible with it, but Muslims have shown that their faith in the American experiment is unwavering. By the time she finished writing her book, Zohran Mamdani was elected New York’s first Muslim mayor. The night of the vote, Ali writes in the epilogue, “felt electric with possibility, charged by the promise that the American experiment was not yet worth giving up on.” Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: What in the World?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.59
What in the World? Test yourself on the week of Sept. 12: Modi and Xi meet, the Houthis fire on Saudi Arabia, and EU leaders gather in Finland. Is that chill in the air the first sign of fall in the Northern Hemisphere, or the realization that you haven’t paid attention to what’s happening in the world this week? Find out with our international news quiz! Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. Is that chill in the air the first sign of fall in the Northern Hemisphere, or the realization that you haven’t paid attention to what’s happening in the world this week? Find out with our international news quiz! 1. The Indian Foreign Ministry stated on Saturday that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had pledged to strengthen ties in what areas? 2. What did Yemen’s Houthi rebels target with dozens of missiles and drones in the Saudi city of Khamis Mushait on Monday? The Trump administration has recently begun blaming Ukraine for high oil prices. The real culprit for the latest spike, however, is the Iranian-backed Houthis’ attacks in the Red Sea, FP’s Keith Johnson wrote last week. 3. European leaders met in Finland on Monday to call for greater European Union engagement in which region? The EU is seeking to address rising security concerns from Russia, as European leaders worry that Moscow may launch an attack from the Arctic in the coming years, FP columnist Christian Caryl wrote last month. 4. Africa’s richest person, Aliko Dangote, launched the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering on Monday, floating 4.1 billion shares for his business in what field? 5. Thailand and Cambodia’s foreign ministers delivered their opening statements on Tuesday as part of the countries’ meeting to settle a border dispute concerning what in particular? 6. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested on Wednesday that the EU could make which country an “associate member” of the bloc? Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has been pitching the idea for months—especially as the United States under the Trump administration has become the biggest threat to Canada’s peace and prosperity, Casey Michel argued in February. 7. Ahead of next month’s election, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed a decree on Thursday that did what? 8. Why did Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson resign on Thursday? 9. The United States confirmed for the first time on Monday that it had deployed weapons where? 10. A Paris court awarded Kim Kardashian 1 euro on Tuesday as compensation for being the victim of an armed robbery in 2016. Due to the robbers’ age when they were found guilty last year, what have they come to be known as? With time already served in pretrial detention, none of those found guilty went back behind bars. Kardashian has sought to move on from the case and expressed gratitude to the French justice system, The Associated Press reports. You scored It’s a big world out there! Brush up on global goings-on by subscribing to World Brief, Foreign Policy’s flagship daily newsletter. Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. item.title: The Houthi Advance Is About More Than Just Iran
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.48
The Houthi Advance Is About More Than Just Iran The Saudi-Emirati rivalry is driving moves across the region. On Sept. 8, the Houthis launched a major offensive against Saudi-backed forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, seizing key points across the country’s west coast and suddenly establishing a commanding position on the Bab el-Mandeb. That same week, Algeria declared that it was severing diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates and subsequently closed its airspace to Emirati planes. These two events, in countries almost as geographically distant as possible within the bounds of the Middle East and with dramatically different geopolitical stakes, may seem to have little in common. But developments in Yemen and Algeria are bound together by three powerful processes shaping regional order at this moment: the failure of the United States to defeat Iran or protect its Arab allies, the Saudi-Emirati conflict, and the rapid erosion of the artificial divides between the Middle East and Africa. The escalation in Yemen has received the most attention, for good reason. The Houthi seizure of the port town of Mokha, most of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, and several key islands in the Red Sea allow the group to disrupt and deny shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb. That entryway to the Red Sea has always been one of the most important maritime chokepoints for global trade, with transit through the Suez Canal connecting Asia to the West (with associated toll revenues keeping the Egyptian economy afloat). It took on even greater importance after Saudi Arabia sought to circumvent Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz by redirecting oil shipments through its East-West pipeline to its Red Sea outlet. The Houthi offensive, combined with drone strikes on the pipeline attributed to Iraqi militias, has suddenly and dramatically closed that outlet, putting unprecedented pressure on Saudi Arabia and the global economy. That same week, Algeria declared that it was severing diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates and subsequently closed its airspace to Emirati planes. These two events, in countries almost as geographically distant as possible within the bounds of the Middle East and with dramatically different geopolitical stakes, may seem to have little in common. But developments in Yemen and Algeria are bound together by three powerful processes shaping regional order at this moment: the failure of the United States to defeat Iran or protect its Arab allies, the Saudi-Emirati conflict, and the rapid erosion of the artificial divides between the Middle East and Africa. The escalation in Yemen has received the most attention, for good reason. The Houthi seizure of the port town of Mokha, most of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, and several key islands in the Red Sea allow the group to disrupt and deny shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb. That entryway to the Red Sea has always been one of the most important maritime chokepoints for global trade, with transit through the Suez Canal connecting Asia to the West (with associated toll revenues keeping the Egyptian economy afloat). It took on even greater importance after Saudi Arabia sought to circumvent Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz by redirecting oil shipments through its East-West pipeline to its Red Sea outlet. The Houthi offensive, combined with drone strikes on the pipeline attributed to Iraqi militias, has suddenly and dramatically closed that outlet, putting unprecedented pressure on Saudi Arabia and the global economy. While the impact of the Houthi offensive has been felt most profoundly on the Iran front, Yemen’s war has its own dynamics. Saudi Arabia triggered the most recent round of fighting in July by bombing Sanaa’s airport, and fighting had escalated for several months. But as with everything in the Middle East these days, there was a Saudi-Emirati angle as well. Last December, Saudi forces suddenly and unceremoniously drove Emirati-aligned forces out of Yemen, pushing back against a Southern independence movement that it viewed as part of a broader Emirati campaign to promote secessionist groups across the region. It had been particularly concerned about potential Emirati support for Israel’s recognition of the breakaway Somali province of Somaliland. The prospect of Israel gaining a strategic foothold on the other side of the Bab el-Mandeb, particularly if that facilitated Emirati encirclement of Saudi Arabia, struck Riyadh as a major strategic threat. Riyadh followed its Yemen moves with a bid to assemble a regional coalition, including states such as Turkey, Egypt, and Qatar, that would become a third pole competing with Iran’s Axis of Resistance and the Emirati-Israeli-led Abraham Accords project. Pushing the UAE out of Yemen was the easy part, though. The quick defeat of the UAE’s allies left the Saudis responsible for supporting and leading the remaining forces defending the territories under the control of the internationally recognized government. While Riyadh made a show of pouring support and reorganizing those forces and pledging air cover (while reportedly quietly paying off the Houthis), much of that aid proved short-lived. Saudi strategy did not seem much improved from decades of previous failures and underperformance, with the influx of cash, episodic airstrikes, continued blockade, and ample propaganda failing to substitute for the absence of human capacity or strategic competence on the ground. Reporting suggests that as many as 80 percent of the Saudi-backed forces were ghost fighters, drawing salaries and little else. Saudi communications seem to have been thoroughly compromised by the Houthis, while promised air cover largely failed to materialize. In the fever swamps of Arab social media, rumors run rampant about the UAE covertly activating its former allies to undermine the government forces—payback for Riyadh’s December humiliation and in support of Israel’s concerns about the new Saudi-led coalition. Houthi motivations therefore cannot be reduced solely to Iranian grand strategy or even to the opportunity to strike a decisive blow in the ongoing war with Saudi Arabia. Their advance also responded to the potential transregionalization of the conflict. Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, and rumored covert deployments on the ground, could potentially bring Israeli, Emirati, and even U.S. forces directly to the other side of the strait to contest control and serve as a base for counterstrikes into Yemen. That could, in turn, turbocharge Houthi ties with the Somalia-based al-Shabab terrorist group, which has been organically growing for several years, raising the risks of a transregional expansion of the war across the Horn of Africa. No doubt these East African concerns were on the mind of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman dropped in for an unusual visit to Cairo this week. Egypt took Riyadh’s side in the December crisis but has thus far declined to join the Saudi-led Mecca Pact with Pakistan and Turkey. The economic impact of the potential closure of the Bab el-Mandeb on the Suez Canal on top of the effects of the Iran war would be devastating to an Egyptian regime already struggling with profound economic problems. The expansion of the Yemen conflict into the Horn of Africa also intensifies the pressure on Egypt, which is locked in an ongoing struggle with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Egypt seems no likelier to be willing to join a ground war against the Houthis than it was when Mohammed bin Salman asked a decade ago, but in many ways the stakes are now higher and the choices more fraught. In a region defined by a fierce struggle between Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Cairo can no longer count on financial support from both, since choosing either side could cost it dearly with the other. Saudi Arabia, frustrated by the refusal of the United States to intervene against the Houthis on its behalf, had hoped to get assistance from its new alliance partners, Pakistan and Turkey. But both countries seem content to offer moral support and stay out of the Yemeni quagmire. Pakistan quickly clarified that its alliance commitments only extended to new conflicts. But such a stance may be untenable as Saudi options rapidly narrow. Pakistani intervention in Yemen in support of Saudi Arabia, though not currently in the cards, would represent a new frontier for transregional security competition and for the necessity of thinking beyond the Middle East. Which brings us to Algeria. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s decision to sever diplomatic relations was a response to the surge of Emirati activities across the Sahel and especially its support for Moroccan claims to the Western Sahara. Algeria’s problems with the UAE center on its support for Morocco as part of the Abraham Accords, which manifests in the Western Sahara as well as across the Sahel, where Rabat has sought to increase its influence at Algeria’s expense—with Emirati backing. Algiers accused the UAE of expanding its influence in Chad, Mali, and Niger and perpetuating destabilizing and bloody wars through support for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan and Khalifa Haftar’s Libyan National Army in Libya. Algerian pro-regime media also accuse the UAE of attempting to manipulate the country’s own 2019 presidential election, though evidence is thus far scarce. Like Riyadh, Algeria sees the UAE’s ambitions in part through the lens of the Emirati alliance with Israel and blames it for the acceleration of Morocco’s diplomatic ties with Israel and American recognition of its sovereignty in Western Sahara. All this points to a Middle East map that is bigger than the one U.S. policymakers tend to hold in their heads, with countries across North and East Africa advancing their own alliances and interests in ways that stubbornly refuse to follow the traditional lines of Middle Eastern politics. A few days after Algeria’s diplomatic moves, Eritrea accused the UAE of “port imperialism” in collaboration with Israel. Like the Houthis, Eritrea has watched Emirati expansion in the Horn of Africa and Israeli support for Somaliland with concern while keeping an eye on Ethiopian military preparations warily. And all of this unfolds amid growing international and regional condemnation of the UAE’s support for the brutal RSF, credibly accused of massive war crimes. Houthi gains in Yemen may prove ephemeral. There is a long history of sudden surges and reversals in Yemen’s long internal war, and a new status quo may eventually emerge that avoids the worst-case scenarios. But the bigger lesson is that regional politics today are not a bipolar struggle between Iran and a U.S.-led coalition. The Saudi-Emirati conflict, which is in turn a proxy for a regional argument over Israel’s place in the order, has now entrenched a three-way competition unfolding across regional boundaries. Marc Lynch is a professor of political science and international affairs at the George Washington University and the director of the Project on Middle East Political Science. His most recent book is America’s Middle East: The Ruination of a Region. X: @abuaardvark Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Will Russia Ever Be ‘Normal’?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.04
Will Russia Ever Be ‘Normal’? Empires inevitably decline, and Putin’s project will be no exception. When asked “how’s it going,” average Russians usually respond with one word—normalno. Life is normal when you’re doing neither exceptionally well nor exceptionally poorly. The English-language equivalent might be somewhere between “hanging in there” and “I’m OK.” Normalnost—or the condition of normalcy—is obviously a relative notion. What is normalno for a Russian pensioner eking out an existence is not normalno for President Vladimir Putin and his minions. Even so, most Russians would probably agree that life is normalno when you’re getting by financially, your kids don’t hate you excessively, your spouse drinks too much only occasionally, and the authorities mostly ignore you. When asked “how’s it going,” average Russians usually respond with one word—normalno. Life is normal when you’re doing neither exceptionally well nor exceptionally poorly. The English-language equivalent might be somewhere between “hanging in there” and “I’m OK.” Normalnost—or the condition of normalcy—is obviously a relative notion. What is normalno for a Russian pensioner eking out an existence is not normalno for President Vladimir Putin and his minions. Even so, most Russians would probably agree that life is normalno when you’re getting by financially, your kids don’t hate you excessively, your spouse drinks too much only occasionally, and the authorities mostly ignore you. Putin’s fascist regime has put normalnost to the test. Life was fine for your average Russian—and for Russian elites—before Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Now, four and a half years into a bloody war that is killing or wounding around 1,100 Russian soldiers per day while pushing the country’s militarized economy to the brink of collapse, life is anything but normalno for Russians living outside the protected bubbles of Moscow and St. Petersburg. Now, even the residents of these two cities have begun experiencing first-hand what seemed for so long to be a faraway, fantasy conflict. At a minimum, a return to normalnost presupposes the end of the war. That, in turn, more or less presupposes the end of Putin. Although Putin’s removal in a coup is possible even as the war continues, it cannot end as long as Putin remains committed to it for the sake of his own personal and political survival. But the relationship between normalnost and war goes deeper than Putin and his determination to destroy Ukraine. Unfortunately for Russia and its neighbors, normalnost will always be susceptible to breakdown—and Russian aggression will always be possible—as long as two structural factors remain in place. The first is Russia’s political culture and sense of national identity. Central to Russians’ self-perception is the culturally sanctioned, deeply ingrained belief that their country is uniquely predisposed to greatness with a quasi-right to dominate others. Russia’s world-historical mission is thus the very opposite of normalno: Its mission is not to rest on its laurels and enjoy life within its borders, but to fulfill its historical destiny and spread Russian civilization—a messianic concept that is deeply rooted in Russian Orthodoxy but largely devoid of any religious content today. Variants of these views were held by imperial Russian officials and cultural figures (such as Fyodor Dostoevsky), as well as anti-communist dissidents (including Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn). These same views are currently held by Putin; Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox church and reputed former KGB agent; Putin’s propaganda attack dog Dmitry Medvedev (known for his eagerness to incinerate European capitals with nuclear weapons); the crackpot philosopher Aleksandr Dugin; the rabid television personality Vladimir Solovyov, and scores of other propagandists. Most Russians espouse them as well—if not explicitly, then as part of the cultural waters in which they swim. The fact that these views have been dominant in Russian discourse over decades and even centuries suggests that we’re dealing with a deeper structure—a stable political-cultural norm, not a set of transient views. Given this tenacious political culture, the many Russians who strive for normalnost in their everyday lives are hard-pressed to resist that culture’s claims about the greatness of their nation. In the final analysis, this undermines Russians’ desire for quotidian normalnost. Could these cultural mindsets change? Other nations with megalomaniacal views of themselves were able to abandon them and focus their attention on daily life only after suffering humiliating military defeats. Britain and France lost empires; the once-aggressive Germans and Japanese were bombed into pacifism during World War II and afterward refocused on domestic prosperity. The United States may be getting its comeuppance today. These examples suggest that Russia can finally embrace normalnost if and only if it suffers a clear defeat by Ukraine. A mere ceasefire won’t do. Neither will Putin’s departure. Defeat would have to be of such a magnitude as to get even the most vociferous supporters of greatness to question their assumptions. Right now, it is difficult to imagine that anything short of a spectacular collapse would finally enable Russians to do what the Germans did after 1945: Accept responsibility for their leader’s crimes and become average citizens of the world. The second factor standing in the way of Russia becoming a normal nation is the Russian state—not the type of regime, whether imperial, Soviet, fascist, or something else, but the size and complexity of a political entity that spans 11 time zones and is populated by a plethora of nations with different cultures, religions, histories, and identities. Such a state is structurally imperial, with defined metropoles and outlying colonies whose residents have the choice of being voiceless subjects, de facto collaborators, or persecuted oppositionists. Tsarist Russia was openly imperial; the Soviet Union, with its hyper-centralized political and economic systems, was arguably the apotheosis of empire; and Putin’s Russia certainly remains an empire both domestically and in terms of its grand ambitions in its region and beyond. All three empires adopted repressive policies toward their non-Russian subjects, ranging from cultural repression to imprisonment to deportation to genocidal war. With just a few exceptions, the ethnic Russian majority appears to be perfectly happy with the imperial state. How many protested Putin’s Chechen wars or invasion of Georgia? How many managed to restrain their glee at Crimea’s becoming “ours” in 2014? How many Russians truly believe that Ukraine is an independent state entitled to go its own way? How many are refusing to fight in a genocidal war that is killing them at an extraordinarily high clip? (Surely arrest for draft evasion is not worse than death within an estimated 30 minutes of being sent into battle.) The supposedly liberal oppositionist Alexey Navalny supported Russia’s invasions of Georgia in 2008 and Ukraine in 2014, spouting various nationalist and openly racist views toward non-Russians before reevaluating only in 2022. Ukrainians are fond of pointing out: Scratch a Russian liberal and find a Russian imperialist. That doesn’t apply to everyone, but it does address an unfortunately common Russian trait. Empires inevitably decline, and Putin’s project will be no exception. The reasons for decline are many, but central is the dynamic between the imperial nation that vies for greatness and the colonized nations who invariably question that claim upon attaining some degree of identity. It was the Soviet revolutionary Vladimir Lenin, after all, who said that Russian chauvinism gave rise to non-Russian nationalism and separatism. But how are Russians committed to their nation’s greatness supposed to respond to non-Russian demands for greater autonomy and cultural identity that threaten the unity and size of the mighty imperial state and the political culture that sustains it? As the tsars, communists, and now Putin have consistently done, greatness demands that non-Russians be silenced. (That some of these leaders—such as Joseph Stalin—were non-Russians themselves does not invalidate the structure of their rule.) Ironically, Russians are trapped in a vicious circle of their own making. Abandoning the political culture of greatness and imperialism would pave the road to normalnost, but it would also upend a key source of affective empowerment and national pride. Dismantling or at least slimming the imperial state would go a long way to making more normalnost possible, but that too would require either a massive Ukrainian victory that undermines the current state’s integrity or a Gorbachev-style perestroika that loosens the internal bonds of empire. Normalnost isn’t just a desirable goal for Russia. It’s also of great importance to Russia’s neighbors. Although neither the culture of greatness nor the imperial state are necessary or sufficient for Moscow to start wars, both facilitate war-mongering and make aggression much easier to sell to Russian elites and the public. They thus make war more likely. Imagine a counterfactual: Would a normal Russia bereft of its imperial culture and all-powerful, centralized state have embarked on a genocidal war against Ukraine? Possibly, but not likely. The sad but inescapable truth is that Russia will be an existential threat to its many neighbors, especially Ukraine, as long as its infatuation with greatness persists—as long as normalnost is only a quotidian aspiration, not a political goal. A modern-day Cato, echoing his Roman predecessor’s insistence that “Carthago delenda est,” might be right in saying that “Russia must be destroyed.” But who, besides the Ukrainians, Balts, and Poles, would agree? The Trump administration appears committed to Russia’s revival as a great power. The Europeans are only just beginning to realize that Russia has already declared “hybrid war”—or, more honestly, war without a mitigating adjective—on them. Much of the rest of the world sees the United States as more of a threat today than Putin’s Russia. That’s the bad news. The good news is that, while Putin may be killing Ukrainian civilians in greater numbers, Ukraine’s determination to achieve victory remains undiminished, as does its ability to kill Russian soldiers faster than Putin can recruit them. The even better news is that Putin is putting into practice Cato’s demand by continuing a war that is undermining the economy, exterminating Russian soldiers in staggering numbers, demoralizing and angering his population, and demonstrating to the world that Russia is a has-been great power. Putin is destroying Russia. Putin promised to make Russia great again. Instead, he’s making it weak—so weak that its disintegration due to his self-destructive policies becomes more likely each day. Russians may take heart: Once they let go of the conviction that their country and state have a special destiny of imperial greatness, they will finally be able to enjoy the normalnost to which they aspire. Alexander J. Motyl is a professor of political science at Rutgers University-Newark. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: When a Team Member Underperforms—but Has Organizational Capital
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.12
When a Team Member Underperforms—but Has Organizational Capital September 18, 2026 Summary. Leaders sometimes inherit an underperforming employee they cannot remove, leaving them responsible for results without the authority to address the problem. They can limit the damage by testing Some of the most damaging performance problems have nothing to do with who you hired. They’re about members of your team you’re not allowed to remove.

item.title: Is Your Strategic Plan Too Ambitious? Or Not Ambitious Enough?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.06
Summary. How ambitious should your strategic plan be? Aim too low, and you may settle for incremental gains. Aim too high, and you risk overwhelming the organization. Finding the right balance requires You’re weighing a plan to enter a new market, launch a new offering, or create a new business division. You have benchmarks in mind and a rough sense of the cost. What you don’t know is whether your idea is ambitious enough to be worth it.

item.title: When There’s More Work Than Your Team Can Handle
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.86
Summary. When demands increase while resources shrink, leaders can’t simply absorb the extra work or push an already-overextended team harder. Both approaches carry costs: When my coaching client, Chris* became chief legal counsel at a financial services firm, he didn’t anticipate how fast the workload would escalate. Within his first year, the company closed three major acquisitions back-to-back, producing an avalanche of contract reviews, compliance filings, and regulatory matters. Every time Chris tried to hand something off, his team would say, “we’re doing our best, but we’re at capacity.” He understood, but since the work still had to get done, Chris absorbed it himself. Working nights and weekends to keep up soon compromised Chris’s ability to drive the very high-level strategy he’d been tapped to lead.

item.title: Will Your Organization Stand By Its Values—Even When It’s Hard?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.55
Will Your Organization Stand By Its Values—Even When It’s Hard? Summary. Organizational values often emphasize what companies stand for, but their real power may lie in defining what they refuse to do, Thirty years ago, Ralph Larsen, then the CEO of Johnson & Johnson, was interviewed by Jim Collins and Jerry Porras, who quoted him in their 1996 HBR article, “Building Your Company’s Vision,” which would become the defining playbook on organizational values. “The core values embodied in our credo might be a competitive advantage,” Larsen said, “but that is not why we have them. We have them because they define for us what we stand for, and we would hold them even if they became a competitive disadvantage in certain situations.”

item.title: When Is It Time to Step Down?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.24
Summary. In this week’s HBR Executive Agenda, editor at large Adi Ignatius speaks with Craigslist founder Craig Newmark about recognizing your leadership limits and stepping back before it costs the Welcome to the HBR Executive Agenda for September 17, 2026.

item.title: Research: Gen AI Is Collapsing Creative Processes
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.10
Summary. Generative AI is transforming creative work by making it faster and easier to brainstorm and visualize ideas. But a new, yearlong study following senior creatives in charge of television and Imagine a photographer reviewing a concept image for an advertising campaign that the client has already approved. He notices a problem: The man in the image is wearing a baseball cap that casts his face in shadow, but his eyes are clearly lit, showing his intense stare into the camera. The photographer’s trained eye tells him immediately that that lighting is impossible. No real-world set up could produce it. The image had been created by a senior creative using gen AI, and the client had loved it. Now the production team has been tasked with recreating—with cameras and human actors—something that reality can’t match.

item.title: Some California cars will get to skip smog checks. What to know about Jay Leno's Law
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.41
Some California cars will get to skip smog checks. What to know about Jay Leno’s Law - Click here to listen to this article - Whether it’s a sleek, low-slung Impala, a candy apple red Monte Carlo or a roaring T-top Trans Am — the classic cars of the late 1970s and the ’80s are an iconic part of California’s automotive heritage. But many of these vehicles have been relegated to driveways and garages due to the challenge of passing a smog check. Auto lovers have pushed for years to lessen emissions regulations for collector cars, arguing that these vintage vehicles are only driven short distances to parades and meet-ups where they deserve to be seen and cherished. Enthusiasts found a powerful champion in famed comedian and auto aficionado Jay Leno, who boasts more than 150 vehicles in his personal collection. On Wednesday, he secured a big win for the classic car community when Gov. Gavin Newsom paid a visit to his Burbank garage to sign Senate Bill 1392, also known as Jay Leno’s Law, legislation that expands smog check exemptions for certain collector cars. How smog check waivers will be applied to classic cars Over the next few years, Jay Leno’s Law will phase in smog check exemptions for collector cars built from model years 1976 through 1985 that are not used as a primary mode of transportation. Under current law, cars manufactured before the 1975 model year are already exempt from smog check requirements. The new exemptions will take effect beginning Jan. 1, 2028, and apply to qualifying cars manufactured before the 1981 model year. Each year, eligibility extends by another model year until 2033, when vehicles manufactured through the 1985 model year will be included. In order to be eligible, owners must prove that their collector car isn’t used for everyday transport either by holding collector-car insurance or documenting that the car is driven fewer than 1,000 miles per year. The exemption is designed to apply to cars used primarily in shows, parades, charitable functions and historical exhibitions. “California can protect clean air while also recognizing the historic and cultural value of collector vehicles,” said bill co-author state Sen. Dave Cortese (D-San José). “SB 1392 establishes a carefully limited exemption for cars that are preserved, driven sparingly, and maintained as part of California’s automotive heritage.” What the bill means for classic cars, lowriders Maintaining vintage vehicles is a labor of love, and the biennial smog check requirement poses an additional challenge for collectors, as not all gas stations are equipped to provide this service. “So you have an old car, it’s been legal your whole life, and now it’s illegal because you can’t find a station to do the emissions test,” Leno said at a rally for the bill in August. “What do you do? It’s your car, so you keep driving it, and you keep hoping a policeman doesn’t see you. And now you’re just making criminals out of people that want to do the right thing.” And assuming collectors can get their car to an appropriate testing location, there’s no promise it will pass. It is notoriously tough to get vintage vehicles up to current emissions standards because decades-old emissions systems frequently deteriorate, and replacement parts are hard to track down. Waiving the smog check requirement will make it easier for collectors to bring their cars to shows and celebrations without running afoul of the law. This is a major win for the lowrider community, which submitted more than 1,700 letters in support of the bill. These customized classic cars, featuring modified suspension that allows them to cruise extremely close to the ground, are a cherished tradition in California’s Chicano community, but for decades have been the target of fines, restrictions and local cruising bans. Though the culture never disappeared since the heyday of cruising in the 1980s and 1990s, interest in lowriding has surged in recent years. Have you noticed? Every weekend, caravans of lowriders and custom cars are cruising and hopping in a resurgent ritual. Van Nuys Boulevard is one of the city’s oldest sites of this resilient SoCal obsession. While at Leno’s garage Wednesday, Newsom also signed Assembly Bill 2541 into law, creating a special license plate to honor California’s lowrider heritage. “Lowriding is more than a car; it is cultura, it is art, it’s family, and it is a powerful expression of Chicano and Latino pride,” said AB 2541 author Assemblymember Mark González (D-Los Angeles). “For generations, our communities have used lowriders to tell our stories, celebrate our heritage, and create something beautiful out of the streets we call home.” Why getting this law passed was an uphill battle Getting California’s Legislature to sign off on Jay Leno’s Law, a bill that will increase emissions to some degree, was not a simple feat. Environmental and public health advocates have consistently opposed new smog check waivers, noting they increase exhaust emissions such as nitrogen dioxide that are damaging to human health. Exhaust is the biggest source of greenhouse gas emissions in California, which has some of the worst air pollution in the nation. At least three other attempts to loosen smog check requirements for older cars have failed to make it to the governor’s desk since 2016. They include a similar law, SB 712, which Leno also rallied for and which died in the Assembly Appropriations Committee last year. This legislative cycle, supporters of the revised Leno-backed bill successfully argued that the environmental impact would be limited in scope, as the waivers will apply to a small number of vehicles that are only driven short distances every year. Sen. Cortese pointed to the fact that less than 1% of registered cars in California fall within the model-year range covered by the law. State Sen. Shannon Grove (R-Bakersfield) signed on as a co-author of the bill and celebrated that it passed with notable bipartisan support. “We have worked for two years to get this law to the finish line,” said Grove. “It was only made possible by the overwhelming support of car enthusiasts, mechanics, and families across the state who have passed these vehicles down from generation to generation.”

item.title: In chaotic L.A. skies, news helicopter pilots juggle competition, camaraderie, risk
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.29
In chaotic L.A. skies, news helicopter pilots juggle competition, camaraderie, risk - Click here to listen to this article - Whether it’s a brush fire, a mass shooting, a car chase or the aftermath of a major storm, viewers in Los Angeles are used to getting the news from above. Television news helicopter coverage has become one of the most important elements of any local newscast, with the high-flying helicopters roaring overhead a common fixture of breaking news scenes. These images are so ubiquitous, it may have been easy to take them for granted, until Tuesday, when an NBC4 helicopter carrying reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw crashed while covering breaking news in Chatsworth. Both died, along with a bystander on the ground. The tragedy has prompted soul-searching in the world of TV news helicopter pilots and focused attention on safety issues. Pilots describe a high-stakes race in the skies of Los Angeles, with the TV stations battling to get breaking news on the air first. The airspace easily becomes crowded, and in the case of moving stories like car chases, a bit unpredictable and chaotic. The crews who take to the air in Los Angeles must not only navigate one another, but air traffic to three regional airports and smaller, local airstrips across the Southland when doing their job. The crash that killed three people on Tuesday night, including two NBC4 journalists, involved a single-engine AS350 B2 helicopter. Questions surround why it suddenly dropped from the sky. They say that safety is always the top priority and that everyone in the air works together to avoid problems. The NBC4 crash marks the most serious incident involving an L.A. news chopper crew since 2000, when a Fox 11 helicopter covering the Academy Awards crashed and burst into flames at Van Nuys Airport. Nationally, National Transportation Safety Board data show that 16 people have died in eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the United States since 2000. A cause of Tuesday’s crash has not been determined, but some experts have said they believe mechanical failure might be responsible. “It crushed us all,” said Tim Lynn, a now-retired helicopter pilot and reporter who flew for 16 years for KTLA-TV. Lynn worked with Moreno and knew how much she cherished her job. “She loved the job so much that she put her all into it,” he said. Camaraderie, competition in the air For all the camaraderie in the air, there is also some competition. Stations want to be first to get to the scene of breaking news. Kurt Deetz, a former news helicopter pilot who retired five years ago, said it’s a difficult business to be in. “It’s very competitive, and at what cost?” Deetz said. At a news conference Wednesday, federal transportation officials said the most critical information available so far has been video captured from the helicopter during its final, live broadcast moments before it crashed. News pilots tend to have plenty of experience, former pilots said, and dangerous incidents are rare. But Deetz said pilots are pushed to be out in the air first, get to the scene, and remain on scene for extended periods of time. “If you can be the first on the scene, you’re a hero,” Deetz said. “I think about that now and think, that is so dumb.” Deetz started his career with KMEX in 1995, and worked for nearly every station in the area while working with Helinet, he said. In the sky, reporters and pilots keep an eye out for one another, warning when one is drifting too close to another or if there is something else to keep an eye on. “We all know each other,” Lynn said. “Maybe we never met, but we’ve all talked on the radio and know the names.” There are unspoken rules that news helicopter pilots learn once they join, Lynn said. During a police chase, for example, the first helicopter on the scene immediately takes the front position left of the fleeing vehicle, he said. The next helicopter takes a position behind that helicopter. The third takes a spot in the front right side of the chase, and the fourth sits behind it. All four maintain those spots throughout the chase, regardless of the turns and twists throughout the area. And when the pursued begins to circle a residential area — a common occurrence during police pursuits — all news helicopters are expected to stop and hover in place, even if their shots are temporarily blocked by trees and buildings. That’s because the tight turns and circles could result in a crash if all helicopters remain in pursuit. “You never move unless you say something,” Lynn said. “It’s a well-coordinated operation.” Your morning catch-up: SoCal remembers two news veterans, the driver accused in a fatal Metro bus crash had multiple drug arrests and more big stories. Lynn remembers at least once when a new pilot joined in a pursuit. “We were all stopped and he’s just chasing the guy like he’s the police,” he said. Lynn got on the radio and, as the other three choppers kept their position, Lynn asked him to stick to “one of the corners.” “That was a learning curve for that guy,” he said. But Lynn said there’s respect for new staff and veterans in the field. Regardless of what station they work for, reporters and pilots are constantly helping one another, abiding by unspoken rules to keep them all safe. ‘A dangerous place to be’ There is one maneuver that pilots say brings them particular anxiety. Jack Cress, a former helicopter pilot for the Marine Corps and a helicopter accident investigation instructor for USC’s Aviation Safety and Security Program, said news helicopters will often spend time hovering over an incident, sometimes at a low altitude. “That is a dangerous place to be,” Cress said. For Deetz, he said he’d often say that he wouldn’t hover low for extended periods of time, especially if he didn’t see a place he could land in case of an emergency. “You set up, get your shot, and then you move on,” he said. “I made a point of saying, ‘I’m not going to hover here for hours.’ ” He knows the practice is still popular among current pilots, which he thinks needs to be rethought. A helicopter crashed into flames Tuesday night in Chatsworth, not far from a serious accident involving a Metro bus that left three people dead. “In this day and age, there’s no need to hover,” he said. “Those cameras are so powerful. There’s no need to be so low.” Helicopter pilots are trained to stay away from those conditions because, in case of trouble like engine failure, the lack of altitude and forward momentum gives the pilot little recourse. If the engine were to fail, for example, a pilot can sometimes perform an “autorotation” procedure to use altitude and forward momentum to force the rotors to turn, easing their descent. The procedure is one that Lynn is familiar with. In 2012, he was covering an incident in Hollywood for KTLA when his helicopter started to smoke heavily. He had no idea until one of the other choppers radioed him to tell him. “As soon as I turn it, he said, ‘You need to put it on the ground now,’ ” Lynn said. Lynn headed down and started getting the helicopter ready for an autorotation, as heavy smoke started to shoot from the engine. Lynn looked toward the ground and was eyeing Highland Avenue or Los Feliz Boulevard for a makeshift landing spot. He gripped the controls and expected the engine to give out at any second, until he spotted a parking lot. He watched for the wires, watched for the trees and set it down. The motor never gave out. Pilots will constantly eye one another in the formation. News helicopter pilots will normally stay around 1,200 to 1,500 feet above the ground, Lynn said. That is to stay above police helicopters, under commercial flights, and still have enough space in case they need to perform an emergency autorotation procedure.
