item.title: 'Machine Gods' explores the latest developments in the world of AI
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Score: 4.34
'Machine Gods' explores the latest developments in the world of AI NPR's Steve Inskeep talks to tech journalists Casey Newton and Kevin Roose about their new show 'Machine Gods,' which is coming to NPR. STEVE INSKEEP, BYLINE: Two leading tech journalists are founding a new video show on AI, and it's coming to NPR twice a week. The hosts are Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, previously known to the tech world for the New York Times podcast "Hard Fork," among other things. Their new venture on NPR is called Machine Gods, and it launches in October. Gentlemen, welcome. KEVIN ROOSE, BYLINE: Thanks so much, Steve. CASEY NEWTON, BYLINE: Hey, Steve. INSKEEP: And I want listeners to understand each of your voices. Will you each just say your names? ROOSE: Yes. I'm Kevin Roose. NEWTON: And I'm Casey Newton. INSKEEP: And the program is called Machine Gods. What's the big idea? ROOSE: So Machine Gods is how people out here, where we are in San Francisco, talk about what's happening in AI. They talk about the fact that we are creating these rapidly improving AI systems. Some people sort of jokingly refer to them as the Machine God. And also, we're - we've been spending the past four years making a show about the latest developments in the world of tech. We're very excited to bring this show to NPR because we think this is a really important time for the public to understand what we see here, which is this industry racing ahead towards something that we've never really seen before. These AI systems are becoming quite capable, quite dangerous, and we're both excited by the potential as well as a little terrified of the risk. INSKEEP: Isn't this almost a literal title in that there are some people in this field who think they're creating God? NEWTON: Absolutely. There is a religious element to the way that lots of folks out here talk about what they're doing. The name is also sort of a play on some of the leaders of these companies who also sort of styled themselves as religious figures. So that's definitely an element we hope to capture in our reporting. INSKEEP: What has obsessed you about this topic in recent years? ROOSE: One thing that I'm fascinated by is that the people who are building this technology are in some sense the most scared of it. You know, we've seen this just in the past couple of weeks with the Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, who resigned, saying that he was scared about how quickly things were progressing. We've seen this in the call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to pace the frontier and kind of slow down AI development. This has not been true for other waves of technology that Casey and I have covered in our careers. You didn't see people at Facebook saying how terrified they were of the godlike superintelligence they were trying to build. But this is really a feature of the modern AI era, is that the people on the inside who have the most exposure to the technology are in some sense the most concerned. INSKEEP: I feel that you have a unique challenge, which I certainly experience as a journalist, as a broadcaster, when I touched this topic, and that is trying to understand myself what is going on and then explain it to laymen. It's extraordinarily difficult. NEWTON: It's very difficult, but I think it's a challenge that Kevin and I both relish. We have seen firsthand the power of explanatory journalism to get people interested in a topic and give them the tools they need to make better decisions about the kind of world that they live in. ROOSE: And, Steve, it's really not that complicated. I mean, if two idiots like us can understand it, I have high hopes for the NPR audience. (LAUGHTER) INSKEEP: That's good. That's good. I'd like to understand how you think about the developments of the last several days. You already referred to them. Jacob Coxon was a relatively junior employee who quit and issued this warning. Dario Amodei, the CEO of the entire company, talks about pacing AI differently and wanting antitrust exemptions so that companies can collaborate on safety. There are all kinds of theories about why all of this discussion is happening now. There are some conspiracy theories about why it's all happening now. What do you think is going on? NEWTON: You know, at the most fundamental level, it is the CEOs of really two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, who have the best window into the present state of AI development. And when they look at the models that they're building right now that haven't yet been released to the public, they're seeing things that make them really, really worried. And they're saying, hey, even if we were to stop individually, we're not confident that other companies around the world would stop. And so this is the time to figure out how we would initiate a slowdown if we felt like we were getting to that point. ROOSE: Yeah. And I don't buy the conspiracy theories, Steve, because these people have been talking about these risks for years. I think what's new is that other people outside the bubble are starting to talk about it as well. INSKEEP: What keeps you guys awake at night when you think about this topic? NEWTON: I mean, I think for me, it would be what they call recursive self-improvement. The idea that eventually these systems will just build and improve themselves and they will just improve at a rate where human beings can't understand what's going on. And, you know, if that were to happen, we may enter some kind of scenario where we see ourselves losing control over this technology. ROOSE: And I'll throw in another bit of AI insider jargon, which is I worry about the alignment problem. This is the classic dilemma of how you build a system that is aligned with human values. It's an unsolved technical problem, and as these systems get closer and closer to human-level experts, it's even more urgent that we figure out how to make them behave not just predictably, but to also behave in line with our values, to not go off and conduct cyber attacks or build bioweapons. So that's what keeps me up at night. INSKEEP: And let me ask you about the other side of this. When you peel away the hype, what excites you about the possibilities of this technology, for real? NEWTON: I mean, Kevin and I both get really excited about applications in medicine, the potential of this technology to help us discover new drugs and otherwise improve medical care. If you're on the side of human progress and you'd like to see us make great scientific discoveries, it seems like AI could be a really great tool to get us there as long as we're able to manage all of the risks. ROOSE: And I'm excited about some of the more sort of mundane daily applications of this stuff. We're creating this company now and this new show and we needed a website. And I've been building websites for more than 20 years and I've spent untold weeks, months, years of my life struggling through some sort of programming problem related to a website I'm building. And now we were able to just give an AI a set of instructions about our company and what we're doing and some visual assets, and it went off and built an amazing website that was better than anything I could have done. INSKEEP: Casey Newton and Kevin Roose are the hosts of the new show Machine Gods. You will see their work on NPR starting in October. It's video first. A full radio program will be available on NPR member stations early next year. Gentlemen, thanks. ROOSE: Thanks so much, Steve. NEWTON: Thanks, Steve. INSKEEP: And because we mentioned Anthropic, I will note that Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. item.title: Poland's prime minister warns of Russian 'accidental' attacks on Ukraine's allies
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 4.14
Poland's prime minister warns of Russian 'accidental' attacks on Ukraine's allies BERLIN — Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia is planning strikes on countries supporting Ukraine. Addressing Polish lawmakers on Thursday, Tusk said Russia intends to send drones or missiles into NATO territory and then claim that these incidents are "accidental." His warning followed a series of incidents blamed on Russia along NATO's eastern flank. Tusk said that these potential strikes "intend to paralyze NATO" or "at least weaken the alliance's willingness to respond collectively" in an attempt to demonstrate that Article 5 "exists only in theory." NATO's Article 5 states that an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all members. Tusk said he'd received intelligence from NATO, Ukraine and U.S. agencies but did not specify which ones he was citing. He stressed that "there is nothing to suggest an invasion" but warned that Poland is about to face a real test as one of Ukraine's staunchest allies. Tusk, who was addressing the Polish parliament on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, also warned that political shifts within Europe are undermining NATO's commitment to Ukraine. He appeared to refer to Russia-friendly political parties currently gaining ground in Europe, such as Marine Le Pen's National Rally in France and the far-right Alternative for Germany. Tusk said that although those parties ostensibly invoke symbols of peace, they are calling for the capitulation of Ukraine. Tusk also questioned whether NATO members in the West were giving any thought to the alliance's eastern flank, pointing out that Poland is more likely to need allied loyalty under Article 5 than Portugal or Ireland due to its proximity to Russia and Ukraine. But just after Tusk spoke, President Trump announced progress in establishing a permanent U.S. Army base in Poland, where troops are currently hosted on a rotational basis. "If this happens, the location will be announced very soon," Trump said in a social media post. "This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance." A European military official, who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, said two sites in western Poland are under consideration for the base. Tusk's warning comes at the end of a week of airspace violations and incidents that European countries are blaming on Russia. On Sunday a Russian drone hit a passenger train in Ukraine just over a mile from the Polish border, shortly after former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European security officials had traveled through the area. On Monday, the Polish military said it retrieved a Russian drone just off the country's northwestern coast, which authorities say was carrying a warhead. On Tuesday, NATO jets shot down a drone in Lithuania. European countries are starting to speak up directly about what they perceive to be a coordinated campaign of hybrid attacks on their soil. These incidents include acts of sabotage, cyberattacks or disinformation, but do not reach the bar of an act of war. Earlier this month, the German government blamed Russian operatives for an attempted drone strike on an airport that serves as a major NATO hub. Russia's Foreign Ministry denies the accusations, calling them "contrived" and "far-fetched." But Tusk's warning was as much for NATO as it was for Moscow. He ended his speech by appealing for unity and a resolute response to any attacks and underscored Poland's own commitment to NATO's defense. Greg Myre contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

item.title: As Europe warms, Italy sees West Nile virus spread
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 3.88
As Europe warms, Italy sees West Nile virus spread Italian health authorities see evidence that rising temperatures and longer warm seasons are helping mosquitoes spread West Nile virus across a wider area, during more months of the year. More than 650 infections have been reported in Italy so far this year, accounting for roughly half of all cases recorded in Europe, according to local health authorities. "Higher temperatures linked to climate change help mosquitoes reproduce and extend the transmission season, increasing the chances that infected mosquitoes will spread the virus to people," said Antonino Bella, researcher at Italy's National Institute of Health, or ISS. West Nile has been considered endemic in Italy since 2020, when cases started to surge, and is now reported every summer and early fall. About 80% of infected people develop no symptoms, while most others experience a mild flu-like illness. Severe neurological complications occur in a small minority of cases, mainly among older adults and people with underlying health conditions. Experts say this year's case numbers are broadly in line with recent seasons. But warmer temperatures favor mosquito reproduction and can mean the transmission season sometimes lasts as late as November, Bella explained. Areas once largely unaffected are increasingly reporting infections, reflecting a gradual expansion of the virus across the country. Italy's experience with the virus is drawing attention from European countries located farther north. A Belgian research team visited the ISS last May to study Italy's research and surveillance system after the country began recording locally acquired West Nile cases. The Netherlands this year has reported more than two dozen West Nile cases, the first since 2020, as well as several deaths, according to its public health institute. "There's no doubt that warming weather will expand the period of replication for the virus and the vector in more countries," said Marc-Alain Widdowson, who leads the Pandemic Threats, Communicable Diseases, and AMR Division at the World Health Organization's Europe office. "You've got to be careful not to say that climate change is all of it, but certainly a warming climate means that we have a longer mosquito season, so that the vectors can survive for longer. Warm temperatures also mean that the virus itself will survive better," he added. Experts note that Italy's extensive monitoring network, which tracks mosquitoes, birds, blood donors and human infections, also helps explain why the country detects so many cases. "There are definitely trends which we think are contributing to increased activity," Widdowson said, citing a warming climate, loss of biodiversity and changes in land use. A longer mosquito season creates more opportunities for transmission, he added, while declines in bird diversity may favor species that are efficient reservoirs of the virus. In June, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control, or ECDC, warned that because Europe is experiencing a warming trend — with heat waves and flooding becoming more frequent and severe, and summers getting longer and warmer — the conditions are more favorable for invasive mosquito species such as Aedes albopictus and Aedes aegypti. Aedes aegypti — known to transmit dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya, zika and West Nile viruses — has been established in Cyprus since 2022 and may spread to other European countries. A decade ago, the Aedes albopictus mosquito was established in eight European countries, with 114 regions affected. This year, the mosquito is established in 13 countries and 337 regions, the ECDC said.

item.title: What to know after a week of Houthi attacks that threaten Saudi oil
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 3.26
What to know after a week of Houthi attacks that threaten Saudi oil CAIRO — It's been a week since Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels stormed down the Red Sea coast, extending their reach to a key maritime chokepoint and threatening Saudi Arabia's oil exports. The Houthis' biggest land grab in years reignited Yemen's 12-year civil war and pushed up global fuel prices. It also gave Iran another potential source of leverage as the United States has started to loosen Tehran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. The Houthis are also firing at Saudi oil facilities and tankers. An attack on Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline, blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq, added to an unfolding nightmare for the kingdom and rattled world markets. The rebel blitz has forced some 125,000 Yemenis to flee their homes. The civil war has killed over 150,000 people and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine. Now the rebels appear to be eyeing Yemen's oil-rich east. So far, the only thing standing in their way is Yemen's Saudi-backed government and an array of forces that have fought each other as recently as January. Saudi Arabia's most important ally, the U.S., appears to be sitting this one out. The Houthis are fighting on several fronts The Houthis captured the important Red Sea port city of Mokha before taking several islands near the narrow Bab el-Mandeb strait, through which some 12% of world trade passes in peacetime. They are also just 32 kilometers (20 miles) from Djibouti, a small African nation hosting U.S. and other military bases. The Houthis first swept down from their northern heartland in 2014, capturing the capital, Sanaa, and much of northern Yemen. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year, and fighting raged until a 2022 ceasefire. In recent days, there has been heavy fighting in and around Marib, a central city in an oil-rich province of the same name. Previous Houthi offensives have failed to capture the city, which also serves as a military hub for Saudi-backed forces. The Houthis also threaten the western city of Taiz, a front line for much of the conflict. Tightening the noose on the world's largest oil exporter The Houthis want Saudi Arabia to lift a long-running blockade on the territory they control. "It is Saudi Arabia that closed the Bab el-Mandeb strait to shipping traffic to and from Yemen and imposed an unjust blockade on the country," Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, told The Associated Press. The Saudis and their allies have long struggled to contain or deter the Houthis, and may be tempted to seek a diplomatic solution to halt the attacks. That might ultimately require U.S. concessions to Iran, the only country with leverage over the Houthis. The U.S., which bombed the Houthis under the Biden and Trump administrations, has shown no interest in getting involved this time around, and the Houthis appear keen to keep it that way. They say they are only attacking Saudi shipping. Traffic has recovered in the Red Sea, for now Windward, a shipping firm, reported a dip in traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb from 35 daily transits before the Houthi advance to 25 after, but traffic has already recovered and climbed to 45 transits on Sunday. The Houthis could still expand their target bank beyond Saudi ships and tankers. During their self-styled blockade of Israel at the height of the war in Gaza, the Houthis attacked ships in the Red Sea with no known connection to that conflict. "At the moment, their focus is on Saudi-linked shipping," said Valentin d'Hauthuille, a Middle East analyst at ACLED, a conflict monitor. But they might "extend the criteria according to which vessels are assessed to be 'Saudi-linked' to increase pressure on both Saudi and the global economy." There are signs of diplomacy, but the cost could be high Regional mediators have sprung into action, but a diplomatic agreement appears unlikely without some kind of breakthrough in the wider Iran war. Iran wants the U.S. to lift a blockade and sanctions that have devastated its economy, while the U.S. seeks the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a deal to roll back Tehran's nuclear program. Neither side has shown any sign of budging since a preliminary agreement quickly crumbled over the summer. Last weekend, Oman hosted a meeting between U.S. and Houthi representatives, a Houthi official and another individual familiar with the talks told The Associated Press this week. The U.S. says it has been in "constant contact" with the Saudis, a close ally and the recipient of billions of dollars in American military assistance. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman recently visited Egypt, which has served as a regional mediator. A government official in Turkey, another potential mediator, said this week that it was in talks with Iran and the United Arab Emirates to try and lower tensions. The Houthi attacks are the first test of a new defense pact among Saudi Arabia, NATO member Turkey and nuclear power Pakistan. But officials from Turkey and Pakistan say they have not received a Saudi request for support. The humanitarian situation in Yemen is worsening The latest fighting has killed eight civilians and wounded another 32, according to the U.N. humanitarian office, which says an estimated 125,000 people have fled their homes. The Health Ministry in the Saudi-backed government says the Houthis have killed around 150 civilians since Sept. 3. Saudi Arabia said Thursday that debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed one person and wounded two others in the kingdom. Yemen was the poorest Arab country even before the civil war, and has experienced widespread hunger in recent years because of the conflict and the Saudi-led blockade. The Houthis' detention of U.N. and aid workers has hampered international assistance in the territories they control. Experts say the Houthis have struggled to pay civil servants, leading to some unrest, and have diverted much of their tax revenues to their military wing. The U.N. humanitarian office, known as OCHA, says only 20% of its humanitarian appeal for Yemen has been funded, and that "millions risk losing access to food, healthcare, nutrition, water and protection services." "The needs are extremely high right now," said Sara Ahmed, a supervisor with Doctors Without Borders in Mokha. Doctors are working under difficult conditions to keep essential services running despite hearing airstrikes, she said. Mahida Ahmed fled the fighting in Mokha and is now sheltering in a displacement camp in Aden, where the Saudi-backed government is headquartered. She said she left in a hurry, with her children but no belongings, while her husband is still stranded in Mokha. "This war has been completely devastating for us," she said.

item.title: France, Poland and European allies warn of escalating Russian 'hybrid' attacks
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 2.71
France, Poland and European allies warn of escalating Russian 'hybrid' attacks The leaders of France, Poland, and other leading European nations are alarmed over what they describe as Russian "hybrid" attacks. SCOTT SIMON, HOST: And now to Europe, where leaders in France, Poland and across the continent this week are saying the Russians are coming. Their warning stems from what they say are increasingly brazen Russian attacks. NPR's Russia correspondent, Charles Maynes, joins us now. Charles, thanks so much for being with us. CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott. SIMON: When these European leaders mention Russian attacks, they call them hybrid. What's that? MAYNES: Well, they're referring to moves that fall into a kind of gray zone. You know, they're not traditional military attacks but nonetheless undermine Europe's sense of security. So we've seen what looked to be attempts to sabotage defense or logistics infrastructure. For example, attack drones were found hidden at an airport in Germany that serves as a transit hub for NATO. There are also allegations of cyberattacks, election interference or misinformation. And in the U.S., the Trump administration's Justice Department last week said it had foiled a Russian plot to assassinate an exiled dissident. You know, of course, all this comes in the context of Russia's war in Ukraine, which is now in its fifth year, and we've repeatedly seen drones fall on or near bordering NATO member countries like Poland and Romania. And while some are believed to be errant drones that had really just gone off course, there's growing evidence that's not always the case. It seems they're there to provoke and maybe even strike targets. SIMON: But is there proof that Russia is responsible? MAYNES: Well, that's tougher to say. Western intelligence agencies say they have no doubt these are acts carried out by Moscow. As to proof, they point to communication intercepts, messages essentially sent by Russian security services where third parties are offered money to carry out assignments. So in other words, they're kind of task rabbits hired to do the dirty work. SIMON: And what does Russia say? MAYNES: Well, they say there's no proof, and this is just scaremongering against Russia. In some cases, like this German airport incident, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said outright this is an elaborate false-flag operation with these attacks staged by Ukraine or the West to rally the European public against Moscow. And I have to say the Kremlin is quite good at exploiting these denials at home. You know, they say to the Russian public, look how they blame us, how they blame you for everything, whether it's doping in sports, atrocities in Ukraine, threatening Europe, election interference, you name it. You know, Russia is always the guilty party, and I think some Russians, as a result, say, well, maybe they do hate us. SIMON: If it is Russia, what's the rationale? What would Moscow be trying to achieve? MAYNES: Well, Russia's long argued the West, through its military support for Ukraine, is de facto a direct participant in the war. And so the theory here is that Russia's punishing Europe for this in particular to the point where European leaders - or at least their voters - eventually say, enough's enough. Ukraine's just not worth the trouble. SIMON: But doesn't that risk a direct conflict with NATO? MAYNES: Well, that's the fear that one of these attacks proves deadly, and NATO may feel it has to respond. Perhaps even by triggering Article 5, the concept that an attack on one member of NATO is an attack on all. And so the theory is that the Russian approach here is to keep it just below that threshold and instead undermine the alliance gradually. You know, think of it as death to Article 5 by a thousand cuts. SIMON: So what does Europe or the West do then? MAYNES: Well, European leaders like France's Emmanuel Macron or Poland's Donald Tusk have made clear they intend to get tougher with Moscow through more sanctions on Russia, support to Ukraine, perhaps even some military action if necessary. The Trump administration's approach seems quite to be the opposite. You know, they want to engage and talk up a future of deals and prosperity to help get issues like Ukraine settled, and the rest, they think, will take care of itself. You know, which approach - carrot or stick - is better? I don't know. I don't think anybody does. But we're at a dangerous moment as we wait to find out. SIMON: NPR's Charles Maynes. Thanks so much. MAYNES: Thank you. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. Transcript text may be revised to correct errors or match updates to audio. Audio on npr.org may be edited after its original broadcast or publication. The authoritative record of NPR’s programming is the audio record.

item.title: The 10 best places to visit in Alaska, ranked
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.16
The 10 best places to visit in Alaska, ranked From glacier-fed fjords and towering peaks to wildlife-rich islands, these Alaska destinations showcase the state’s wild beauty Alaska defies easy summary. The state covers more than 663,000 square miles, contains eight national parks, and holds more coastline than the rest of the United States combined. It is also, for a place of that scale, more accessible than the statistics suggest: Anchorage is a three-hour flight from Seattle, the Alaska Marine Highway ferry connects the southeastern communities without requiring an airplane, and several of the state’s most dramatic landscapes are reachable by road or day trip from the main population centers. Alaska rewards travelers who make the effort to get there with an experience of wild scale that no other American state delivers. The state's variety is as impressive as its scale. A single Alaska trip might include whale watching in a Southeast fjord, a flight over glaciers from a small mountain town, bear viewing on a remote island with no road access, and a morning hike above treeline, with North America’s tallest peak within sight. The distances between these experiences are real, but the infrastructure that connects them, small aircraft, ferries, and a network of outfitters with deep local knowledge, makes multi-stop Alaska itineraries achievable for travelers willing to plan ahead. The 10 destinations below appear in Travel + Leisure, covering the best places to visit in Alaska as recommended by Travel + Leisure editors and regional experts, drawn from the first 10 entries in the publication’s list of 20 top Alaskan destinations. They span the genuinely full range of what Alaska delivers: the state’s largest city, one of the most remote bear-viewing sites in North America, the continent’s tallest mountain, and a state park that begins where Anchorage’s eastern suburbs end, putting half a million acres of mountain wilderness within bus distance of the city. 1. Anchorage works as a base and a destination in itself Wonderlane / Unsplash Anchorage is often treated as the place you fly into before getting to Alaska proper, a gateway to the state, not a destination within it. That framing undersells what the city actually is. Alaska’s largest city by a significant margin, Anchorage has excellent restaurants, a genuine local culture built around outdoor recreation, and mountain views from downtown that few cities in the country can match. The Chugach Mountains rise directly behind the city to the east, and on clear days Denali is visible 130 miles to the north, a reminder that Alaska operates at a scale where the continent’s highest peak is a distant backdrop from a city of nearly 300,000 people. Diana Rhoades of the Anchorage Park Foundation points visitors to the Moose Loop, a 32-mile, mostly flat path around the city shaped like a moose. The path passes through dozens of parks where moose and other wildlife are regularly spotted, giving Anchorage a wildlife-viewing dimension that most urban park systems cannot provide. The Tony Knowles Coastal Trail, an 11-mile paved path running along the western edge of the city above Knik Arm, delivers views across the inlet to the Alaska Range and is one of the most scenic urban recreational trails in the country. The city’s restaurant scene has grown considerably over the past decade and now includes serious dining options alongside the seafood-focused casual restaurants that the fishing culture sustains. The Anchorage Museum, housed in a contemporary building downtown, is one of Alaska’s strongest cultural institutions and provides essential context for the state’s Indigenous heritage, natural history, and contemporary art scene. Anchorage functions best as a multi-day stay at the start or end of a broader Alaska trip, with day trips to Girdwood, Talkeetna, the Matanuska Glacier, and the Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center at Portage all accessible by road in under two hours from the city center, making Anchorage one of the most versatile base camps in American travel. 2. Admiralty Island teems with brown bears at Pack Creek Credit: Travel Alaska Admiralty Island in Southeast Alaska, accessible only by floatplane or boat from Juneau, holds one of the highest densities of brown bears anywhere in North America. The island’s Pack Creek bear-viewing area, managed jointly by the U.S. Forest Service and the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, provides structured viewing platforms and guided access during the July-through-September salmon season, when bears congregate at the creek to fish. Jordan Lambe of Maple Leaf Adventures describes Pack Creek as a highlight for wildlife lovers, and the word highlight undersells what Pack Creek offers: standing near fishing brown bears at distances most national park bear encounters don't approach. The island covers about 1,664 square miles of old-growth Tongass National Forest and is sometimes called Kootznoowoo, the Tlingit name meaning Fortress of the Bears, a designation that reflects both the density of the bear population and the island's cultural significance to the Tlingit people, whose traditional territory it is. The bear population is estimated at roughly one bear per square mile, a density that makes encounters on hiking trails a possibility even outside the managed viewing areas. The forest itself, old-growth Sitka spruce and western hemlock, is among the most intact temperate rainforest ecosystems remaining in the world. Access to Pack Creek requires a permit during peak season, and the permit system limits the number of visitors at the viewing platforms at any one time, which helps preserve the quality of the experience. Tours from Juneau operate by floatplane and typically include a full day on the island. Visitors who want a longer experience can arrange multi-day camping with outfitters familiar with the island’s regulations. Admiralty Island is the version of Alaska wildlife viewing the state’s reputation promises, but many more accessible destinations cannot fully deliver. Old-growth forest, salmon-rich streams, and managed access at Pack Creek together make it one of the most complete bear-viewing experiences available anywhere in North America. 3. Denali National Park guards North America’s tallest peak Credit: Alaska.org Denali National Park and Preserve covers six million acres of subarctic wilderness anchored by Denali, the 20,310-foot peak and highest mountain in North America. As Scott Claggett of the National Park Service describes it, travelers on the park’s single road watch low-elevation taiga forest give way to alpine tundra and snow-covered mountains, culminating at the continent’s tallest summit. The transition happens gradually across the 92-mile park road, and the scale of what the road reveals grows with each mile: wider valleys, larger glaciers, higher ridgelines, and eventually the full profile of Denali itself, visible from the road on clear days as a mass so large it reads from a distance as a range, not a single peak. Private vehicles are restricted beyond the first 15 miles of the park road. Everything beyond that point is accessible only by the Park Service’s bus system, which runs from late May through early September and operates as both transport and wildlife-viewing platform. The restriction concentrates the park’s human presence on the road itself and leaves the vast majority of the six million acres as genuine wilderness, which is why the wildlife viewing from the bus, grizzly bears, wolves, moose, caribou, and Dall sheep moving through terrain unhabituated to vehicles, is as good as it is. Pulling up to a sleeping grizzly from a bus window at 50 feet is an experience the park’s management structure specifically enables. The weather at Denali is famously unpredictable, and the summit is obscured by cloud on roughly two-thirds of days. Visitors who build extra days into their itinerary, planning for the possibility of a clouded-in day at the Eielson Visitor Center at mile 66, give themselves the best odds of seeing what they came to see. The park’s backcountry permit system, which distributes backpackers across the landscape using zone maps instead of maintained trails, offers one of the most accessible genuine wilderness experiences in the American park system. 4. Girdwood packs adventure and mountain scenery year-round Credit: Alaska.org Girdwood sits about 40 miles south of Anchorage in the Chugach Mountains and operates as Alaska’s most complete year-round mountain town. Nicole Geils of the Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center describes Girdwood as packed with adventure and incredible scenery, and the description applies across every season: Alyeska Resort, the state’s most developed ski area, provides winter skiing on terrain that rises to 3,939 feet above sea level, while summer brings hiking, glacier viewing, and wildlife activity in the surrounding Chugach State Park and national forest terrain. The town’s setting in a narrow valley surrounded by peaks that exceed 5,000 feet creates the compressed, dramatic scenery that distinguishes Girdwood from the more open landscapes that characterize most of Alaska’s accessible mountain areas. The Alyeska Aerial Tram ascends from the resort base to 2,300 feet in summer, offering views over Turnagain Arm and the surrounding peaks with no hiking commitment. The Crow Creek Mine, a placer gold operation active since 1898, offers gold panning and a window into the small-scale mining history that shaped many of Alaska’s mountain communities. Girdwood is also the gateway to the Matanuska and Knik Glaciers, both accessible by road, and to the tide flats of Turnagain Arm, one of the best locations in Alaska to watch bore tides, the wave-like surge of water that the arm’s unusual geometry generates during certain tidal conditions. The round trip from Anchorage to Girdwood by the Seward Highway is one of Alaska’s most scenic drives, running along the edge of Turnagain Arm with the tidal water on one side and the Chugach peaks on the other for most of the route. The highway also passes through the small community of Portage, where the Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center provides drive-through wildlife viewing and the Portage Glacier is accessible by cruise. Girdwood is within easy day-trip range of Anchorage but rewards an overnight stay for visitors who want to use it as a base for the surrounding terrain. 5. Kodiak Island earns its fame through bears and fishing Credit: Travel Alaska Kodiak Island in the Gulf of Alaska is home to the Kodiak brown bear, a subspecies whose isolation since the last ice age has produced the largest brown bears on earth by average body weight. The Kodiak National Wildlife Refuge covers 1.9 million acres of the island’s rugged interior and supports an estimated 3,500 bears whose primary food source is the salmon that fill the island’s streams during the summer and fall runs. Viewing platforms above salmon-bearing streams allow visitors to watch Kodiak bears fishing at close range during peak season, one of the most concentrated wildlife encounters available in Alaska for non-backcountry travelers. Kodiak’s fishing reputation extends well beyond the bear-viewing season. The island’s commercial fishing fleet is one of the largest in the United States by volume, and the king crab, halibut, salmon, and black cod fisheries operating from Kodiak’s harbor give the city a working-port character that sharply distinguishes it from Alaska’s more tourism-oriented communities. Charter operators in Kodiak offer sport fishing for king salmon, silver salmon, halibut, and Dolly Varden char, with some of the state's most productive halibut grounds accessible within a day’s boat ride. The island’s rugged coastline, accessible by small boat and floatplane, holds seabird colonies, sea otter populations, Steller sea lions, and orca whales in the surrounding Gulf waters. The Baranov Museum in Kodiak covers the Russian colonial period, when the island served as the capital of Russian America, adding historical depth to a destination whose contemporary identity centers on wildlife and fishing. Access is by daily jet service from Anchorage or by the state ferry system, and Gulf of Alaska weather can change quickly enough that travelers benefit from building flexibility into any Kodiak itinerary. Fog and wind can ground flights and affect boat operations without much warning, and a spare day is sensible planning, not excessive caution. 6. Kenai Fjords National Park sends 40 glaciers to the coast Credit: U.S. National Park Service Kenai Fjords National Park sits on the southeastern edge of the Kenai Peninsula, about 130 miles south of Anchorage, and its defining feature is the Harding Icefield, one of the largest icefields in the United States, from which nearly 40 glaciers flow to the coast. As Scott Claggett describes it, the park exists at the edge of the Kenai Peninsula where the Ice Age still lingers, with wildlife thriving in the icy waters and lush forests along the fjords carved by that vast expanse of ice. The park’s most dramatic features are its tidewater glaciers, which reach the sea and calve house-sized blocks of ice into the fjords below, with a crack and splash audible across the water. The park is primarily accessed by boat from Seward, and day tours from the town’s small boat harbor provide the most efficient introduction to what the park contains. The marine wildlife in the fjords is exceptional: orca whales, humpback whales, Steller sea lions, harbor seals, sea otters, Dall’s porpoises, and puffins all inhabit the waters, drawn by the nutrient-rich environment that glacial meltwater creates. Tours that travel to the outer coast beyond the sheltered fjords reach the park's most remote sections and offer the best opportunities for humpback whale encounters. Exit Glacier, the park’s only road-accessible feature, provides a different kind of glacial encounter: a series of maintained trails through glacial moraine, with dated markers showing the glacier’s position in previous decades, making the scale of recent recession tangible in a way that a boat ride past an active calving face does not. The Harding Icefield Trail, a strenuous full-day hike from the glacier’s parking area, climbs approximately 3,500 feet above the treeline to the edge of the icefield itself, providing one of the most physically demanding and visually extraordinary experiences available to non-technical hikers anywhere in the state, with total elevation gain of approximately 3,500 feet over eight miles round trip. 7. Frederick Sound fills with humpback whales each season Credit: Holland America Frederick Sound in Southeast Alaska is a body of water between Admiralty Island and the Alaskan mainland that has earned a reputation among wildlife photographers and marine biologists as one of the world's most reliable locations for observing humpback whale behavior. The nutrient-rich waters that flow through the sound during the summer feeding season attract large numbers of humpback whales, often creating, as Jordan Lambe of Maple Leaf Adventures puts it, remarkable encounters that exceed what most dedicated whale-watching tours elsewhere deliver. Bubble-net feeding, in which groups of humpbacks cooperate to herd fish into a concentrated column before lunging through the surface together, is observed at Frederick Sound more frequently than almost anywhere else on earth. The sound is best accessed by boat from the small community of Petersburg or from Juneau, and expedition-style tours that spend multiple days in the sound provide the sustained time near the whales that single-day excursions cannot. The Southeast Alaska ecosystem that Frederick Sound is part of supports the full range of North Pacific marine life: orca whales, Steller sea lions, harbor seals, Dall’s porpoises, and seabirds including marbled murrelets and pigeon guillemots all inhabit the sound alongside the humpbacks. The geography of Southeast Alaska, with its protected inner channels and nutrient-rich fjords, creates conditions that support this marine diversity across the full summer season. The best months for Frederick Sound whale watching are July through September, when humpbacks reach peak feeding density before migrating south to winter breeding grounds. The surrounding landscape, with the peaks of the Coast Mountains rising above the spruce-hemlock forest on the mainland and Admiralty Island’s old-growth forest on the western shore, provides a visual backdrop that makes the whale encounters feel embedded in an intact ecosystem, not staged as a managed attraction. Frederick Sound is one of the experiences that Alaska offers that genuinely has no close equivalent elsewhere in the accessible world. 8. Talkeetna lifts visitors over Denali and charms below Credit: Travel Alaska Talkeetna is a small town at the base of Denali, accessible by road about two hours north of Anchorage or by the Denali Star train that stops at the community’s historic depot, and it serves two distinct visitor functions that reinforce each other without competing. The first is as the primary departure point for flight-seeing tours over Denali and the Alaska Range, operated by small air services that fly ski planes onto the range's glaciers and land on the ice for guided walks in terrain otherwise accessible only to mountaineers. The glacier landing experience, standing on the Kahiltna or Ruth Glacier with the peaks of the Alaska Range rising above, is specific to this part of Alaska and is among the most dramatic accessible experiences the state offers. The second function is the town itself. Talkeetna’s walkable downtown is a compact collection of colorful storefronts, local breweries, independent restaurants, and the kind of authentic Alaska character that more tourist-oriented communities spend considerable effort recreating without achieving. The Talkeetna Historical Society Museum documents the town’s history as the primary staging base for Denali expeditions, with photographs and equipment from the mountain's climbing history spanning a century of summit attempts. The Fairview Inn, open since 1923, is the social anchor of the downtown and serves as a gathering place for the mix of climbers, pilots, river guides, and travelers that gives Talkeetna its specific social character. The Talkeetna River and the confluence of the Talkeetna, Susitna, and Chulitna rivers just outside town provide kayaking, jet boat tours, and fishing access in terrain that looks north toward the peaks the town exists to serve. The view of Denali from the town’s airport area on clear days, with the mountain’s full profile visible above the taiga forest and river flats, is one of the most satisfying ground-level views of the peak available at any accessible location. Talkeetna rewards a full day or an overnight stay, not a drive-through stop. 9. Sitka layers Tlingit and Russian history on the Pacific Credit: Alaska.org Sitka occupies Baranof Island on Alaska’s southeastern panhandle, surrounded by the Pacific Ocean and the Tongass National Forest, and holds a concentration of historical significance unusual even by Alaskan standards. The city was the capital of Russian America from 1804 until the Alaska Purchase of 1867, and the Russian colonial period left behind Saint Michael’s Cathedral, the most prominent Russian Orthodox church in North America, and the Russian Bishop’s House, one of four surviving examples of Russian colonial construction on the continent. Layers of Russian architecture, Tlingit cultural sites, and the natural setting of ocean and forest give Sitka a depth of character its modest size would not suggest. Sitka National Historical Park preserves the site of the 1804 Battle of Sitka, the last major armed resistance by the Tlingit people to Russian colonial expansion, and presents Tlingit totem poles along a two-mile trail through old-growth forest that leads to the battle site. The park’s cultural center documents Tlingit history, craftsmanship, and the political and cultural dimensions of the colonial encounter, providing essential context for understanding Alaska’s Indigenous cultures. The Alaska Raptor Center rehabilitates injured birds of prey, including bald eagles, allowing close observation of birds in active recovery. Wildlife viewing around Sitka extends to sea otters and whales offshore, and the coastal trail system provides access to the meeting zone between old-growth forest and Pacific coastline. The Sitka Sound Science Center runs marine research and education programs open to visitors during the summer season. Sitka is accessible by Alaska Airlines jet service from Juneau and Seattle and by the Alaska Marine Highway ferry on the western Baranof Island route, and its historical depth, natural setting, and cultural richness together make it one of the most complete destinations in Southeast Alaska for travelers whose interests extend beyond wildlife and scenery alone, and whose itinerary has room for the kind of unhurried exploration the city rewards. 10. Chugach State Park gives Anchorage a wilderness backyard Credit: Travel Alaska Chugach State Park sits immediately east of Anchorage and covers approximately half a million acres of the western Chugach Mountains, making it one of the largest state parks in the United States and the piece of genuine wilderness that gives Anchorage a relationship with the landscape that few cities of comparable size enjoy. Diana Rhoades points visitors specifically to the Little O’Malley Peak trail, a 4.5-mile out-and-back that passes through wildflower meadows and alongside a creek before reaching summit views of the city, the inlet, and the Alaska Range beyond. The trail is well-maintained, family-accessible, and still produces the wildlife encounters that the proximity of actual wilderness to a major city makes possible. The park’s trail system ranges from easy valley walks accessible to all fitness levels to multi-day backcountry routes into the park’s remote interior, where glaciers, alpine lakes, and high-elevation terrain deliver the Alaska wilderness experience visitors might expect to require a plane to reach. The Flattop Mountain trail, among the park’s most popular, reaches a 3,510-foot summit above the treeline with views over Anchorage, the inlet, and, on clear days, Denali and the Alaska Range. The trailhead is accessible by city bus, which is an unusual amenity for a wilderness hiking destination. The park’s proximity to Anchorage means it absorbs the city’s resident outdoor population on weekdays and weekends alike, and popular trailheads fill early on clear summer days. Visiting midweek and starting before 8am improves the chances of a quieter experience on the most frequented routes. Chugach State Park is what makes Anchorage’s claim to be a gateway to Alaska’s wilderness more than a marketing statement: the wilderness actually begins at the city’s eastern edge, and the park is accessible to anyone staying in Anchorage without a car, a charter flight, or any additional planning beyond finding the right trail and arriving at the trailhead before the popular routes fill on clear summer mornings.

item.title: What it actually costs to run a DMV-authorized registration service like NeedTags in California
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 5.20
California's Department of Motor Vehicles licenses a small category of private businesses to do something most residents assume only a government office can do: process vehicle registrations, ownership transfers, renewals, and lien sales on the state's behalf. NeedTags, a North Hollywood-based registration service and authorized California DMV partner, operates inside that category. Getting there, and staying there, involves a specific set of state requirements that most customers never see. Registration services have drawn scrutiny over the fees they charge on top of what the DMV itself collects. What that scrutiny tends to skip over is what those fees fund: a business model built around state licensing, a mandatory bond, background-checked staff, a DMV computer connection, and continuous compliance obligations that never expire quietly on their own. Getting Licensed Comes First Anyone who wants to operate a registration service in California has to apply for an Occupational License through the DMV's Occupational Licensing Branch, a process governed by California Vehicle Code Section 505.2 and 11400 et seq. and Title 13 of the California Code of Regulations. The application includes a background investigation on the business owner and every employee who will handle DMV transactions, live scan fingerprinting for each of them, and photographs of the business location and signage for DMV review. An inspector visits the office in person to confirm the business is in an approved location and that its records meet state standards before a license gets issued at all. Licensing isn't a one-time hurdle. Every employee added to the operation has to be added to the DMV's approved employee listing, and every change to that roster, the business address, or the business name triggers its own filing and fee. The Bond Nobody Sees Before the DMV will license a registration service, the applicant has to post a $25,000 surety bond, filed on DMV Form OL 605 under CVC Section 11402. The bond isn't insurance in the traditional sense. It's a financial guarantee that if a registration service mishandles a customer's money or paperwork, the state or the harmed customer can collect against it, and the business then has to reimburse the bond company for whatever gets paid out. The bond has to be renewed annually to keep the license active, and letting it lapse is one of the fastest ways to lose the license entirely. Businesses that also want same-day plate and sticker issuance, rather than mailing paperwork to Sacramento and waiting, apply separately for the DMV's Business Partner Automation program, established under CVC Section 1685, which lets a licensed registration service process registration and titling transactions electronically and issue validated registration cards, stickers, and plates on the spot. That enrollment carries its own $305 nonrefundable application fee, plus $232 for each additional branch location, and requires a Statement of Personal History screening form and live scan for every employee directly involved in BPA transactions. DMV takes the system access seriously enough to require its own security review before granting it, separate from the review that produced the original license. Where the Money Actually Goes Once licensed, a registration service runs a business with the same fixed costs as any other storefront: office lease, staff wages, and the software and hardware needed to interface with DMV systems, plus costs that are specific to this industry. Bond premiums renew every year. Employee background checks and live scan fees apply to every new hire before that person can handle any customer paperwork. DMV filing and correction fees apply anytime a business changes address, adds a branch, or updates its employee roster. None of that touches the registration fees the DMV itself charges the customer. Those pass through the service untouched; the service fee covers the operational costs of processing the paperwork correctly the first time. Founder Eddy Asmerian said the fee reflects what a same-day, in-person transaction actually requires on the business side, not markup for its own sake. "We are exponentially faster, provide a personalized experience, and afford no wait times,"* Asmerian said. The Process, From Walk-In to Plate A typical transaction starts with the customer bringing in a title, a Manufacturer's Statement of Origin for a new vehicle, or out-of-state registration paperwork. Staff verify the documents, confirm a smog certification is on file where required, run a VIN verification if the vehicle was never registered in California, and calculate the DMV fees the customer owes. For licensed BPA partners, the transaction can be submitted and completed on the spot, with plates or stickers issued the same day rather than mailed weeks later. Every transaction has to be logged and retained in the business's records, which the DMV can audit at any time as part of the same compliance framework that governs the license itself. Why the Fee Exists The value case for a service like NeedTags is time and certainty rather than a discount. California's DMV offers direct online registration for many transactions with no service fee, and a customer with an afternoon to spare and no unusual paperwork can complete them on their own. What a licensed registration service sells is the difference between that and someone who doesn't know which form applies to their situation, is on a deadline they didn't know about, or wants a same-day plate instead of a mailed one. The fee funds the licensing, bonding, staffing, and system access that make that same-day, no-wait transaction possible, and it exists because the DMV built the private registration service category specifically to require all of it.

item.title: Live Five: Safety Orange, Gregory Page, We the Commas, Jason Graham, Adams Avenue Street Fair
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 4.34
Safety Orange at the Holding Company September 19 Reggae rockers Safety Orange came together in 1996, founded by singer-bassist Sol Turpin, a San Diego native from Sublime tribute band 40 Oz to Freedom, with guitarist/vocalist Greg Karlo (who once played with Turpin in a Cure tribute band). Their debut full-length Life as a Fish was followed by Troll Rock High and extensive touring. A third album called State of Where I Am, released on their own Wabasa Records label (Turpin’s middle name is Wabasa), included a cover of a song by the Cure. Their single for “Better Now” was featured on Spotify’s Reggae Summer Beach playlist, and a 2022 single called “Get Outta My Way” came with a sleeve illustrated by Dead & Company gig poster artist Mark Sgarbossa. They’ve released several new songs recently including “Salt Water,” “My Town,” and “Smokin’ Love.” The Ocean Beach event includes Gun Shy and Tropical Drip. Adams Avenue Street Fair in Kensington & Normal Heights September 19 and 20 Enjoy over 75 musical acts on six stages, taking place along Adams Avenue in Kensington and Normal Heights. The 44th annual event features around ten blocks of carnival rides, beer gardens, beer tastings, festival foods, and 300 exhibitors. Kicking off at 10 am each day, attractions include special performances like the Fern Street Circus, comedy shows hosted by the Adams Avenue Theater, and full craft beer pours and specialty drinks across multiple dedicated tasting areas. Among the local acts slated to appear are The Amandas, Auz Fontaine, the Beard & the Bird, Boostive, Euphoria Brass Band, Fred Heath & the Sidewinders, Gayle Skidmore, Grampadrew, Lord Howler, Manganista, Manzanita Blues, Midnight Rivals, MohaviSoul, Please Ask For Paul, Rookie Card, Sara Petite, Scary Pierre, Sue Palmer, Tigers In Cairo, Wild Wild Wets, and Ypsitucky. Gregory Page at Pilgrim United Church of Christ September 20 The son of a traveling Armenian pop singer and a mother who was the lead singer and saxophone player in one of Britain’s first all-girl groups, roots Americana rocker Gregory Page melds traditions of folk, Celtic, jazz, ragtime, blues, swing, and French romanticism. He has performed in a wide range of iconic venues such as the London Palladium, London’s 02 Arena, and The Paradiso in Amsterdam, playing events like the Woodford Folk Festival in Australia and countless international music fests, headlining as well as opening for Bob Dylan, Leon Russell, Judy Collins, Chris Isaak, and frequent collaborator Jason Mraz. Since Page’s first solo album in 1990, he has released over 20 more and appeared as a guest on dozens of others. He performs from time to time as a member of the Rugburns (who scored a big regional hit with “Hitchhiker Joe”), as well as famed acoustic duo the Hatchet Brothers (with Frank Lee Drennen of Loam), and he’s produced music for over two dozen artists, including Jason Mraz and Tom Brosseau. He won a pair of San Diego Music Awards in 2021, taking home trophies for Album of the Year and Best Pop Album for his full-length One Hell of a Memory. We the Commas at the Belly Up Tavern The three Comma siblings who make up alt-surf R&B rockers We the Commas play what they call Surf Alternative R&B, or SARB (the name of their first EP). The band members ranged in age from 17 to 23 when they began hosting a series of weekly three-hour gigs at the Bunker House in Oceanside, as well as appearing on San Diego’s KUSI Morning Show and at a March of Dimes charity event in Balboa Park. They released their debut single “Sherry” in 2020, followed by a single and video for “Custom Made” and a debut EP called Sarb later that year. They’ve been championed by supporters such as The Head and The Heart and Young the Giant, who both shared the group’s covers online, and they've worked with A-list production talent like Rex Kudo (Post Malone, Young Thug, Lil Uzi Vert) and Charlie Handsome (Khalid, The Weeknd, Drake). They released a new single in May called “As Of late.” The Solana Beach bill includes Isabella Erardi with guests Josue Vazquez and Zach Wolf. Jason Graham at L’Auberge Del Mar September 21 “I specialize in playing fun covers in a wide variety of genres,” says indie folk artist Jason Graham, who grew up studying music and performing in the Midwest. Known for his high-energy solo sets that blend pop, rock, folk, country, and top-40 hits, he uses live looping technology to create a dynamic one-man-band experience. “I have been lucky enough to travel the world playing music on cruise ships for the past few years,” he says of the four years he spent traveling and performing with Norwegian cruise lines playing six shows a week, three to four hours a night. Now married and newly settled in San Diego, he’s become a fixture at area nightclubs, hotels, and restaurants, including the Hotel Del Coronado, Barleymash, Andaz, Union Kitchen & Tap, Cannonball, Fairmont Grand Del Mar, La Valencia Hotel, and the Bahia Resort Hotel. Comments

item.title: Tours in Town: Thievery Corporation, Wave to Earth, Pierce the Veil
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 4.05
Thievery Corporation For over 20 years, Rob Garza and Eric Hilton have been expanding the dancefloor boundaries of EDM as Thievery Corporation. Though early efforts were paint-by-number exercises in straight dub and acid jazz, their evolution toward stadium spinning has been fueled by melding world music into their jams, particularly Middle-Eastern, Latin, and Indian sounds. Since the breakthrough release that landed them a worldwide audience, 2005’s The Cosmic Game, it’s not uncommon to find multiple languages represented on any given album, from Spanish and Italian to French, Portuguese, Romanian, Persian, and even Hindi. The band’s political and social stances are trotted out and propped up from time to time, as in “History” where Boston rapper Mr Lif complains about how “I can’t look at a cop without second-guessing.” The duo recently re-released their sixth studio album Culture Of Fear as a 15th Anniversary edition, and they’re currently on their 30th Anniversary Tour. Wave To Earth South Korean indie rock band Wave To Earth is known for their dreamy blend of lo-fi indie pop, surf rock, jazz-inspired percussion and drumming, and English-language songwriting. They create warm, melancholic, and atmospheric soundscapes with cinematic flourishes on tracks such as “light,” from their debut EP, which earned them early underground traction. They went viral on TikTok in 2020 with "seasons" from their album 0.1 Flaws and All, which surpassed 500 million streams, and their single "bad," which climbed to number one on Spotify's Viral 50 Global Chart. Promoting their work as "All Self-Made," members Daniel Kim (vocals, guitar), Cha Soon-jong (bass), and Shin Dong-gyu (drums) handle their own recording, mixing, mastering, visual art, and direct all of the band’s music videos. They have become one of the most-streamed South Korean indie acts globally, selling out major tours across North America, Europe, and Asia, and performing at major international festivals like Lollapalooza. Pierce the Veil Pierce the Veil was founded by singer/guitarist/songwriter Vic Fuentes and his drummer brother Mike, both former Mission Bay High School students who previously played with Early Times and Before Today. Their debut album Flair for the Dramatic - recorded in Seattle and in the studio that their parents had built for them in their home near Mission Bay - came out in summer 2007, during which the band took part in that year's Warped tour. In 2010, their album Selfish Machines debuted at number one on Billboard’s Heatseekers chart, and they toured that summer again with the Warped Tour, as the proggy metal band’s album racked up over 700,000 downloads. 2012’s Collide With the Sky became their biggest selling album, going gold and selling over 500,000 copies, while their fourth studio album from 2016, Misadventures, entered the Billboard Top 200 Chart at number four. Their most recent full-length, The Jaws of Life, dropped in 2023. This final date of the tour will be Pierce The Veil's only mainland U.S. headline appearance of the year.

item.title: Lynyrd Skynyrd: American rock band comes to town
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 3.36
Lynyrd Skynyrd is dead. Long live Lynyrd Skynyrd. Gary Rossington, the band's last surviving original member, died in 2023. Ronnie Van Zant, its original singer and principal songwriter, has been gone since 1977. But Lynyrd Skynyrd is still out there playing “Free Bird,” “Simple Man,” and “Sweet Home Alabama” — with Ronnie's younger brother Johnny Van Zant at the microphone, as he has been for nearly 40 years. The last of the street survivors is gone, but the show goes on, and next Thursday, Van Zant & Co. will bring that show to Del Mar. Street Survivors was, of course, the band’s fifth album, released just three days before the band’s plane crashed, killing Ronnie Van Zant, guitarist Steve Gaines, backup singer Cassie Gaines, and three others. That was the end of Lynyrd Skynyrd, until the fan response to their 1987 tribute tour —“Free Bird” closed the shows with an unmanned mic in honor of Ronnie and the crowd supplying the vocals — helped convince them to start up again. “My brother once said that recording music and making studio albums is great and fun, but Skynyrd is all about playing live,” says Van Zant. “That still stands today. It’s an awesome thing to see younger generations come out and experience the band live. To walk onstage and have those people loving the music — that’ll get you up on your bad days. I’ve played with kidney stones. I once played a show in San Diego with my appendix bursting” — at Viejas in May of 2006. “I did two shows not knowing” about the inflamed appendix, he recalls. “I just felt like crap. Then I got to Shoreline Amphitheater up in Mountain View and ended up going into Stanford Medical Center and having an emergency operation. But I got through those two shows, with help from Skynyrd Nation. Whoever wrote ‘The show must go on’ really lived it. That’s what we do. I woke up from surgery saying, ‘You think I can do the show tomorrow?’ And the doctor was like, ‘Oh no, Mr. Van Zant. You’re going to be here.’” When Van Zant got back on his feet and the band got back on the road, they stayed there, doing 80-100 shows a year until Rossington’s failing health led them to launch the Last of the Street Survivors Farewell Tour in 2018. The title echoed the earlier album, but it also belonged to a new song they had written about Rossington — and about the joys of doing it live. “I think it was myself, Tom Hambridge, Gary, and Rickey Medlocke in a room, and we just started writing about Gary: the last of the street survivors." Out here on 75, keepin’ the dream alive/ Highway brothers and midnight riders/ We’re the last of the street survivors. “COVID came along and blew that tour out,” recalls Van Zant. “We were off for 15 months” — long enough for the band to re-think their long goodbye. “We started back up, and we haven’t stopped since.” "Last of the Street Survivors" came easy. “I had the first few lines and the melody. Melodies are my schtick. Sometimes, God puts that on you and it just rolls. Those are really the best kind.” It isn’t always like that. “Me and my brother Donnie from .38 Special, we did a country record, and there’s a song on there called ‘The Things I Miss the Most.’ Me and Donnie and Jeffrey Steele were up in Nashville at a Residence Inn. I had been on the road, and I had given up drinking, but I was like, ‘Boy, a little Crown Royal sure helps the vocal cords.’ And I came up with the opening of the song: I swear I gave up drinking/ Sometimes I have no choice/ After singing hard six nights straight/ Another sip sure helps my voice. But there were about two words in the bridge that just didn’t come that night. It was three in the morning, and we were like, ‘Maybe we should come back to this tomorrow.’" That was 20 years ago. Today, what he misses most is what he leaves behind: “being at home, just being around the house. Right now, I’m in my sunroom in Florida, looking out at a pool and some green trees. I sold my brother Donnie some swampland, and now he’s my next door neighbor. I’m watching him go back and forth, cutting grass with his zero-turn John Deere. We’ve got a little studio in the back, and a little garage apartment back there, and that’s the hangout for the guys. His wife and my wife are good friends.” It's a serene scene for a guy who sings for a band that once had to take the engulfing flames off an album cover. “God puts you on a roller coaster,” concludes Van Zant. “But I believe everything happens for a reason. I don’t know why; I’m not smart enough. And I’m not supposed to know why. But life is very, very short, and there’s a better place than here. I try to get up every day and say, ‘Thank you, Lord, for the breath than I’m breathing. I’ve got another day to maybe make an impact on somebody’s life.’” For now, that means touring and singing the music that never went away. “I think my brother was a genius and wrote for God-fearing, common, hard-working people — patriots. I think that each generation has a lot of us, and it just goes on and on. The ‘Southern Rock’ tag came from MCA Records. But we always considered ourselves an American rock band.” But one day, it may mean sitting back down in the studio and paying proper tribute to Rossington. “We have a bunch of songs that we never got to record because Gary got too sick,” says Van Zant. “Hopefully, one day we’ll finish what we started. It would be a great thing to finish that in his honor.”

item.title: Puddles Pity Party isn't just clowning around
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 3.13
Quick, name a comic-book clown who’s upset about the state of the world and who, for some reason, sings a lot. What’s that? The Joker from the godawful bite-the-hand-that-applauds-you sequel Joker: Folie a Deux? Well, you’re not wrong. But happily, that’s not who’s on stage tomorrow night, opening for Weird Al Yankovic at Rady Shell. No, the crooning clown of the hour is Puddles from Puddles Pity Party, seen here in full comic color on the cover of his new album No One’s Free. “I wanted a cover that invites people in,” writes Puddles. (Our interview was conducted via email; Puddles saves his spoken words for his songs.) “The imagery is like a little sugar to make the medicine go down. I think comic books have traditionally been a vehicle for imagining justice served in a perpetually cruel world. The thought bubble is basically my ‘wtf’ reaction to all the division and intolerance and violent rhetoric permeating our society lately.” The album title is also the name of its first song, and in case that bit about division and intolerance wasn’t enough, you can tell from the outset that we’re a long way from “Royals,” the Lorde cover that first made Puddles an internet phenom back in 2013. (Mainstream stardom came four years later, when he reached the quarterfinals of America’s Got Talent.) “Royals” is the story of a poor girl from a torn-up town who can’t help but notice the difference between pop-star life — jet planes, islands, tigers on a gold leash — and her own. But, she says, we’re fine with this; we didn’t come from money. “No One’s Free” has none of that serenity. Right away, the song warns, The world is getting’ much too small, and there’s really no room at all, and if one of us starts to fall, we all go down. No one’s free ‘til we can see ourselves in every stranger. It's almost unsettling, hearing such an earnest sentiment from an ostensibly comic figure. (One of his most popular stage bits is singing the theme song from Gilligan’s Island to the epically varied tune of “Stairway to Heaven.”) It’s one thing to listen to him cover Radiohead’s “Creep” in all its plaintive angst. It’s another to hear him sing something you haven’t heard before — the songs were written by longtime friend Andrew Douglas Quinn — that includes a sentiment as naked as In the end, my friend/ We all stall/ We’ll all fall/ Ya lose it all/ But you can have a ball/ In spite of it all. It put me in mind of "Cloony the Clown" from Shel Silverstein’s poem about a clown who can’t make people laugh — until he tells them how sad he is. “And after he finished his tale of woe/ Did everyone cry? Oh no, no, no/ They laughed until they shook the trees/ With ‘Hah-hah-hahs’ and ‘Hee Hee-Hees…and while the world laughed outside/Cloony the Clown sat down and cried.” I asked Puddles if he’d read Cloony, and wondered if there was a kind of dare to the audience at work: can you listen to this from a clown without wondering if you’re supposed to laugh? “Shel Silverstein is my jam,” replied Puddles. “Telling a compelling story in an uncomplicated, sincere way leaves room for wondering. But nobody is ‘supposed’ to laugh or not laugh. Reactions are personal to the listener, purely subjective. Some folks laugh when faced with uncomfortable or sad subject matter. It may be a nervous reaction, but it’s authentic to them.” Or maybe it’s enough to just turn our attention to a song that will likely show up in Weird Al’s setlist: the similarly sincere "Skipper Dan." I’ve never quoted a YouTube comment before, but this one from @TheAncientTale is worth it: “I was at a weird Al concert when he actually explained this song. He was on a Disney water ride, and the tour guy was talking about his failed acting career. Weird Al said to himself ‘that’s a song.’ And he went home that day and worked on this song tirelessly. This isn’t a joke, he actually said that.” Give it a listen: the chorus is an absolute banger. But that’s the exception for Yankovic; usually, he’s a little more layered, as when he gives us a peppy anthem about executing people on behalf of the Deep State with “Party in the CIA.” As Puddles notes, “Weird Al’s crowd is dialed in for a wild time. They appreciate absurdity. That said, there are a few poignant moments in my set that can catch some off guard. I’ve seen grown men in the audience get moved to tears. I’m sure they did not expect the feels to overtake them in such a festive environment while sporting a tinfoil hat.” On “No One’s Free,” the absurdity is that, like Cloony, the clown is quite sincere. Puddles: “I sing what I mean, and I mean what I sing. I like the Mark Twain quote, ‘When in doubt, tell the truth.’” The callback to Twain — another humorist with a strong moral bent — led me to ask Puddles about his heritage. Pagliacci? Bozo? Some other clown? “I’m descended from a long line of roustabouts and raconteur shrimp boat captains. Watching TV as a boy with my MeeMaw, I was inspired by the physical comedy of Carol Burnett, the absurdity of Monty Python, and the cringe antics of Andy Kaufman. And listening to the scratchy AM radio on PeePaw’s shrimp boat, I was always moved by the more dramatic vocalists, singers like Tom Jones, Freddie Mercury, and Shirley Bassey.” (It’s easy to hear Mercury’s influence on Puddles’ “Wasting Time.”) But despite the social concerns underlying Todd Phillips’ take on The Joker, the Clown Prince of Crime does not fit into Puddles’ pantheon. And "Creep" or no "Creep," he is not put off by the cultural ascendence of the Creepy Clown. “Joker and Pennywise are not real people. They don’t scare me. There are actual humans in real life who are far more sinister and frightening — many of whom are currently in positions of power and doing far more damage to the world than The Joker could have ever dreamed.”

item.title: The mystery of San Diego pollution
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 2.40
Beginning our tour of San Diego’s most befouled spots (air, land, or water), we stop first for three summer holidays — Memorial Day, July Fourth, Labor Day — when local beaches turn from sun havens into trash dumps. When party-hardy masses overrun Mission Beach, west of Belmont Park, they leave behind swaths of crap. There, at dawn, Cathy Ives, in her sandals and sun visor, surveys the carnage. She’s a citizen trash-trawler, she and her little red wagon, holiday or not, scour the beach for the non-biodegradable: styrofoam and booze bottles (though both are banned); plastic water bottles; torn Mylar balloons; boogie boards that crumble into foam beads, becoming bird or fish “food”; fast-food wrappers for sandwiches; cardboard boxes for pizza; and those little packets of hot sauce. (Predacious gulls pick through the piles or hungrily eye human junk-haulers.) Top finds in a year (from Ives’s website): bottle caps (20,000), broken toys (4000), whole toys (2142), 1/2 flip-flops (500), pairs of shoes (397), socks (343), plus T-shirts, cigarette butts (the nicotine and tar they release can be toxic to sea life) underwear, plastic bags, straws, cup lids, lighters, tennis balls, and Frisbees. Ives piles the goodies she can’t recycle behind her home, encouraging people to make trash projects of them, like flip-flop art. Cathy Ives One peculiarity of the American need to trash is its treasure: there’s a market for picking up stuff, not only for Cathy Ives — she recycles or donates $10,000 to $20,000 worth of goods to the Encanto Boys and Girls Club each year — but also for the metal-detector sweepers who scan the sand for coins, jewelry, and cell phones. Then there’re city workers, who arrive, post-holiday, at 4 a.m., bucketing, bagging, and front-loading in headlighted trucks hillocks of sandy trash for the dump. (July 5th, I arrived at 6 a.m., two hours late to get the full trash Monty. That weekend, city crews took out 1700 pounds of crap and 15,000 cigarette butts.) Workers earlier stationed refrigerator-size boxes to make recycling obvious. According to the Natural Resources Defense Council, San Diego spends $14.1 million per year to “stop litter from becoming pollution.” Video: Cathy Ives talks about Mission Beach pollution Mission Beach is one of San Diego's most polluted areas. Cathy Ives discusses the origins and consequences of trash at the beach and shows off her remarkable collection. ^^^^^^^^^^^ The Reader has started this series of its best stories from the past 52 years — 2600 cover stories and some remarkable interior features — to help make up for the loss of its physical edition, which was once large enough to hold whole oceans of print. These stories will feature all the original illustrations and photos (plus easy-to-read typography). ^^^^^^^^^^^ You’d think beachgoers would want to take care of Southern California’s most precious natural resources — the ocean’s welcome mat — beach and breaking wave.
